div.head: PLEASAM! ,PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASAM! ,PARAGRAPHS.

WHEN the captain wants to stop the vessel does he hoist a stay-sail? THERE is a new kind of 'alf-and-'alf sold now in the saloons—'alf beer and 'alf froth. THERE is only the difference of an s between woman's weakness and man's weakness—One is gossip and the other is go sip. A DANDY asked a barber's boy if he had ever shaved a monkey. "No, sir," answered the lad; but if you will take a seat I'll try."
ACCORDING to an advertisement in the American paper relating to a town contract a condition is— " The contractor to expire on the 30th April, 1889."
" MOTHER'S always telling me not to bolt my food," said a small boy, "and now she gone and bolted the cupboard that has got all the victuals."

YOUNG WIFE—" John, mother says she wants to be cremated." Young husband—" Tell her if ahe'll put on her things I'll take her down this morning." "How do you feel this morning?" asked a doctor of a patient who the preceding night had attended a fancy dress ball. "I feel just like a rain-soaked poster," he limply replied.
TEACIIER—" What is the feminine of friar ?" First boy—" Hasn't any." Teacher—" Next ?" Second boy—" Nun." Teacher—" Correct." First boy (indignantly—" That's what I meant—hasn't any—none.'

" ARRAII, thin, Mrs. Divins, will yez go to the circus wid a select party this day ?" "Faith, thin, Mrs. Moriarty, minny thanks, but I ixpect a little circus of me own. This is the ould man's day for gettin dhrunk." THE New York Sun speaks bitterly of a fellow editor as the " omnisicolistical princox who daubs darkness over the vast editorial page of the Brook- lyn Eagle." WIFE—" Swear to me, Augustus, that you will only take one drink." Husband—" I swear it." -(Hall hour later at cafe). "Waiter, give me some whisky in one of those large lemonaele glasses." BOBBY—" I guess you must be a lady-killer, Mr. Sissy." Mr. Sissy (complacently)—" Aw, d'ye think so, Bawby?" Bobby—" You must be; Clara said that after you left last night she nearly died laughing." As William bent over her fair face he whispered —" Darling, if I should ask you in French if I might kiss you what would you answer ? " She, summoning up her scanty knowledge of the French, replied, "Billet doux

GREAT STATESMAN (doing some figuring)—" Eh? What ? " Wife (looking up from newspaper) "What does 'labour question' mean?" Great statesman (absently)—" The question is, what 'll catch the labour vote?"

PROPRIETOR of fine grounds, to young landscape. gardener—" Have you ever studied—er—er—path- ology ?" Landscape gardener—" No, sir." Pro- prietor—" Well, then, you won't do. I must have a man who thoroughly understands laying out paths." PROPRIETOR—" Have a good dinner, sir ? " Guest—" Can't say I did, but you have two things on the bill as fine as anywhere in the United States." Proprietor (flattered)—" Ah ! and they are ?" Guest—" The salt and the ice-water."

LAWYEIt—" Did you not kiss the plaintiff con- tinually when you called on her ?" Defendant (in breach of promise suit)—" Yes, I never stopped kissing her while I was in the house, but I did that in self-defence to keep her from singing." HE—" And so you are really attending a cook- ing school, Miss Clara ?" She (brightly)—" Yes, and it is such fun." He—" I suppose you can make nice bread already ?" She—" No, I have nothing to do with making bread; but I can inake lovely angel cake. lam only taking the classical course."

WIFE—" If I were to be kidnapped, John, and spirited away from you, what would you do?" Husband—" No danger of that, my dear." Wife —"Well, just imagine it, you know." Husband —" My dear, don't you know that there is a limit even to the imagination." AN old farmer of some 70 winters astonished onlookers at the Upper Town market on Saturday by making on a wager a series of continuous somer- saults, which would do credit to a young and lively acrobat, on top of a large load of hay.— Ottawa (Canada) Free Press. DUMLEY (bitterly)—" They say that (hic) fortune knocks once at every man's door, but (hie) if she ever knocked at mine, I wasn't there to hear it." Brown—" No, Dumley, fortune does not go around knocking at people's door at two or three o'clock in the morning." A Pious DISTINCTION. Brother Simpson (examining a neighbour s horse behind the church sheds)—" I ain't a-tryin' to work up no hoss trade on the holy Sab'th. 'Tain't my style o' doin' business. Sunday's for relig'ous d. oties. But I say, if you'll bring that thar mare o' yourn round to-morrer' morning', I'll swap even, and throw in that old ram o' mine."

A WELL-KNOWN umbrella maker was married the other day, and at the wedding breakfast, when the usual healths had been drunk, the beat man rose and said, "There is one more toast which, for the sake of the future prospects of the happy couple now present, I call on you to drink, ladies and gentlemen, with all sincerity, the health of—St. Swithin."

YOUNG wife (at dinner table, sobbing)—" I think you—you—are just as mean as—as—you can be. I made that--that apple dumpling as a pleasant surprise for yo, and—and now—you -- want me to bring a handsaw to cut it in two with." Young husband—" Good heavens, Maria! Is that a dumpling? I took it for a. cocoa-nut." (With desperate firmness). "I'll eat it now, Maria, if it kills me."

AN Irish priest, a moderate drinker, was asked to address a meeting in favour of totafabstinence. He met the difficulty thus :—" Bhoys," said he, "I would recommend to ye moderation in all things. Moisten yer clay a little by all means, but don't make a bog of it. If I hadn't meself moistened me own clay sometimes, I'd 'a' been dust before now."

A GENTLEMEN from the Highlands of Scotland, attended by his trusty servant Donald, a native of the wild mountainous district of Lochaber in Inver- ness-shire, when travelling through the fertile and delightful plains of Italy, asked Donald what he would do if he possessed an estate there? Donald Instantly replied, "Please your honour, I would sell 'him, and buy an estate in Lochaber !" CLERGYMAN should be brief and to the point. A Boston clergyman once had a broad hint to that effect :—" We would have, you short when you marry us," said a prospective bridegroom, "be- cause we are going west." "How long after the ceremony will you start ? " asked the clergyman. "In about a week" was the reply. Then the minister realised he had a reputation as one posses- sing the gift of continuance.

WHEN the Rev. Mr. C- was minister of the U. P. Church in Sanquhar, he called one day, in the course of his pastoral visitation, on a decent old woman who was a member of his congregation. Engaged in friendly conversation with her he said, "I hear your potatoes are not very good this year, Jennet r, "'Deed are they no, sir, said Jennet, "they're very bad; but I've reason to be tha.nkfu' that ither folks are as bad as my am."

IT is recorded of a rich old farmer that in giving instructions for his Nyill he directed a legacy of £lOO to be given to his wife. Being informed that some distinction was usually made in case the widow married again, he deuhled the sum, and when told that this was quite contrary to custom, he said, with heartfelt sympathy for his possible successor, "Ay, but him as gets her'll deserve it." AN amusing story is told of the Rev. Myron Reed, of Colorado, who two years ago ran as the Democratic Congressional candidate in that State. It seems that during the canvass the Rev, gentle- man was interrupted in the midst of a public prayer by a man who shouted " Louder ! Reed stopped short, looked at the interrupter, and said coolly, "I wasn't addressing you, sir; I was ad- dressing the Almighty." Theri he went on with his prayer. "Do you believe there is any such thing as luck 2" asked a young man of an old bachelor. "I do. I've had proof of it." "In what way ?" "I was refused by five girls when I was a young man."

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

The news of the death of The O'Gorman Mahon reached the House on Tuesday evening and created some excitement in Irish circles. The Parnellites intend to contest the seat at Carlow, and hope ta make a good fight for it. They believe themselves to be very strong in the constituency.

The biographers of that fine old Irish soldier The O'Gorman Mahon, have omitted to mention that he was the original of the famous portrait of the O'Mulligan drawn by Thackeray in ." Mrs. Perkin's Ball." The fact is placed beyond dispute by Thackeray's own illustrations in the original edi- tion, in which The O'Gorman's ontwardtharacteris- tics are reproduced with a fidelity and skill which rival those of the letterpress.

The throwing out of the Bill promoted by the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Co. for the extension of their line to London, came as a surprise upon the House generally. The promoters of the measure are more or less comforted by the assurance that if the Commons .Committee had not thrown out the Bill, the Lords would have made short work of it.

Mr. Willis, Q.C., will, it is believed, return an affirmative reply, if he has net already done so, to the invitation of the Chester Liberal Association to contest the borough at the next election in the Gladstonian interest. Mr. 'Willis, who enjoys a lucrative practice, is not new to political life, hav- ing sat for Colchester in the Parliament of 1880- 85. He is an active member of the Congregational body.

Much regret was expressed on Tuesday evening in artistic circles at the death, on Tuesday after- noon, of Mr. J. C. Farrer, the well-known landscape painter and etcher. Ile was attacked a short time ago by influenza, and, the lungs becoming affected, he was unable to rally. Mr.Furrer began his career in America,and his work is highly esteemed on both sides of the Atlantic. lie had scarcely reached the prime of life.

Although several amendments to the second read- ing of the Education Bill stands on the paper in the names of Liberal members, there is no intention of insisting upon them to the point of a division. It is probable that therefore the second reading is reached they may be withdrawn from the Order Book. Unless opposition comes from the Conserva- tive side it is practically certain that the second reading of this Bill will be passed without a divi- sion..

It is getting on for three months since the Royal Commission on Labour was appointed. The session will end in less than eight weeks from now. At this rate, what will the Government have to show for their much-vaunted Commission by the time next year's inevitable general election comes upon them? They will be able to point proudly to the fact that they have collected evidence—et voila toed. How eminently satisfying to the labouring classes! How calculated to secure their 6upport at the poll.

The answer given by the Secretary for War on Monday, to the question concerning the Tranby Croft baccarat scandal is generally regarded as virtually terminating, as far as the House of Com- mons is concerned, the unpleasant incident. It is felt by the more sagacious of those who have taken up the matter that it would not merely be unad- visable but unnecessary to mpve,as had been origin- ally contemplated, the adjournment of the House of Commons, in face of the Prince of Wales's frank admission of error.

Miss Jane Eirkaldy and Miss Catharine Pollen, the two students who were placed in first class in the .Oxford Natural Science Honours Examination List issued last week, were not only the only ladies who offered themselves for examination, but the first who have taken up the special subject—Animal Morphology—in which they secured their honours. Both ladies are students at Somerville Hall. Miss Pollard was for a year at the Royal Holloway Col- lege, and has held the Clothworkers' Scholarship at Somerville Hall.

Two of the three counsel who are pleading Miss Valerie Wiedemann's cause against the Hon. Robert Horace Walpole are novelists. Mr. T. Terrell, her leader, is the author of "Lady Delmar," a novel that has been much borrowed trom the libraries; and Mr. F. C. Phillips, one of her juniors, is a well known fictionist—the author of "As in a Looking Glass," "Young Mr. Ainslie's Courtship," "Jack and Three Jills," and several other stories. Miss Wiede- mann's whole life has been a romance—a very pain- ful one since she became connected with Mr. Walpole, and it is becoming that her counsel should be romance writers.

Mr. Walpole himself is a harmless looking little man, who does not appear capable of anything in particular, wicked or good, except succeeding to an earldom, and legislating for his country. He is not handsome, is rather diminutive in stature, sports a kind of a beard, and is becoming bald. Miss Wiede- mann is head and shoulders taller than he is, and decidedly more interesting in appearance.

Mr. Stead, Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P.., and other gentlemen associated with the social purity move- ment, found the funds with which Miss Wiedemann continued her litigation against Mr. Walpole after the first action, in which she was non-suited by the late Baron Huddleston. Now that Miss Wiedemann has established her case her friends are not likely to allow her to be at a disadvantage from lack of means, should Mr. Walpole succeed with the appeal for still another trial of the action, which he yester- day statea he intended to make.

Another strike now threatens. The tramway rien are uneasy. Some Of their employers have already granted them the twelve hours and other privileges. The other companies threaten to hold out, but in their case the twelve-hours day is as certain to be adopted as though Parliament itself had passed a Bill for the liniitation of hours. Whatever may be said of the eight hours movement, it is certain that no trade or enterprise of any kind will hence- forth be able to conduct itself on a system which requires more than twelve hours' continuous work from any class of men.

Mrs. Grimwood, who is being lionised a good deal here, and has been the object of royal solicitude in recognition of her heroism in conneation with the i Manipur disaster, s said to have displayed even more fortitude and courage during that terrible crisis than the public are aware of. Although the i incident has not been reported n the newspapers, she is credited with having used her revolver to some purpose on the enemy, and to have disposed of no fewer than three assailants. Having regard to her wonderful bravery and unflinching spirit, it is little wonder that she has been a profoundly in- teresting personage since her return from the East, and that the sir.cerest sympathy is felt for her.

A party of some fifty Jews have just shipped from Antwerp for Boma, in the Congo. country. This is the first party of Jewish emigrants which has sought a resting-place in the new African State. What would Mr. Stanley have so say to this plan of Jewish settlement? The Congo territories, accord- ing to Mr. Stanley's account of them, are naturally rich and fertile enough to support millions of Jews, supposing they could stand the climate. But from the climatic view point, Baron Hirsch's Argentine scheme seems the more promising. There are ten million Jews in Europe, of whom five millions are in Russia. For these five room mnst be found somewhere—if Russia means to carry her senseless, savage policy to its bitter end.

Lord Coleridge's observation in his charge to the jury in the baccarat case, that the truest and grandest of all sayings was, " Let us die, but let us not stain our honour," has puzzled a good many persons who are nevertheless tolerably well con- versant with the Scriptures. It has been found at last in the Apocrypha, and the "great Hebrew Chieftain "to whom the Lord Chief Justice subse- quently attributed it has thereby been identified as .Judas Maccabeus. The verse is the 'tenth of the ninth chapter of the First Book of Maccabeus as follows :—" Then Judas said, God forbid that I should do this thing, and flee away from them; if our time be come, let us die manfully for our brethren, and let us not stain our honour."

The common belief that woman has a proportion ally longer trunk than man finds no confirmation in the researches of the Professors of Hygiene at Amherst College, United States. Some two thous- and students of this great institution have been subjected to scientific measurergents,with the result that although the average male is found to be only just over seven per cent, taller than the average female, in length of trunk he exceeds her by eleven per cent. In the length of the lower limbs there is

Schopenhauer appears to have overlooked this point of superiority when he un- gallantly described women as "that undersized, narrow-shouldered, broad-hipped, and short-legged race."

More in sorrow than in anger, Mr. W. H. Smith on Monday night dealt a fatal blow to the linger- ing hopes of many a private member. The Govern- ment must have the whole remaining time of the House. It was painful to have to ask it, and only to be sanctioned by stern necessity. In return he had to offer the prospect of an early prorogation, and perhaps the wrath of his opponents was modi- fied in some measure by illicit joy at the abandon- ment of several Ministerial measures. Mr. Smith had to part with some of his pet lambs, and choae the least promising among the flock. The Private Bill Procedure (Scotland) Bill goes over to next session, together with another Scotch measure. The India Councils Bill is abandoned, the Regimental Debts Consolidation Bill postponed, Lord Salisbury's Public Trustee Bill, the Summary. Jurisdiction Bill, and the Law of Evidence Bill are abandoned. The Clergy Discipline Bill waits upon the reception which Mr. Gladstone will'give it. Thus the session is considerably lightened, but there remains much more than is likely to be got through by the first week in August.

ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

"Batsmen wanted !" is says the "Manchester Guard- ian," now the general cry in Lancashire cricket circles. We have some of the best bowling in England in the team, and Lancashire fielding is second to none, but our batsmen don't get runs; and men sigh for the days when the captain and Barlow were in their prime, and when, with Eccles and Robinson, they gave the fielders a long day in the country. Men we have, add to spare, who make a brave show in club matches, but somehow fail to play up to their reputation when Lohmann and Hearne are on the warpath. The two MacLarens would be invaluable if they could play regularly, but their ap- pearance in the team must necessarily be intermittent to the great loss of Lancashire, which has, in "Mr. A" at least, perhaps the most promising young batsman in the country.

But the reasons which debar Messrs. MacLaren from assisting the county do not, we may presume, apply to some other players, and one of these, A. Smith, of old- ham, is, in the opinion of many, thoroughly worth a good trial. Hewitson, of Preston, is not required as a bowler whilst Briggs is in the team, even if it were cer- tain that his delivery would pass muster ; but he made a respectable figure as a batsman, and might be worth another trial. But, after all, we are not inclined to take a despondent view of the position of the county. The men usually train "on" instead of " off," and when the last trases of influenza have disappeared and Mr.Hornby is himself again, we look for a very different state of things from that which prevailed at Lord's on Thursday and Friday.

Speaking of Mr. S. M. Crostield's fine performance on Monday in the match against Yorkshire, when he carried out his bat for 82, the "Sporting Chronicle" says, "It is not too much to say that the Warrington amateur has never been seen to such conspicuous advantage in a big match, and this is certainly the highest innings he has ever played for the county. He has always been a good, sound, and enthusiastic cricketer, but without meeting with the best of luck, and he is to be congratht- lated on his excellent display to-day. His defence was perfect; he hit splendidly all round the wicket, and the only two bad strokes he made happened to be chances. Wardall was the culprit each time, missing him in the slips off Buttner at 29, and eight runs later off Peel at extra cover-point. Both catches ought to have been easily taken, and the double blunder made a vast difference to Lancashire's score. Crosfield, who laid on with great power when he got a ball to hit, obtained ten 4's, one 3, and eight 2's, and he was loudly and de- deservedly cheered on his return to the pavilion."

The close of Tuesday's play at Bradford left scarcely a doubt as to the result of the match, Lancashire having an innings to play and wanting only 72 runs to win. Therefore, the concluding day's cricket (Wednesday) ex- cited a very small amount of interest. Only a few visitors came up to the ground, and an hour and ten minutes' actual play proved sufficient to bring the game to a conclusion. No rain had fallen during the night, and Lancashire entered upon their light task with the wicket only a little worn. The weather was dull and close. It cost Lancashire two batsmen to hit off the re- quisite number of runs, Sugg being bowled at 20 and Ward playing on at 64; but the Yorkshire fielding was again at fault, Barlow,who scored 32 not out, giving two palpable chances. Lancashire won the match by eight wickets, and at nearly every point of the game they ' showed superior form to their opponents.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

Amongst the successful candidates at the recent Cam- bridge University Examinations the names of several prominent athletes are enrolled, many of them being included in the list of Wranglers. The pursuit of physi- cal exercises ought to be of the greatest assistance in the attainment of higher intellectual honours,and it is satis- factory to notice that in the Universities at any rate the enjoyment of the former does not seem to interfere with more important work. The sixth in the list of Wranglers is F. J. Selby, the well-known rowing man, while A. W. Charles, the Trinity Hall quarter-mile runner, will be re- membered as having represented his University with success against the London A.C. and the United Hospi- tals; he was also first string in the " quarter " at the inter-University meeting.

Several of the members of the Manhattan A Club have arrived in England during the last few days, and they are to make their first appearance at Huddersfield on Saturday next, preparatory to competing in the cham- pionships at Manchester the following week. L. E. Myers, who four or five years ago furnished the greatest attraction in the English athletic world for one season, and who at that time made his home in Manchester, is again coming over. He was a few years ago the finest 440 yards runner in the world, and we very much doubt whether he has ever had a superior in either amateur or professional ranks.

Queckburner is the giant of the Manhattan Club, and on the strength of his arm his friends ,depend for the hammer and shot. We shall, however,rely on the gigan- tic Irishman Barry, whilst R. A. Greene, if he can 'only get strong and well, ought to want a lot of beating with the shot; Greene has never shown his best form in pub- lic, but when practising at Old Trafford he has more than ones very nearly managed 42ft.

We all know Conneff, the Irish runner, who emigrated after winning the two miles northern championship in the days of the Manchester Exhibition and whose match against E. C. Carter in Dublin roused his countrymen to such a frenzy of excitement, but Roddy and Carey are strangers. We confess that Carey is the athlete we are most anxious to see, as' we have never produced in this country an amateur capable of '.eating evens in a 100 yards level race. On June 10 three excellent watch holders timed Carey to run the distance in 9:I sec., and he himself claims to have accomplished 93/4. If these times can be believed he is much superior to any sprinter we have, and ought to win the championship by about four or five yards at least. Somehow, we do not believe that he will have such a runaway victory, although we cannot name a competitor likely to give him even a hard race.

Michael Bruce, the well-known Scottish cyclist, on Wednesday, broke the record on the occasion of a fifty mile handicap of the Edinburgh Cycling Club. Bruce gave the limit man 42min. start, and still came in first. His time was 2h. 59 min. ssec., being 10mia. less than the previous record. He rode a pneumatic safety.
LORD SALISBURY ON IMPERIAL FEDERATION.

Lord Salisbury, replying to a deputation from the Imperial Federation League on Wednesday at the Foreign Office, particularly as to their request for a conference of the self-governing colonies, said he was convinced of the importance of Imperial Federation, for it meant neither more nor less than the future of th e British Em- pire. Owing to the external causes there was unrest in Canada, and even in Australia a feeling of unwillingness to acquiesce in the present state of things. A large por- tion of our foreign difficulties arose entirely from our colonial connections, and great vigilance had to be exer- cised to avoid dangers. The League claimed that they had no cut-and-dried scheme. He thought that was a slight mistake,for a time had come when a scheme should be prepared. The solution of the problem would be difficult,for in order to make a united empire they would have to form a union for war and also for Customs policy. The question was not one for vague sentiments, but for close examination and the highest patriotism, and in solving the problem it would not be possible to leave our Asiatic dependencies out of sight.

div.head: JNE 20, 1891.
div.p: THE DRINK QUESTION (No. 2). HIGH LICENSE.
BY H. WEITHAM.

There are few amongst us, be they never so dull, but are satisfied that in the drinking habits of the people lies at least one source of all our troubles. It is no compensation to the workers to say 'Oh well, the rich man has his club and his wine cellar; why shouldn't Lhe poor man have his pot of beer?' It is not liberty we cry for when we ask that on every corner lot, and near every factory, saloons should be erected. It is the right to disgrace our- selves we ask for, a far different thing from liberty. Talk of compensating the trade for the loss of its vested interest! Whose loss has been the greatest, say, sincellBoo ? In Great Britain, during 1800, a population of 15,000,000 consumed 12,000,000 gallons of spirits. In 1874 a population of 32,000,000 con- sumed 41,000,000. That is, while the population in- creased 113 per cent., the consumption of spirits in- creased 241 per cent. In the United States the con- sumption of beer has increased, since 1841, 1,675 per cent. of wine 401 per cent., and of ardent spirits over 200 per cent. The official reports state that the people of the United States used four gallons of intoxicating drinks per head in 1840, and twelve gallons per head in 1883. During the five years preceding 1884, while the population increased about 15 per cent., the consumption of distilled spirits increased 44.5 per cent., and that of malt liquors 60.2 per cent. The production of the latter has risen from 1,628,934 barrels in 1863 to 18,998,619 barrels in 1884. I have no more recent figures by me, but the above clearly shows who has benefited in the past, and should be enough to put aside the criminal idea of compensating " the trade" so much talked of just now in the United States.

THE BREWING INTERESTS are well looked after. In every city the unions are strong: every man employed about a brewery is expected to belong to it. The employers, or boss brewers, look favourably upon the unions; both parties work together, and what money can do at elections, it does to a certainty. In this city of San Francisco, the Secretary of the Brewery Work- men's Association is President of the Federated Trades Unions, and with this power behind him can do just a little. I have before me heaps of state- ments and figures given in evidence before Com- mittees as to the actions of these unions, and the money spent in log rolling and lobbying to put hack temperance measures. Trade Unionism in America is engaged rolling up the hill a big stone ; each time the stone gets near the top, the brewery workman will send it rolling down again. The legitimate working-man, will and must dissociate himself entirely from the brewing business. Then he will feel independent, and see his course clear. In stating my views on this, "the greatest thing in the world," I know I lay myself open to sharp criticism, because I am neither an abstainer, nor am I likely to become one, nor yet would I do away with public-houses. I would take the management of them ou of private hands; their number would then be a question for the people to settle and would not be left to the cupidity of the individual who thought he saw a chance of making a profit at his fellow man's expenses. The way is not clear to do this just yet. In the meantime we resort to another method, and we say we will limit the num- ber of saloons by putting the price at which a liquor license can be bought as high as poSsible, .to a party called

THE HIGH LICENSE ASSOCIATION has been brought into being to accomplish this de- sirable object. Of course this Association has been at work, more or less, for some years, in vari- ous cities . throughout the Union, but it is only recently that it has made its existence felt in this city. It commenced work by calling public meetings and providing good speakers. Notice was given at these meetings as to time and place of meetings for arranging propa- ganda. This has resulted in a petition, signed With over 3,000 names, being placed before the super- visors, a Board which acts as (but has more powers) your own Town Councillors. it prcwses to raise the license fee from 23 dollars to 150 per quarter. The association makes no protest against the sale or use of liquor as a beverage,but points out " that one saloon to every fourteen voters is out of all propor- tion to the necessities of the city,' and that all in excess of this is generative of the crime and de- bauchery with which the city is afflicted and is the chief cause of the burdensome taxation. That the High License system works well, where adopted there can be no doubt. In Vineland, N.J., where there were .no saloons in 1877, the municipal expenses for the preservation of order for the year were reported at 75 dollars, the population being 11,000. In Gothenburg, Sweden, the town made famous some years ago by friend Chamberlain, with a population of 80,000, experiment has reduced the number of saloons to twenty. In the city of Bergen, Norway, the wants of a population of 45,000 are met by twelve saloons. In Philadelphia, under the high license law, 1,202 saloons were sufficient for a population of 1,000,000, in the year 1889. San Fran- cisco has scarce 300,000 population but it has 5,000 drinking places. The association does not propose to interfere with the honest and just liberty of the citizen. It does not say drinking is a crime, but it does insist, that a man has

NO RIGHT TO GET DRUNK, and that drunkenness creates disease and adds to the burdens of the sober. The Association sets forth that high license "gives ample room for the legitimate sale of liquors for dietetic, hygienic, medicinal, mechanical, and sacramental purposes." The ends it seeks are nobler manhood, and happier homes, by bridling a traffic which is productive of more personal, social, and domestic misery than all other causes put together. It urges on the side of economy that the acceptance of its proposition will gradually diminish taxation, and obliterate State jails, prisons, and the scaffold. There is no word here of "compensation." It is proposed to raise the price of licenses as they expire. The Associa- tion does not, and justly so, recognise the moral obligation to continue the issue ot licenses until the end of all time at the original, or any traditional rate. On this point it is well to cite the pre- cedents set by the higher English Courts. In 1882 Mr. Justice Steplien said :—" The Legislature says, when we talk of a renewal of a license, we do not mean that, but we mean a new license granted to a man who had one before." In 1878 Lord Chief Justice Cockburn said: "According to the Act of 1828, the justices had the some 'discretion to refuse a renewal as they had to refuse a grant of a new license." In 1882 Mr. Justice Field said : "In every case in every year there is a new license granted, you may call it enewal if you like. The Legislature is not capable of calling a new license an old one. The Legisla- ture recogniQes no vested right' at all in any holder of a license. It does not treat the interest as a vested one." In :1884 Mr. Baron Pollock said: "The notion that there is a property of the landlord in a license cannot be considered sdimd law," and in 1883 the trade's particular advocate; the late Mr. Thomas Nash, counsel for the retail liquor vendors of England, frankly admitted that, "there cannot be the smallest doubt that, in the strictest sense, no such thing as vested interest 'exists in a license." I suppose this is all good law and as such will appeal, no doubt, to the patriotism of the Eng- lish Tory party. Parliament in 1853 closed all the public-houses in Scotland on Sunday, and subse- quent legislation has enforced Sunday closing in Ireland and Wales.

NO COMPENSATION in these cases was given for the loss of one-seventh of the time and profits of the publican. In 1869 a bill was passed raising the rental qualifications of beer-houses, and 300 beer-houses in Liverpool alone were closed. There was no compensation. When "The Canadian Temperance Act" passed, the Canadian Parliament, in 1878, the liquor men appealed to Her Majesty's Privy Council to declare the law unconstitutional, inasmuch as it granted no compensation for the suppression of licenses' • but their appeal was rejected, and thousands of licenses have been revoked under the provisions of the Act. The late General Secretary of the liquor trade of Great Britain estimated that the compen- sation to which the trade would be entitled for the suppression of licenses since the passages of the recent laws would amount to at least £400,000,000. What is wanted is, not the suppression, but the control of the business. It stands in ground alto- gether peculiar to itself, and because it appeals to the weakest side of our nature, should be held in closest control.

div.p: SATURDAY,
" Honest, Felix. If I let you up, will you give back what you took from my desk ?" " I—l—didn't--"
"Oho I We'll quickly see. Take care I None of that I By the heavens above me, I'll have what you've got in that pocket, if I have to throttle you 1" And TOM tore away another button.

"0, yes, yes 1 I'll give it up ! I will, truly. Tom—say—let me up, and I'll tell you everything. I certainly will." As the sergeant drew his hand across the bosom of the prostrate man, he felt a suspicious some- thing on the opposite side from the pocket at which he had been aiming; and before he let him up, he took that something away—a double-bar- relled pistol. He opened one of the pans, and found it fully primed: and he reclosed it without emptying it. "Now, get up; and mark you, if you prove treacherous, I'll shoot you as I would a dog. Re- member, you are my prisoner, captured by legal warrant; and you know what an officer may right- fully do to a prisoner whom he can hold in no other way. So, my man, beware !" McAllister, once more on his feet, shook himself back into his clothing, and then said: "Toni, what'll you give me if I'll give you back them papers—every one of' em—safe and un- harmed ? "

"Give you!" cried the sergeant, indignantly. "'What'!! I give? I'll give you over to the tender mercies of a drum-head court-martial. I needn't tell you what that'll amount to." "But, Tom, they are worth more than you know."

"Not a bit of it. I know just what they are worth. Come, come, don't waste more time. I know just what you hoped to do with those papers, and who, you fancied, would purchase them of you, but it won't do. They must go back to their true owner.—Give you? Why, bless your impu- dence, I'd give you a good sound whipping at the stake before you went to prison, with a ball-and- chain dangling from your ankles I that's what I'd give you." The wretch gasped for breath, and seemed to consider.

"Look 'e Tom," he said at length, in a cringing groveling manner, "you 've got the upper hand, and Jam helpless. But if you get back the papers all safe, you 'll let me go, and never bring it up against me. You 'll do that, I know. And I 'll tell you more. I may be able to give the young heir help, who can tell 7" Tom had a wonderfully soft spot in his heart. The recovery of Percival's packet in this easy and unexpected manner, without the least publicity, was good enough for one day's accomplishment. The punishment of the thief would not help the matter in any way, nor could it benefit anybody, not even the thief himself, for such another tempta- tion would, in all human probability, never be set before him. He considered the proposition for a brief space, and then replied: "Give me the packet, Felix, and we'll talk of that afterwards. I mean what I say. I don't want to push you too hard, but I won't speak a word in that direction until the packet is in my hands."

The culprit caught the relenting light in the ser- geant's eyes, and felt that he was saved from public trial, at least. With trembling hands he unbut- toned his waistcoat, and from an inner pocket brought forth the stolen prize. "it's been opened, Tom, but not a soul has fieen the contents saving myself. And they are all there every one just as I found 'em." A dark cloud came upon Tom's brow when he saw that the time-honoured seals had been broken, and the ribbon cut. McAllister was quick to detect the cloud, and the feelings that had called it into being, and after a moment's thought, he con- tinued:

"Pm goin' to make a clean breast of it, Tom. Here are two copies that I made of two of those papers. They're of no use to me, and I give 'em up, so that you may have everything, I keeping nothing at all." "What did you make those copies for ?" Tom asked, as the other gave him two neatly folded papers. For this reason," he promptly answered: "I didn't want to expose the original documents. They were too precious. So I made these copies, that I might show them to the man to whom I meant to offer them for sale. My soul I wouldn't he have jumped at 'em This adroit turn had the effect which its maker had hoped for. It touched Tom's tender spot, and he said to his captive that he was free to go. "You won't let this out at the arsenal, Tom ?" tive man pleaded, beseechingly. "No, Felix I'll keep faith with you. Let me look; yes, Felix, are all right, I believe." The number of the papers contained within had been set down upon the envelope, and the old hussar found the contents intact. "And let me tell you, you've done a blessed thing. S'pose'n you'd kept these papers. You never could have sold 'cm. Leastwise, I don't believe you could. But, if you had, the man who would be villain enough to buy them would be very apt to be just villain enough to want you out of his way. D' you see ?" Yes, he saw it, and he had thought of that very thing before. Said he, as the twain had turned back towards the castle, for McAllister had no more occasion to confer with the old man of the mill:

"Tom, old mate, I'm glad you 'ye got that cum- bersome parcel. P'rhaps you won't believe me, but I tell the solemn truth, nevertheless. I 'vs lived to be two years over threescore, or nearly that, and that's the first, last, and only thing I ever stole. I tell you I don't want no more of it. Bot 0 such visions of golden heaps—of guineas in- numerable—floated before my distorted imagina- tion, that my better sense was held in thrall. I knew, from what you had told me of Percival Gor- don—and, mind, I never asked you for the story I knew that he must stand somewhere very near to the title of Ambleton •' for, Tom, I was born and reared on the estate." And he was going on to tell further, when his hearer interrupted, and told of his own researches at the grand old place. "Well," pursued Felix, when he had heard, "then you know all about the true worth of Am- bleton. Sir Edward, the present baronet, I knew must be near his end; but when I had come back and found who was the man to succeed if your boy's claim should be kept out, my heart sank. I feared to trust him. In fact, I don't know hut I sheuld have tried to quietly get the papers back into your desk if a now hope hadn't unexpectedly presented itself." "What was that?" Tom asked, quietly. "Eh ! Don't you know ?" "I 'm sure I dont. How should I?" McAllister stopped short in his walk, and looked his companion squarely in the face. "Tom, I thought you said you knew everything there was in them papers." "So I do. Leastwise, I think I do." "And I," returned the old clerk, "am very sure you don't know anything about it Ho ! ho! I'll open your eyes when we can fiud a quiet nook in which to look at one or two of them papers." Tom sought to gain the information while afoot on the old mill road, but Felix would not speak. He would not offer a word of explanation until they were where they could refer to the papers. As they approached the castle they saw signs of commotion. Servants were passing to and fro with hurried steps; there was no gossiping; and windows in the upper chambers were being thrown open. We may remark here that Oxton Castle had been greatly modernised since the days of the first earl. Under its old feudal barons, the last of whom had fallen at Naseby, fightino. for Cromwell, it had been maintained as a knightly stronghold and fortress, pure and simple ; but since that time the moat had been filled up • the massive outer walls removed; thedonjon enlarged and beautified; the old loopholes changed into high ,nd broad gothic windows; wnile numerous outbuildings had been erected upon the verge of the rear court. The only purely distinctive features of the feudal castle which had been preserved were the draw- bridge, the ponderous portcullis, and the twin barbicans.

"Tom 1" cried the clerk, when he had seen cer• tam n windows on the second floor of the castle thrown open, "the earl is dead 1" "Ah 1 Think you so "I know it. Let us hurry on." Reaching the stable, they found it true. Walter Buckley, seventh Earl of Oxton had been gathered to nis fathers upon the other side. Tom saw one of the grooms leading a horse, all caparisoned, around to the main vestibule—a horse which he recognised as belonging to the Earl of Elmdale. The impulse was upon him to hasten forward and speak with his lordship. Percival was at his place, and he would ask the earl to tell him that the lost papers had been found. But he did not go. A little further reflection decided him to proceed in person, and at once, in quest ef the young captain, and shortly af tel. wards he saw Lord Elmdale_ride away.
The old serge tut had learned all there as to learn of the death of Oxton's late lord, and had siamified his intention to call for his horse, Y.-hen

LThAllister took him by the arm. " Tom ! come with me. You don't know what you've got in your pocket. Bless you, man! you need to have every wit awake and sharp. Come, come; I know what I say, and if you are not satisfied when I am done you may kick me." Putting away his last qualm against opening the packet, the old hussar followed Felix to an out-of- the-way room in the servants' quarters, where, when the doors had been secured, McAllister asked Tom to produce the papers. "Do you lay them out," he said, "and I'll show you those we want."

- The faithful guardian, having resolved on his course, made no hesitation. The packet wa.e opened, and the papers so placed that their respec- tive characters could be told at a glance by the Ulorsements on their backs.

Three of the oldest—the very oldest of the lot= McAllister separated from the rest, and took them into his hand. He ran his eyes over the writing, yellow with age on the inside, and finally turned to his companion. "Tom, old fellow, here we have the birth of Mary, wife of Captain Archibald Gordon. She was daughter of George Patten, George was younger son of Sir William.' " Yes ; I know all that."
"Ah !but wait. Let us look now after the other side of the house. Here—this paper gives us the mother of George Patten, Lovina, her name was. Here we have it. See." * * * • • * *
Half an hour later Tom Crawford was in the saddle, speeding away towards Wenham. He must see the general before he suffered himself to be questioned by Percival.
(To be confined).

div.head: PERCIVAL GORDON; OR,
div.p: PERCIVAL GORDON; OR,
THE CHILD OF HE REGIMENT.
BY SYLVANITS COBB.
CHAPTER XVI. TOM'S CAPTIVE-A REVELATION.

Fortune favoured the old sergeant. By one of those chances that sometimes befriend a man when and where he least expects it, he obtained a clue that was to lead to success. When he parted with Percival, at the entrance to Elmdale Park, he had thought to continue his way to the east- ward without stopping; and his youthful companion fully believed he had gone on. But he had not done so.

He had watched the captain until he had disap- peared beyond the great gate at the park entrance; when, in drawing rein for a start, his •eye chanced to fall upon a small, neat stone cottage, on the opposite side of the way, not more than fifty yards distant; and he saw a woman coming from a low- roofed shed, or barn, with what appeared to be a pan of milk in her hands. Now Tom was a dear lover of milk. He loved it far better than he loved grog, or even punch. Since his happy boyhood, when milk, fresh and rich, had been one of the chief articles of his sus- tenance, he had not lost his keen relish for it. If that woman had a pan of fresh milk, he would enjoy a draught, if he could. So he rode over to the cottage, and having dismounted, and secured his horse to a hitching-post that stood conveniently at hand, he went to the vine-embowered door and rapped; and the self-same woman whom he had seen in the yard,—a kindly-faced, good-looking matron she was,—answered his summons. Would she give him a draught of fresh milk? Yes,—with pleasure. Evidently she liked the appearance of the old soldier. She said she had just milked a cow that had strayed away over night, so he should have it fresh and sweet. While Tom sat in the neatly-kept living room, waiting for his draught, a man came in, from a side porch—a man of about his own age, hale and hearty, with a frank, honest face, and homely, who limped in his walk. "What !—Tom ! Bless me! is it possible!" "Jack,-,-.old fellow 1 Well,—this a joy I had not anticipated." _ .

Just then the matron—Jack's wife—came in with the milk, and when she learned that her visitor was the veritable Sergeant Tom Crawford, of whom her husband had told her so much,—of whom he never tired of telling, nor she of listening,—when she knew this, she was rejoiced. _ _ . _

Jack Loomis had been with Maxwell's Hussars in Spain, and at Waterloo; and after that, badly wounded in the right leg, he had returned to his Lorne at Elmdale, and settled down, the present earl having given him the cottage and the garden, and made him chief forester.
Tom drank his milk, and chatted pleasantly with his old comrade. By and by Jack asked him to let him put up his horse, and enjoy his company through the night. But Tom shook his head.
"No, Jack, I would do it if I could, and it would make me very happy; but I must keep on. I must reach Dorchester to-night." And thereupon he told of what he was in search.

"Nay, nay, old fellow! You won't go to Dor- chester to-night," exclaimed Jack, with a jubilant light in his clear grey eyes. "I happen to know Felix McAllister. We were in the same ward in hospital, at Woolwich, and after I was well enough to get around, I acted as assistant nurse, and he came under my care. You'll find him at Oxton."

"At Oxton!" repeated Tom, in glad surprise. "Are you sure ? " "I am sure he left this very cot, and the very seat in which you now rest, yesterday for that place. My good Molly, here, assured him that the old earl was surely dying, upon which he hurried off. He said he would like to speak with his lord- ship of Oxton, if the thing was possible; but Molly told him she didn't think it was at all possible. Howsomever, away he went, headed direct for Oxton."

Tom thanked his friend kindly for the informa- tion, and having finished his milk, and promised to look in again when he should find himself in that neighbourhood, he took his leave, and was quickly in the saddle and on the road, retracing his steps. Should he proceed directly to the castle ?—and, if so what excuse should he offer for his intrusion? A happy thought presenttd • itself. He would claim to be a messenger from Lord Wenham, which in fact he was, and, as such, inquire after the master. And this he did. He had dismounted in the main stable-yard ' • one of the grooms had very pleasantly taken his horse in charge and he had made his inquiries concerning the condition of the earl, when he saw Lord Elmdale ride up. By and by, of a veteran of the servants' corps, he ventured to ask after Felix McAllister.

"He was here not an hour ago," was the ready answer; "and I guess you'll find him over at the old mill, where he's gone to see Arthur Grundy." "Who and what is this Grundy ?" Tom asked. He wondered if he was a man whom this McAllister would be likely to wish to see on the business he had in hand. -

He was informed that Arthur Grundy, now four- score years of age, had formerly been valet and confidential attendant of Stephen Buckley, the earl who had preceded the one now dying. "Just the man," said the old sergeant to him- self, "whom Felix would be likely to want." He learned the way to the mill and at once set forth: The mill was an old pyramid of Portland stone, its motive power being afiorded by four great wings exposed to the wind. It was more than a mile distant from the castle, on a considerable eminence, with a comfox table cottage close at hand. Tom had gone half the distance, having reached a point where an old stone bridge spanned a beautiful stream, and where the path was over- arched by large willows. As he approached the bridge he saw a man standing at the far end, leaning over the railing, with his gaze fixed upon the water below. He stopped, with a, great thump at his heart, and slipped aside into the shade of the willows; for in the man at the other end he had recognised Felix McAllister. He waited a few moments, until he had composed himself and gathered his thoughts, and then moved carefully forward, taking the opposite side of the way, and gliding on Without noise. So successful was the sergeant in his manceuvre that he had come up behind his whilom room- mate with his hand upon his shoulder, before he had been aroused from hid reverie. "Ah I Tom!" •

"Yes, old fellow, it is myself." And as he spoke, he transferred his hand to the man's collar, where it was fixed with a grip of steel. McAllister turned pelf', and shook like an aspen. His first movement—an impulse without reflection —was to early his hand to his left breast, to a spot over the inner pocket of his closely-buttoned waistcok it was done in a second; but Tom's quick eye detected it, and he suspected its mean- ing. Be determined to strike while the iron was hot wad before his man could collect his senses and regain his impudence. McAllister felt the tightening of the grip upon his collar, and tried to free himself. "No, no, Felix, my boy! You are going with me, or I will take you down where we are, and overhaul your pockets—l don't know which. I have a warrant for your arrest, from General Max- well, so you've got to come; and you know as well as I do how a thief is punished in the English army—especially a thief that breaks into a desk and—" "I didn't break in! I aint a thief! I haven't got anything that belongs to you, nor to anybody else I" The culprit brought this speech out in spasmodic, gasping sentences, and at intervals of taking breath. ‘,‘ Look you, man,, give me what you've got in that breast pocket." "I habit got nothin' in there," he cried, clapping his Wand over the spot in mortal terror. "Now by the royal diadem, we'll see ! " said Tom; and, as he spoke, he put forth a strength beneath the power of which his prisoner was noth- ing more than a child. Tom Crawford was by far a stronger man than was the other; and, moreover, right gave him a moral advantage that was effective. With a quick, powerful effort, he threw McAllister back- ward upon the moss-covered stone floor of the bridge, and in another instant his knee was upon the rascal's breast. With but little trou,le he gained both the captive's wrists within the vice- like grasp of his left band, while with the right he attacked the buttons of the waistcoat. McAllister knew that he was conquered, and utterly helpless; and when the hand of his captor approached his breast-pocket, he gave up the con- test, and surrendered. " Mercy I Mercy, Tom! Don't do it! Let me up, and I'll confess everything. I will, so help me Heaven!"

div.head: THEY ROLLED ON THE FLOOR
div.p: THEY ROLLED ON THE FLOOR
On Monday, November 24th, 1890, the American papers published the following news item :

"Mrs. Sarah S. Hensler, of No. 873, East One-hundred and-Thirty-fourth Strut, New York, shot and killed herself yesterday morning. She was a lady of excellent character and high social position, and a member of the Rev. Dr. Ramsay's Presbyterian Church. She was well- to-do and very active in various public and private charities. Since last July she had suffered fearfully from indigestion and dyspepsia, which brought on melancholia and then a kind of insanity; under the influence of which she took her own life."

Here is another story, not so tragical, but with the same moral. The narrator tells it of himself. "Mostly," he says, we dread and fear death, yet once I prayed to die, and the reason was in this wise. Up to Christmas, 1888, I had been a healthy man, but at that time (a period of rejoicing with so many) I felt deprcssed, lan- guid, and tired. My appetite left me, and I was much distressed after eating the lightest food. My skin and eyes became tinged with a dark yellow colour, and the kidney secretion was like blood. The pain in my stomach was almost unbearable and often lasted from 12 to 14 hours without intermission. Sometimes I was in pain night and day, and was so bad that my wife had to sit up with me through the night. I was constantly sick, and troubled with a stomach cough, and expecto-- rated a quantity of green phlegm.

"In spite of warm clothing and every comfort, I was always chilled ; the cold shivers running through me as if my blood were thin and poor. I could take no solid food ; I lived on soups, milk puddings, &c., and after each meal I had empty, gnawing, windy pains at the stomach, which nothing relieved.

" After a time an intolerable itching of the skin spread all over me, as if my blood were poisoned. Our family physician attended me for about a year. Acting upon his advice I went to Harrogate,where I consulted another - doctor, and drank the waters, but feeling worse I re- turned hcme. The bath attendant at Harrogate and others told me I was suffering from blood poisoning,but this the doctors never mentioned. The first doctor said it was the passing of gallstones that gave me such dread• - ful pain.

"I now consulted an eminent specialist at Manches- ter, who confirmed what the other doctor had told me, but none of them afforded me any relief. "In this miserable way I dragged on for six months more, and became so much reduced I could scarcely put one foot beforo the other, and so thin that the rings fill off my fingers and rolled on the floor. I was in such pain that I prayed to die, and one of the doctors told a friend of mine I could not recover.

"In August of last year (1890), whilst my sufferings were at the worst, a book was sent to me by post, tel- ling me of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I cleterkniaed to try it, and sent to Mr. Evans, chemist, Lymm, for a supply. After taking the first bottle, I felt a little better, and by persevering with the remedy I recovered my appetite, and gradually gained strength. My natural colour is now returned, and I feel as well; as lever did in my life ; in fact, as well as I did when a boy. I can eat any kind of food without incon- venience, and hare gained 30 pounds in weight during the past three months. I may add that previous to tak- ing this medicine I was so much altered, that my friends and even my pupils, scarcely recognised me. I tell every one what Seigel's Syrup did for me."
The gentlem•ln who initkes the foregoing statement is a person of position and known to all the people of
Lymm. He declines to permit the publication of his name, but the perfect truth of what is here related is vouched for by Mr. J. H. Evans, the chemist above named.

The case was an aggravated one of indigestion and dyspepsia and its natural consequences. The whole system had been poisoned and disordered by the acids engendered by the fermentation in the stomach, and had not Seigel's Syrup come to the rescue just as it did, a fatal result must have followed in a brief time.
TWO CHILDREN KILLED A T LANCASTER.

- Two little girls,Sarah Ramsden,aged 11,and Ethel Bleas- dale, nine, both of Lancaster, who with several others, were trespassing on the Midland Railway embankment at Lancaster, on Sunday afternoon, to pick daisies, were knocked down by the engine of a passenger train from Morecambe. The engine driver, hearing a scream, and feeling the engine strike something, stopped the train. The girl Ramsden, however, had been instantly killed, and her companion died shortly afterwards. .
