IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

The Lord aTa-n-c-ell(Tito-oir-lais-seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. bum LAND DRAINAGE.—Ihe Drainage and Improve- inent'of Lands (Ireland) Bill was read a second time. EPISCOPAL FEES.—The Bishop of CARLISLE stated that the Charges which he paid on his elevation to the Bis- hopric of Carlisle amounted to £4Ol Bs. 4d. The state- ments which had appeared in some of the newspapers on the subject were greatly exaggerated. •aims ADVANCED.—The Museums and Gymnasiums Bill was read a third time. The Mail Ships Bill was read a second time. . _
The House adjourned at ten minutespast five.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONT.
The Spe;.ie-r-t;ola-he-c-hii7at t6ee o'clock. THE BACCARAT CASE AND THE PRINCE OF WALES.

Mr. Summits asked the Secretary of State for War Whether he had taken, or intended to take, any action with regard to the person or persons who, in the case of Sir William G. Cumming v. Wilson and others, were alleged to have broken or to have been parties to the breach of the re.ulation of her Majesty's Army which Provides that "Every commissioned officer of her Majesty's service whose character or conduct as an officer and a gentleman has been impugned must submit the case within a reasonable time to his commanding officer or other competent military authority for investiga- tion." -

Mr. E. STANHOPE said: Any hon. member who glances at the regulation in question will, I think, see that the chief person who had broken it was Sir William Gordon Cumming, because he did not report his case to his commanding officer according to the regulations. Any offence committed by any other officer can only have consisted in advising him to take any other course than that laid down by the regulations of the service. One of the three officers who are concerned is General Owen Williams, who has retired from the Army, and is there- fore not subject to the Queen's regulations. The other officers are undoubtedly subject to it. The regulation in question (No. 41) has never been specially brought to the attention of his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, but now that his attention has been called to it, and on looking to all the circumstances of the case his Royal Highness has authorised me to say that he now sees that an error of judgment was committed in not requiring Sir W. Gordon Cumming to report his case to his command- ing officer. In this view of the case I concur, but I Should like to give expression to my own personal opinion, that if any of us had suddenly heard that a friend of our own, and one who served her Majesty with honour bad been accused of dishonourable conduct, we should certainly have hesitated before adopting any course Which would have immediately and irretrievably blighted all his future hopes and prospects. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Blecklev Levett, who was in the same position, has ad- dressed in proper terms, a letter to his superior officer expressing his regret at not having acted in strict accord- ance with the regulations. It is not proposed to take any further action in the matter. (Cheers.) EVENING SCHOOLS.—Sir W. HART DYKE told Mr. S. Smith he could hold out no hope of freeing evening BehOOIS. GOVERNMENT BUSINESS.—Mr. W. H.SMITH moved that the Government business should, for the remainder of the session, have precedence on all days. The motion Was carried. THE LAND BILL.—A SCENE.

On the order for the reading of the Irish Land Purchase BM, Mr. J. Morley commented on the measure at some length, and said there were eight chief objections to it as it originally stood, none of which had been met. Mr. LABOUCHERE moved the rejection of the Bill. Mr. Sey- mour Keay endeavoured for several minutes to address the House, but in vain, his utterances being drowned in the loud and determined cries of " Divide," " Divide," Which seemed to proceed from members on his own side of the House as well as from the •Ministerialists. Eight minutes passed in this manner, when Mr. Hums ELivoT moved the closure. The Speaker declined to put the motion, at the same time advising Mr. Keay that as a large sec- tion of the House did not wish to hear him he had better make his remarks as brief as possible. Another five Minutes passed in Mr. Keay unsuccessfully endeavouring to shout down the various cries and noises raised on all sides, the excitement and confusion becoming greater every moment. At length the stern voice of the Speaker was heard loudly demanding oider. Mr. Keay gave way to the Speaker, and sat down. Perfect quiet reigned, while everyone waited breathlessly for the ruling of the chair. The SPEAKER quietly proceeded to put the amendment of Mr. Labouchere for the rejection of the Bill. There was a loud Ministerial laughter at the evi- dent discomfiture of Mr. Ksay.—After a division had been challenged and was in progress, Mr. S. Keay, addressing the Speaker, sitting, and with his hat on. said.: I beg your pardon, sir, but I sat down because I thought you were rising to a point of order.—The SPEAKER: The reason I rose was that the noise and dis- order, which was becoming momentarily greater, were not to the credit of the House, and I thought the hon. member would acquiesce in putting a step to it. (Min- isterial cheers and laughter.)
DIVISION. The House then divided.
For the amendment.. 96 Against
Majority 129 The figures were received with Ministerial cheers. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY.
ThorLorcl Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past five o'clock. --

THE NAVAL ARTILLERY VOLUNTEERS.—Conversation, initiated hy Lord SIDMOITTI, took place on the report of Admiral Tryon's Committee on the Royal Naval Artillery Volunteers, and the proposal of the Admiralty to turn the force into one of Marines.—Lord, SIDMOUTH and Earl COWPER were unfavourable to the proposal, which was defended by Lord Sudelev, Lord Elphinstone, and the Earl of Ravensworth.;---Cord BRASSEY, while maintaining that the existence of the Royal Naval Volunteers had been thoroughly vindicated, advised the men to accept the designation of marine artillery, and to devote themselves to shore training in gunnery. LAND BILL.—The Land Purchase Bill, brought froth the Commons, was read a first time, and the second read- ing 'fixed for Thursdsy week.
Their lordships rose at twenty minutes past seven o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAY,
The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. The Royal Insurance Company Bill was read a third time and passed. Only a few questions were put, and these were of minor importance.

div.head: MANIPUR DISASTERS.
div.p: THE MANIPUR DISASTERS.

Sir W. HAUC-O—II—RT: who was received with loud Opposi- tion cheers, called attention to the disasters at Manipur and the clauses which led to them, and moved—" That a humble addresses be presented to her Majesty that she Neill be graciously pleased to give directions that there be laid before the House further correspondence relating to Manipur." He said the motion was not of a party char- ter. It was rather a motion of inquiry, which would enable the Government to give further explanations with reference to the matter than had so far appeared in the papers at present in the possession of hon. members. He commented on the surprising circumstance that the determination to send an armed force into Manipur terri- tory was taken without any communication from the Indian Government to the Secretary of State at home, and that no opinion with regard to any one of the tran- sactions seemed to have been asked of the Secretary of State. Not even after the disaster was any opinion asked as to the punishment to be awarded, or-as to the policy to be pursued.

- Sir -JOHN GOILST said the Government were prepared' to lay on the table any further information in their power. The reasons why the transactions were carried to the point of a military expedition against Manipur without any previous consultation with the Secretary of State in London was that the universal practice of the Government of India, in all except what were considered important cases, was to take upon themselves the res- ponsibility of dealing with the native States, and of not seeking the previous sanction or approval of the Secre- tary of State; and thu Government of India and every- bedy connected with the Manipur affair regarded it at -the outset as a matter of very little importance, and had • there 'seen no disaster, very likely nothing would ever save been heard of it. Mr. cunzos contended that both upon constitutional .and upon practical grounds the Indian Governrrient were ,actually right in the step taken. Mr. CAMPBELL- BANNERmAN said the speech of Sir J. Gorst was rather a satire upon the Indian government than a defence of it. Sir R. Temple, Mr. Maclean, Sir George Campbell, Sir L. PellY, Mr. Bryce, Sir R. Lethbridge, and Mr. Stanhope continued the debate, and in the end Sir William Har- couit's motion was agreed to. MISCELLANEOUS.—The report on the Customs and In- land Revenue Bill was read and agreed to ; the Markets and Fairs (Weighing of Cattle) Bill was read a third time, and passed. COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS.—In moving the' second reading. of the County Council (Elections) Bill, Mr. RITCTIIE said that under the law as it now stooi the next election of County Councils would take place in Novem- !3er next. This would be inconvenient, and, therefore, In conformity with a wish generally expressed by the County Councils, the Bill would provide that the elec- tions should not take place until March 1892. After some discussion Mr. LABOUCTIERE said that this Was a disfranchising bill, and he was, therefore, not surprised that it was proposed by the present Govern- Meat. (Laughter.)

I After a few words from Mr. Ritchie, the Bill was read I a second time. SUPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Supply. A vote of £15,716 for salaries and expenses of the House of Lords was agreed to ; and one of £32,592, for salaries and expenses of the House of Commons, was under discussion when progress was reported at twelve o'clock. BILLS APVANCED AND WITHDRAWN.—The Allotments Rating Exemption Bill passed through Committee. The Maintenance of Destitute Parents Bill was withdrawn, as was also the Church Buildings Act (Compulsory Powers) Repeal Bill and the Fisheries Regulation (Scot- land) Bill. The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 25 minutes after twelve o'clock. THE SHIP CANAL.—The consideration of the Manches- ter Ship Canal Bill on report was deferred until Thurs- day. - NAVY ESTIMATES.—The house went into Committee of Supply on the Navy estimates.—Mr. SISAW-LEFEVRE moved the reduction of the clothing and victualling vote, and urged that the naval establishment should be moved from Ascension to St. Helena, where it would be much easier to maintain an adequate force. Lord Geo. Hamilton claimed that Ascension was far more useful for the defence of British Commerce than St. Helena, and could be fortified at little cost. Replying to other criticisms, he said 20,090 men would be required to man the ships built under the Naval Defence Act, and they proposed an increase of 12,500 men to the number on the Estimates at the time the Act was introduced. The vote was agreed to. Mr. GOURLEY moved the reduction of the shipbuilding vote by £60,350 ' the amount of the subsidy given to the owners of certain swift cruisers to be used for the protection of our commerce in case of war, contending that the policy was unnecessary. Mr. Forwood replied. The amendment was negatived, and , the vote agreed to. After discussion, other votes were agreed to, and the resolutions reported to the House. , THE BUDGET BILL.—On the third reading of the Cus- toms and Inland Revenue Bill, Mr. PICTON called atten- tion to the large increase in the consumption of tea which followed the reduction of the duty.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER was glad to think that the reduction of the duty had led to the increase of the consumption of tea, but declined to discuss the question further now.— The bill was read the third time. BILLS WITHDRAWN.—The Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, the County Councillors' Disabilities Removal Bill, and the Boilers Registration Bill were with- drawn.

WEIGHTS AND MRASURES.—On the motion of Mr. J. MORE, a Select Committee was appointed to inquire and report upon the various weights and measures used for tho sale of grain throughout the United Kingdom. The House adjourned at half-past five o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIIIRSDAY. The Earl of Morley, in the absence of the Lord Chan- cellor, took his seat on the woolsack at half past four o'clock. In the House of Lords, yesterday, the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill, brought from the Commons, was read a first time. On the motion of Lord HERSCHELL, and after a brief debate, the Mortmain and Charitable Uses Bill was read a second time. The Fisheries Bill— which, Lord BALFOUR of BURLEIGH explained, pro- vided for carrying out an agreement between Britain and Belgium with a view to remove difficulties that had arisen between British and Belgian fishermen in the seas off the eastern coast of this cnuntry—was read a second time; On the motion of the Duke of Westminster, the Brine Pumping (Com- pensation for Subsidence) Bill was read a second time; and a motion by Lord Thurlow for referring the bill to a select committee was negatived without a division. The Russian-Dutch Loan Bill was read a second time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIIIRSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. SHIP CANAL BILL.—The Manchester Ship Canal Bill was read a third time, the new clause proposed by Mr. Stanhope, providing that if seven years after the open- ing of the canal the money advanced by the Manchester Corporation was not repaid the undertaking should be vested in a public trust, having been withdrawn after some discussion. CLERICAL FEES.—Mr. SMITH informed Sir W. Lawson that the statement that the expenses consequent on the last translation to the Archbishopric of York amounted to over £7,000 was largely exaggerated, even with the inclusion of the sum expended on dilapidations at Peter- borough and the purchase of furniture belonging to the previous Archbishop of York. QUESTIONS &c.—Mr. CHAPLIN informed Mr. Howard Vincent that a report by the scientific officers of the Local Government Board on the recent epidemic of influenza was in the hands of the printers. Mr. SMITH, in reply to Mr. H. Fowler, promised to consider the question of the appointment of a Select Committee to inquire into the operation of the existing marriage laws, with a view to ascertaining whether and what alterations should be made therein. Mr. Smith, replying to Mr. De Lisle, said the Government could not interfere with the purchase for the nation, by the trustees of the Chantrey bequest, of the picture purporting to represent an incident in the life of St. Elizabeth of Hungary. The picture was acquired by the trustees in the exercise of the duties entrusted to them, BILLS ADVANCED.—A Bill to amend the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act with respect to the conveyance of animals by sea, and a bill to amend the Coinage Act, 1870, were read a first time. The Lords' amendments to the Savings Banks Bill were considered and agreed to.

CHILD LABOUR IN FACTORIES.—The consideration of the Factories and Workshops Bill, as amended by the Stand- ing Committee, was then proceeded with, an interesting debate ensuing on the question of the minimum age for child labour. The result was a defeat for the Govern- ment, a clank proposed by Mr. Sydney Buxton, prohi- biting the employment of children under eleven years of age being carricd as follows : For Mr. Sydney Buxton's clause 202 Against lB6

Majority against the Government. 16 The result was received with prolonged Opposition cheering. When the Speaker read out the number. The clause having been read a second time. The Speaker said that as there were no amendments on the paper he would at once put the question, that the clause should be added to the bill. Mr. MACARTNEY said that he pro- posed to move an amendment, Thereupon (it being then past twelve o'clock) the debate stood adjourned to this day. BILL PASSED.—The Returning Officers' (Scotland) Bill passed through Committee, and was read a third time and passed. The report of Supply was received and agreed to. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to one o'clock.

div.head: TRADES' UNION DEMONSTRA.- TION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: TRADES' UNION DEMONSTRA.- TION AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday afternoon Warrington was the scene of an imposing trades union demonstration in con- nection with the Local United Trades and Labour Council. About 1,800 men, representing the princi- pal trades of the ditstriet, promenaded the main streets of the town, with a profuse display of ban- ners, and accompanied by a number of bends, and with presentments in realistic form of the processes of manufacture in which the processionists were en- gaged. The procession started from Arpley-st., near the Trinity Church Schools, about half-past two o'clock, and pursued the following route :—Through Sankey-st., Bold-st., Rylands-st., Bridge-st., Mersey- st., Church-st., round the lamp outside the Parish Church, thence back along Church-st., and Irlam- at., through Scotland-road, along Winwick-st., Tanners-lane, Bewsey-st., Horsemarket-st., and past Market Gate, along Sankey-at., through Winmarleigh-st., to the starting point. The pro- cession was headed by Mr. George Armstrong, presi- dent of the Warrington Tanners' Union and delegate of the Warrington Trades Council, who, as chief marshal, wore a white sash, and was mounted on horsebaT.k. After him came the meinbers of the Trades Council with the League of the Cross brass band. 'I hen came the bakers, marshalled by Mr.Nimmo,and carrying a beautiful banner on which appeared a paintitr, which depicted a man reap- ing a field of corn ; and also the passages" By the sweat of his brow man shall eat bread " and " So shall thy barns be filled with plenty." A number of bakers marched behind carrying representations in wood Of the implements used in their vocation. Then followed the representatives of the National Union of Gas Stokers and general labourers, these being marshalled by Mr. Leigh, and having with them a banner, and a band under the direction of Mr. Yorke. Messrs. Crosfield had improved the occasion by having contributed, as the next item in the procession, a lurry from which several men and a boy arrayed in clothes of unexceptionable white, were stamping, boxing, and throwing in all directions samples of

THE CELEBRATED PERFECTION SOAP, • the spectators eagerlycompeting with each other to be- come the recipients of the saponaceous bounty showered upon them. ,The next feature in the procession was one which illustrated a, new and most significant phase of unionism, being no other than tip presence of a number of

INSURANCE AGENTS. This indeed was a striking exemplification of the in- creasing comprehensiveness of trades'-unionism, and of the practicability of that for which agitation has but quite recently been commenced, combination between those conventionally known as working-men, and employes of other classes for common protection of their interests. The ironworkers came next in order with the Catholic United Band, those in front carrying wooden representations of the paddles, robbles, and tongs used in their work. A lurry conveyed a group of puddlers, and a donkey-cart, led by a boy carrying a broom, contained a shingler, these men also being pro-

div.head: Til E EXANINER, SATURDAY, J UNE 20, 1891.
div.p: Til E EXANINER, SATURDAY, J UNE 20, 1891.

vided with wooden imitations of the implements em- ployed by them in their proligio.is toil at the furnace's mouth. In connection with this part of the procession there was a pony cart, prettily decorated with ever- greens, containing two menarrying miniature engines. The coopers came next in order, and carried a very fine banner, bearing on it the device of two barrels,a finished cooped one in perfect condition, and another going to destruction from want of hoops,above these appearing the motto" United we stand, divided we fall." The coopers carried also miniature barrels on rods, and two men bore diminutive figures similarly mounted representing coopers.busily plying their vocation, the hammer of one of these being automatically kept working on a tiny barrel. A lurry laden with barrels on which flags were mounted and coopers riding upon it, added to the pictorial display. The boot and shoe operatives, who were marshalled by Mr. Shute, succeeded the coopers, and lurry on which were seated, a number of DISCIPLES OF ST'. CRISPIN busily engaged in the pursuit of their handicraft and , another stood with a machine in front of him, which he assiduously manipulated, gave quite an aspect of indus- trial ar.imation to this part of the procession. After, the boot and shoe aperative,s marched the tanners, marshalled by Mr. Miller, and with two bands, those of St. Mary's, Widnes, and Lymm Church of England Temperance Society. They carried a magnifi- cent blue silk banner on which appeared a representa- tion of the Leather Exchange at Bermondsey, and repre- sentations of the various processes of work in the tan-yard. This was one of five banners brought by Mr. H. Preece, secretary of the Leather Trades Union, from London, for use in the procession. Two of these were leather banners, on one of 7chich appeared the motto "There is nothing like leather," and on the other "Simon the tanner," this apt citation from Scripture in proof of the antiquity of the trade exciting muck remark. The tanners had the accompaniment of a lurry on which rode representatives of the different departments of the trade surrounded by hides and other appurtenances of their work, with which they busily employed them- selves. To the tanners decidedly must be awarded the chief honours of the day so far as the display made was concerned; and their motto "THERE IS NOTHING LIKE LEXTUER

was strikingly applicable in this connection. The wire drawers, whose marshal was Mr. Wood, and who were very numerous, and had with them the Cockhedge Mis- sion band, brought up the rear of the procession. The sight was an animated and picturesque one, and was watched by thousands of persons in the streets and from the houses lining the route. The police deserve the utmost credit for the manner in which they succeeded under somewhat difficult conditions, in preserving the course clear as they did. But although the demonstra- tion was one which of its kind was unprecedented in Warrington, it was disappointing in some respects. Great surprise was expressed at the fact that the number of tanners present from Penketh was so large as com- pared with that of those belonging to the town ; and, moreover, some of the principal trades of Warrington took no part in the proceedings. The glass cutters, the glass makers, the wire weavers, the bricklayers, the painters, railway servants, filesmiths, navvies, plas- terers, and joiners, though all down in the printed list of trades .that were to join in the procession, were absent. This somewhat damped the spirits of the promoters and detracted from the eclat of the demonstration.

identical; unless the working-men were organised on the principle he had laid down the interests were antagonis- tic. Working-men must send those to the House of Commons who would help them to a better condition of things. (Applause.) There would have to be a great improvement in the condition of the working classes; they could not go on year by year with their noses to a grind- stone and their feet upon the workhouse threshhold as they had done. The slave of America was better cared for than nine-tenths of them, and if they sickened and died it cost nothing to fill their place, but the owner of a slave if he lost him had to purchase another, therefore took care of him. They were not considered of as much value as the good horse their employer put into his stable. No law should be allowed to stand in the statute book by which employers could drain their life blood and then leave them to the parish. (Applause.) If a working- man became invalided he should be as much entitled to a pension as any of the civil servants paid out of his earnings. (Applause.) Mr. W. MATISIN moved the following resolution : "That this public meeting of Warrington working-men rejoices to know that in many towns and pldces fair wage clauses are being inserted in all public contracts, and respectfully requests the Warrington Corporation to insert fair wage clauses in their contracts, the same clauses to apply to all contracts which may be sub-let, ante, as far as practicable, to give such contracts to War- rington firms, persons, or companies, and also desires the Corporation to consider the whole subject as soon as possible, so that clauses may be inserted in the public contracts, which would be one great step towards abolishing that cruel evil known as the sweating sys- tem." (Applause.) He considered there was more in the question of contract, both of Parliamentary and mnnicipal work, than a great many of them were aware of. (Hear, hear.) In London there had been hundreds of schools built for the School Board; and scarcely one of the contracts had fallen into the hands of firms who paid Trades Union wages. The result was that on investigation being made by the new School Board jobbery had been revealed that had been going on for years in the name of economy. It was entirely owing to the apathy of the working-men that these things had been allowed to go on. (Hear, hear.) He congratulated the local Trades Council upon the success of that demonstration for a start. He thought that those trades which had stood aloof that day day would see that if they had thrown in their lot with those who took part in the procession they would have demonstrated to the employers and the Corporation that they were a body of men whom they must listen to and respect in the future. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. JENKINS, in seconding the proposition, said it was merely for the want of looking after the working People had not got what they wanted. Working-men had been guilty of two .mistakes in the past. They had allowed somebody else to think for them, and they had allowed those others to carry out the think- ing. If a thing was worth having it was worth work- ing for, and therefore he advised them not to let other people think for them, and to insist upon carrying out their own ideas. (Hear, hear.) On the question of hours of labour there had been divisions of opinion amongst workmen in the past as to whether they should get their hours reduced by Trades Union effort or by legislation. For his part he did not care which way they got it so long as they did get it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) With him it was a question of the easiest way to get it, and he had noticed that everybody that wanted anything in this country, and knew how to get it, went to the Hoese of Commons for it. (Hear hear, and laughter.) Lawyers and doctors, for instance, had done well for themselves by going to Parliament, and it was his opinion that they should never get reduced hours for all trades un- less they got it through the ballot box. (Hear, hear.) Be- sides if they did get their hours reduced by Trades Union effort, he was afraid that on the first panic in trade em- ployers would be having them lengthened again while if they were reduced by an Act of Parliament they could only be lengthened again after a considerable agitation. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. PREECE supported the proposition, and advised these present to vote solidly for those candidates who were prepared to insert the fair wage clauses in con- tracts. Applause.) With regard to the eight hours day, he had been one of those who believed that it could be secured by Trades Union effort, but he should not hesitate a mment to use those methods of legislation which the landlords and capitalists had taken so much advantage of. (Hear, hear and applause.) The resolution was then put po the meeting, and carried unanimously. Mr. BULLOCK, secretary of the Warrington Trades Council, next moved: "That this meeting agrees to make fair wage contract clauses a test question at all municipal elections, and pledges itself to support only those .candidates, who are prepared to vote for this measure, being returned to the Council." He pointed out that the Corporations of Sheffield, Nottingham and other places had adopted the contracts chases, and he said he did not see why Warrington. Corporation should not. The way to bring that about was to support only those candidates who would support the clauses. (Ap- plause.) Mr. STOREY seconded the proposition and strongly urged upon every workingman to make up his mind to vote for no candidate who would not support the fair wages clauses. This resolution was also carried unanimously with ap- plause. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.

THE WHITEC ROSS WARD ELECTION. LIBERAL CANDIDATE RETURNED. The election of a successor in the representation of Whitecross Ward on the Warrington Town Coun- cil to Mr. E. Greenall, who has been made an alder- Man, took place on Monday. The election excited considerably more interest than municipal bye- elections usually do. Mr.Greenall is a Conservative in politics, and the Conservative party in the town appeared determined to make a desperate effort to retain the seat, although in November last White- cross Ward declared itself distinctly Liberal by re- turning Councillor H. Roberts by the large majo- rity of 193 over his opponent, Mr. A. Woods. ()n this occasion Mr. Woods was again the Conservative candidate, while the Liberals some time prior tol the vacancy, had selected dr. George Plumpton, toolmaker, to contest the seat on their behalf. Bcth sides have worked hard during the election, though their efforts have been mainly confined to canvas- sing, as only two public meetings have been held, one on each side. The pollinc, on Monday morning opened as usual at eight o'clock'. The polling booth was situated in St Barnabas' School, Bostock-st.,where there were two poll- ing stations for the convenience of the 845 electors of the ward. At polling station No. 1, the presiding officer is Mr. F. W. Walker, the poll clerk Mr. H. W. Longdin, and the personation agents—for the Liberals Mr. George Plumpton, jun., and for the Conservatives Mr. William Gleave. Mr. John Fairhurst presides over No. 2 polling station, assisted by Mr. John Harrison as poll clerk. The personation agents are—for the Liberals Mr. John Webb and for the Conservatives Mr. John Brown. During the marning the poll was rather slow, but later in the day, and especially at times convenient for workingmen, vot- ing was much more briskly carried on. The election literature was rather plentiful. The Tories were particularly profuse in their misrepresen- tations as to Mr. Plumpton's relations with the work- people he employed, and on Saturday placards were issued declaring the Liberal candidate's works were a " black " shop. Mr. Plumpton at once issued a strong denial of "the foul slander, and offered to give £lO to the Infirmary if the charge were proved. Another hand- bill, headed Latest Tory Dodge," was also issue.d,relat. ing to the same subject, and contained a letter from workmen in the employ of Mr. Plumpton, in which the , following words occurred: "The statements made by the Tory party about our e.nployer are absolutely false. We are paid as good wages as are received by any toolmakers in any workshop in this county. We can with confidence recommend our employer as an upright and fair-dealing man ; and we trust and believe he will be returned, on Monday next, by a majority." The contest was conducted with the utmost good feel- ing between the two candidates, but strong indignation was expressed by the Liberals at the conduct of the Tories in covering Liberal placards. The posters which Mr. Plumpton issued,on Saturday,replying to the insinu- ation that he was opposed to Trades Unionism were, every cue of them, covered during Sunday night by Tory bills, printed in red ink with a view to conveying the impression that they were issued by the Liberals. Not only were all the private stations, which had been engaged by the Liberals, covered, but bills were placed on the houses of prominent workers for Mr. Plumptel, and two of them were placed on the candidate's garden wall, one on each side of his gate. In one case where one of these posters as being cleaned off a private house, one of the Tory officials added insult to injury by pro- testing against it being touched. It is much to be re- gretted that such tactics are resorted to. It serves no good purpose, excites the worst feeling, and provokes a disposition to retaliate. In larger posters twelve reasons were given why the electors should vote for Mr. Plumpton. Reference was made to the fact that Mr. Plumpton has resided in the ward, and has had business in it for over 20 years, and that he was opposed to "sweating," and had pledged himsslf to support a fair-wage clause in all the Corpora- tion contracts. He contended that the electors had a right to say how many licensed houses they would have in their midst, and was opposed to any member of the Town Council who is directly interested in the drink trade having a seat upon the Watch Committee. He was in favour of the Baths being made worthy of the town, and special facilities being afforded to working-men and school children. He was also in favour of a stipendiary magistrate, if the appointment can be made without being a serious burden upon the rates, and he would vote for a public inquiry into the condition of the depots. Mr. WOODS declared himself strongly in favour of all Corporation contracts being given to Warrington men, and of no tender being accepted where " sweating" was carried on. He was favourably disposed towards en- larged and commodious baths being erected at once,and opened free on certain days to school children, under the centrol of their teachers ; also that the prices charged for the swimming baths be as low as possible,to encourage the art of swimming among all, which was now impos- sible, owing to the present prohibitive charge. He was described OR the posters on the walls as "The popular workingman's candidate, who has the support of all genuine trades unionists." In another placard, Trades Unionists were asked not to be humbugged any longer, but to vote straight for Mr. Woods, "who is the Trades Unionist candidate." DECLARATION OF THE POLL.

The polling booth was closed at eight o'clock, and the ballot boxes were at once conveyed to the Town Hall. Alderman Platt is the retffning officer for Whitecross ward, but, in his absence, Councillor Black burst acted in his place. The counting was proceeded with expedi- tiously. There are 845 persons entitled to vote in the ward, and 685 votes were recorded. It is worthy of note that not a single voting paper was rejected on the ground of its not being properly filled up, and there was no case of attempted personation. The announcement of the result was made by Councillor Blackhurst from the ideps in front of the Town Hall to a crowd of moderate dimen- sions which had gathered below. The result was as follows : For Mr. Plumpton (L) 384 „ Woods (C). 3Ol
Liberal majority B3 The announcement was received with loud cheers. VOTE OF THANKS.

Before the public announcement was made, Mr. WOODS moved a vote of thanks to the returning officer. He added that he must at the same time congratulate Mr. Plumpton upon his success, and also congratulate themselves upon the nice manner in which they had in- dividually conducted the election. (Hear, hear.) Mr. PLusirroN, in sesonding the vote of thanks,moved by his opponent and friend, Mr. Woods, said he was sure the good feeling that had existed between his friend and himself had had a great effect upon the working of the election. He only wished that the same thing had been carried out by the parties that had been working with his friend. He would not, however, say anything about that just then; it was something he might have to say a word about another time. He hoped that if he had to meet Mr. Woods again the same good feeling would exist between them. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BLACICHIIRST, the returning officer, acknow- ledged the vote of thanks. He was pleased to find two gentlemen fighting an election so good-humouredly and parting such good friends. He thought every election

iingfitEci- fie conducted on the same llnes;- ancrtftPre would be less unpleasantness. People in the excitement of the moment often said things they regretted after- wards. (Hear, hear.) 4 SPEECHES AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. -

After the announcement of the poll there was a con- siderable gathering at the Liberal Club, and Mr. Plump- ton was warmly congratulated on his victory. Amongst those present were Councillors H. Roberts, T. Flood, S. J. Beaman and A. Browne; Dr. Gornall, Mr. J. Walker, &c.

Councillor H. Roomers said he supposed the members of the Tory party would try to get what satisfaction I they could out of the fact that they had been beaten by a majority of 83. Moral victories were, no doubt, very pleasant 0 those who won thern,but they did not count. , When they. came to count noses in the local House of I Parliament the moral victory would not be in it. (Hear, I hear, and laughter.) He had had a good deal of experi- ence in electioneering, but he had learned that it was possible for the Tory party to descend to deeper depths than he had even thought it possible for them to do. They had introducezl into that election everything that could possibly be introduced to damage Mr. Plumpton's character, but fortunately for him, and for the Liberal party too, his character as a man had been entirely unassailable. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Liberal party did not bring men before the people of Warrington in the position of candidates whose moral character could be assailed, and they never intended to do. (Hear, hear.) But there had been introduced into the election a side issue which was as contemptible and as base as it was unfcunded. There had been, as they knew, statements made against Mr. Plumpton which had been proved to be utterly foundationless. But the Liberalism of the Whitecross ward had proved staunch and loyal. (Applause.) They had been told that if Mr. Plumpton won he would kave to fight again in November. Well, Mr. Plumpton would fight again in November next, and, without being a prophet or the son of one, li.?. would undertake to say that when those men who had that day been led away by the false:statements of the Tory party in regard to trade matters, had time to reflect and to read some of the state- ment which had been uttered in contradiction of the lies, the majority would be considerably increased. (Hear. hear.) The Tory party had that day done every- thing it was possible for it to do. It had descended to meannesses of which, he confessed, he had not thought it capable of. He would not specify what they were, but they knew them as well as he did. (Hear, hear.) And he would not describe the female members of the Primrose League in the terms in which the defeated candidate had described them. (Laughter.) He had far too much respect for the fair sex to apply to them, even in jocu- larity, any term so coarse as that which as reported to have been made use of by a member of the gentlemanly party at a meeting of the Primrose League last week. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They had now made,White- cross ward as good as they could make it; every repre- sentative of the ward belonged to their own side. They now stood in the Council Chamber as 17 Liberals to 19 Conservatives. It was now nearly 20 years since the Liberals had a majority in the Town C;uncil, but they had now a majority of the elected representatives. (Ap- plause.) The Tory party were only able to hold their ownl by the aldermanic vote, the vote of men who had not to face the electors to give an account of their stewardship as they ought to do. (Hear, hear.) They could not abolish the aldermanic seats, and so they must reform them, and thsy could only do this by increasing the number of Liberal elected members of the Town Coun- cil. (Loud applause.)

Councillor PLIMPTON was received with loud applause. Be remarked that that was not a victory for him alone ; it was a victory for the Liberal party not only in White- crcAs ward but in the whole town. (Applause.) The Tory party had said some very unpleasant things about himself in different ways. He did not think he should refer to any of thein,as there were some of them he might have to deal with in another way. (Loud applause.) They had won a great victory in Whitecross ward. They never expected to win by more than 100 of a majority, and when they had gone round and seen in many caseg the sickness that prevailed—and it had made him sad at heart to see so much sickness in the ward—and in addi- tion to this there had been many deaths and removals, so that they considered if they had a majority of 100 the victory would be as great as it was when Councillor Roberts was returned. (Hear. hear.) The Tories had told them that they would light again in November. (" We are ready for them.") But they told them that before they began, and if they were not frightened then. and if the Tories could afford to fight to lose, surely the Liberals could afford to fight to win. (Applause.) Whitecross Ward was a Liberal ward, and Warrington was a Liberal town. (Hear, hear.) It only wanted unity and harmony, a working together, to disturb the present M.P. for Warrington. The Tories had called him a Liberal Unionist, but he longed for the day when he could see Warrington represented by a Radical or Liberal member. (Applause.) Mr. Plumpton then paid a warm tribute to the services rendered ia the election by Councillor Roberts, the Whitecross Ward Committee, and others. With regard to his action in the Town Council he saidhe should act in an independent manner. He should net bind himself to any individual or any party. If he saw a wrong he would oppose it, but if he saw a right he would support it. (Hear, hear.) But he could tell them this, that if it came to a party question— for instance, if it came to a deciding vote as to who should be Mayor—his vote would not be lost on that oc- casion ; and if it was the making of an alderman he would not stay away. (Loud applause.) Mr.Jomq WerAten moved a vote of thanks to the Chair- man and workers. He remarked that the Tory candidate had said tohim,that they had,at any rate,won a moral victory. He (Mr.Waiker) at once congratulated Mr. Woods on his moral victory, and expressed a hope that the Tories would always hq.ve such moral victories. (Hear, hear. and laughter.) He did not, however, con- sider it could be called a moral victory; he thought it was rather an immoral defeat so far as the Tories were concerned, for there had been nothing like morality in it. (Hear. hear.) Tennyson said that the "lie which is half the truth is always the blackest lie," but he ventured to say that in this instance even that did not hold good, for there had been the blackest of lies without any truth in them. (Applause.) He had never seen such climbing down in placards as they had had in regard to Mr. Plumpton's trade. They started off with stating that he , employed non-union filesmiths, and ended with saying that he dealt in files. If there was anything more ridiculous than that he failed to find it. What was Mr. Woods's position? He dealt in a hundred things, but could he say that every one of those articles had been made by trades unionists. ("No.") He ventured to say that Whitecross ward had got in Mr. Plumpton one of the very best men they could send to the Council. (Hear, hear.) He had told them that he would be inde- pendent, and from what he knew of Mr. Plumpton he was quite sure he would be independent, but that dial, not mean he was going to be independent of the Liberal party. He bad told them that when the Liberal party in the Council was acting co-hesivelvjas a Liberal party he would always be found voting with it. (Hear, hear.) If he might offer a word of advice tothe Liberals in the Council it would bets put themselves in the position of the rank and file that day and work shoulder to shoulder. Unless they did that and formulated a policy upon which they could act together—a policy which should go right to the hearts and interests of the masses—and showed them- selves earnest in carrying it out, he was afraid the Tories would strike in between them, and perhaps they the (Liberals) might not be quite so successful as they hoped at the next election. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. T. BIRCHALL seconded the vote of thanks, and re- ferred to the manner in which the Tories were " Ameri- canizing" their institutions by slandering their opponents. The Tory tactics in Warrington had never been noted for deanliness,but on that occasion they had outdone them- selves. A decent Tory had expressed to him (Mr. Birchall) his disgust at the actions of his party, but un- fortunately the Tory party were not led by their decent members. (ApPlause.) Mr. I. HAYWOOD thought that fight had done the work- ing-men a lot of good,and it had brought Trades Unionism to the front as it bad never been brought before. (Hear, hear, and applause) Mr. S. DUNDODDIN, Councillor BEAMAN, Councillor T. FLOOD, and Councillor BROWNE also congratulated Mr. Plumpton on his victory. The vote of thanks was then put to the meeting and carried, and Councillor Ronsers having responded, the meeting closed. AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB. Immediately after the declaration of the poll, a meet- ing was also held in one of the billiard rooms of the Con- servative Club, under the presidency of Mr. John White. The CHAIRMAN in addressing those present said the re- sult of the poll showed that the Liberals had obtained 62 fewer votes than last November, and Mr. Woods had obtained 48 more than he did then, the result beine, a majority of 83 for the Liberals or an improvement in the Conservative minority, as cr.mpared with the previous contest in the ward of 110. The poll was much the same size as last year, or rather only 14 less. Lie believed there was an old saying, blessed is he. that expecteth nothing ;he won't be disappointed. He supposed no one in that room had expected that Mr. Woods would win the election. He (the chairman) never expected it from the first, but he was agreeably surprised, and they Must all be, that in the great Radical stronghold of the town bhey had been able to reduce the majority by the magnificent sum of 110 votes. (Applause.) This aug,ured very well for their course in November next, and also for the ap- proaching Parliamentary election. By the I time that came about lie hoped the working-men of the Whitecross ward would have found out, as they seemei to be finding out, that their best friends were the Conservatives, whether in the local or the Imperial Parliament. They could not but regret for the sake of the Town Council that Mr. Wobds had not been returned, as he (the Chairman) was sure he would have been a very great addition to it, being a man of great practical experience and of no small ability, and one who would lave walked worthily in the footsteps of his father. The Chairman concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Woods for the splendid fight he Ead made and congratulation on the moral vic- tory he had won. (Applause.)

div.head: MASS MEETING.
div.p: MASS MEETING.

• Late in the afternoon a mass meeting was held on the piece of waste ground adjoining Trinity Schools, a furry being utilized as a platform. Upwards of a thousand persons were present, but it was observed that many of the processionists congregated round the bands in other parts of the ground. Mr. T. B. Malkin of the Warring- ton Trades Council, occupied the chair, and he was sup- ported by Mr. E. Trow, of Darlington, general secretary of the Associated Ironworkers and a member of the Labour Commission ; Messrs. J. Greeley, B. Hall., W. Bullock, and T. Houghton, president, vice-president, secretary, and treasurer, respectively of the Warrington Trades Council, Mr. H. Preece, of London, secretary of the Amalgamated Leather Trades Union, Mr. R. Harrison of Birmingham, general secretary of the Wiredrawers' Association, Mr. Wm. Matkin of Liverpool, chairman of the last Trades and Labour domicil there. Mr. John Jen- kins, of the Manchester and Salford Trades Council, Messrs. R. Storey, S. Dunn, and A. Birch, Houghton, J. Loxley, W. Potter, G. Sambrook, J. Price, H. Lawson, N. Cook, and others. Mr. BULLOCK announced the receipt of a telegram from Mr. John Wilson, M.P., financial secretary of the Durham Miners' Association, who had been expected to attend, stating that he had been suddenly taken ill. The CHAIRMAN then addressed the meeting. He said he felt very proud of that day's demonstration, the first that had been held in Warrington in connection with trades unionism,and he felt that by what they were now doing they were only echoing the voice that had been heard throughout the whole country. Had such a de- monstration been attempted a few years ago it would very likely have been suppressed, but the police officers that day had been helping all they could to make their meeting a success. Gatherings such as that had two very important elements in them. The first was that they showed to the working-men something of their own strength, and second that it showed the capitalists that those who had been tools in their hands were not unorgamised. Too long had the capitalists had their own way and enriched and fattened themselves upon the working-men. The time was coming when they ought to form one,great party, connected with no political side, but only a labour party. (Some applause.) Mr. TROW then followed. He said the demonstration was a proof to them what organisation could do ; a proof to the employers that the men of this kingdom were be- coming alive to the fact that without organisation they weak,and that with organisation they were power- ful, and able to hold their own against the capitalists. There was not a profession into which the sons of the cap- italists were drafted that had not a perfect organisation. The church had it, the doctors had it, the lawyers had it, and the employers had it, and what was good for them was equally good for the working-men. (Applause.) He did not want them to organise to rob anybody, to take from any employer what belonged to him. He did not want them to meet force by force, but he wanted them to organise and put themselves into a position in which, by argument and reason, without force, they would be able to secure their rights. (Applause.) He had been now for over 35 years fighting,not to rob capi- tal, but to prevent capital robbing him ; not as an advo- cate of force or strikes, but trying all he possibly could to prevent strikes. They praduced disasters among those affected by them on both sides, something like those caused by war between nations; and he was a man of peace ; he believed in arbitration between employers and employed for the purpose of preventing the misery and suffering caused by strikes. That object could only be secured by perfect combination and perfect confidence in one another. He was a member of a board of arbitra- tion, that during the last 20 years had settled over a thousand labour disputes without a day's stoppage, and wives and children had not gone shoeless and supperless because of these disputes. He wanted those present to feel that every fellow-labourer was a brother, that the interests of the miner could not be singled out and those of the blast furnaceman left in the lurch, that those of the shoemaker could not be singled out and every other tradesmen ignored, but that they must all combine to- gether in common brotherhood. The cause of one man must be felt to be the cause of all men and the cause of one trade that of every trade They might talk till doomsday about the interests of capital and labour being

div.head: lilt. PARNELL AT BERMONDSEY.
div.p: lilt. PARNELL AT BERMONDSEY.

Mr. Parnell, addressing a meeting at Bermondsey Town Hall, on Wednesday night in connection with the Irish National League, defended his action in regard to the Land Purchase Bill. If properly worked that bill would do more good to Ireland than any measure that had proceeded from the Imperial Parliament. He con- fessed himself quite unable to understand why the Liberals had opposed it, and condemned their policy as false. He was not discouraged by Kilkenny and Sligo, and he would submit the question to constituency after Constituency until the general election.

div.head: TRAGIC AFFAIR IN IRELAND.
div.p: TRAGIC AFFAIR IN IRELAND.

• A Newry correspondent telegraphs that late on Tues- day night the inhabitants of Kilkeel were thrown into a state of great excitement by the intelligence that a shocking tragedy had been committed in the town, that a young man and his wife had been shot, and that the would-be murderer had committed suicide. It appears that on Tuesday night William Sloan, a painter, of Harbour-road, Silkeel, entered his mother's house in Newcastle-St., and observing his sister and her husband sitting in the parlour—they having just returned from their lioneymeon—pointeci a revolver .at them and fired. The shot struck his brother-in-law, named Annett, in the thigh. Mrs. Annett grappled with her brother, and during the struggle the revolver was again discharged, but Mrs. Annett escaped injury. After a sevete struggle the weapon was wrenched from him ,and he walked away. The police, on being communicated with, went to Sloan's house, which they found barri- caded. On forcing the door they discovered Sloan lying dead, he having shot himself through the head. Annett's injuries are not dangerous. There was no motive for the crime, and at the inquest on Wednesday night a verdict was returned that the deceased con mitted the deed while temporarily insane.

- Councillor Mrtrt seconded th-e proposition. He -had not expected Mr. Woods to win the election, but they had won a moral victory even better than he expected,. bringing the Liberal majority of 193 down to 83. In can- vassing the ward, he had found there was a great deal of terrorism--(hear, hear)—intimieation and coercion, and more than 80 people, he was quite sure, dared not vote for Mr. Woods. (Hear, hear.) If all had been fair and above-board the Conservatives would have won theelee- tion. If it had been those nasty-narrow minded old Tories that were doing this he could have understood it— (laughter)—brit they were Liberals. (Applause.) Mr. James RATTERSDY supported the motion. He said he was delighted with the result, although not as satis- fied as he might be. He had not expected the Conserva- tives would poll so many, because having lived in the ward so many years he knew it to be a Radical strong- hold, and certainly when dealing with a class of peo- ple who were very stubborn and stupid and not the best educated people it took a lot to change their views. He was glad Mr. Woods had been so plucky as to come out again, and that he had gained such a moral victory. The vote of thanks was accorded with cheers. Mr. Woons in responding said he must say that with the result of the poll lie was perfectly satisfied. (Ap- plause.) When it was considered that the total poll in the Ward last time was 699. and this time 685, 14 less, and that the Liberal candidate was a man not known at all, what had been said, that the ward was a Radical stronghold, where men must of necessity vote as they were told was clearly borne Out. The in- crease in his total number was due entirely to the work and zeal of the workers of the Conservative party, and he must take the opportunity of publicly •thanking Mr. Hampson and his assistants and all who had come forward not only from Whitecross ward, but from the other wards in the town, for their Services in bringing up their men. He had not succeeded for the simple reason that many of his supporters dare not come to the poll, and had to sneak up the back streets to get out of the way. That did not say much for the Liberal party. Between Mr. Plumpton, and himself there had been the greatest good feeling, and he only wished every election was carried out between the candidates as that had been, because he could not see why two men could not be put forward by two different sides and behave themselves courteously to each other; instead of levelling abuse at each other. It gave him great pleasure to think that by their hard earnest work they had reduced the majority of the other side from 193 to 83. If they in the Henry Roberts' stronghold could do that in a small municipal contest what could they not do in the case .of a Parliamentary election in increasing the majority in favour of Sir Gilbert Greenall ? (Applause.) Dr. CANNEL". proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. John White.—Mr. Jorm HAatesoer seconded. He was very pleased indeed with the result of the election, and the way it had been carried on. He did not think he ever knew an election worked better, or by more enthusiastic workers.—Mr. THOS. MASON supported the proposition, and it was carried heartily and unanimously.—Mr. Wittes having thanked the meeting, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. H. Cookson, secretary of the Ward, on the motion ot Mr. H. HOUGHTON, seconded by Mr. H. ISHERWOOD, and Mr. COOKSON having acknowledged the compliment, the proceedings concluded.

div.p: AFFAIRS IN IRELAND.
PROMOTION FOR ECCLESIASTICS.

The "National Press "announces that the Pope, at the request of Archbishop Walsh, has promoted to the position of private chamberlain, with the title of Mon- signor, Dr. Molloy, rector of the Catholic University Dr. Browne, president of Maynooth ; Archdeacon Walsh, of Kingstown; Canon Fitzpatrick. rector of Holy Cross Seminary: and Canon Plunkett. Dr. Molly, Dr. Browne, and Archdeacon Walsh have further been raised to the rank of domestic prelates to his Holiness. .

MR. GLADSTONE AND THE EVICTED TENANTS. The following letter from Mr. Gladstone was received on Saturday at a meeting of Cork evicted tenants "Dear sirs,—You will probably have understood through the public journals how I was prevented by illness from giving practical attention to the subject opened in your letter of April 29. lam glad to think that notwithstand- ing the unfavourable condition of the present Parliament, something has been gained through the exertions of . several Irish Nationalist members.—Yours faithfully, W. E. GLADSTONE." .

MILLITARY DISTURBANCE AT ENNISKILLEN. A military riot was reported on Saturday from Ennis- killen, where ill-feeling exists between the 3rd Battalion Enniskillen Fusilier Militia, now undergoing their annual training, and the North Lancashire Regiment, stationed in the town. 'rhe pickets of each regiment met in the, street, and a fight commenced, each side being rein- forced by comrades. A number of militiamen fr4m the camp rushed throught the town, and in spite of the police, ran into the conflict with belts off and bludgeons. Several persons were wounded with bayonets, and the police were helpless. Lieutenant Bloomfield went to the militia camp and brought out an armed company, which had the effect of quelling the row. ALLEGED MURDER. Four men, named Conner, Clinch, Mulligan and Brown, were charged at,Rathbeal. county Dublin, on Monday, with the murder of Patrick Tipper, a labourer, who was returning to Suggard from a National Federa- tion meeting at Lucan, on Sunday evening, the accused being members of a deputation which attended the meeting. The case was adjourned for a week, all the accused, except Connor, being admitted to bail.

div.head: O'SHEA DIVORCE SUIT.
div.p: THE O'SHEA DIVORCE SUIT.

The " National Press" London correspondent says : I understand that proceedings in bankruptcy have been begun against Mr. Parnell for the recovery of the costs in the divorce action, amounting to about £7OO, which Mr. Parnell has not paid in spite of repeated applica- tions.
THE WIEDUANN-WALPOLE CASE.

The trial of Miss Wiedeinann's action for breach of promise and seduction against Mr. Robert Horace Wal- pole was resumed before Mr. Baron Pollock in the Queen's Bench Division on Saturday morning. Miss Wiedemann lays her damages at £20,000. This was the fourth day of the trial. Mr. Terrell proceeded to re- examine the plaintiff. She said that the fact that the she had a child in 1883 was a great scandal in her family and her relatives were very angry with her about it. It I was not true that She had a child in 1881. She was ad- mitted into the Church of Rome at Rome on the 28th of May, 1881. She had not in 1880 or at any other time im- proper relations ivithCrenneville in Vienna or anywhere else. She had had no means of conducting this litiga- tion, and all the money she had had for the case had been found for her by a few friends who wereinterested in her. She had made endeavours to find Cook, the de- tective, since the last trial, but he had gone out of the country, and had left his offices in London. Mr. Terell proceeded to read the depositions of the Rev. Charles Wagner, who spoke of the good moral character borne by the plaintiff. On Monday, Mr. Lockwood, for the defendant, sub- mitted there was, for want of corroboration, no case,but his Lordship (Baron Pollock) ruled that the fact of the defendant's leaving important letters unanswered might be urged as corroboration of a promise. Mr. Lockwood, then, opening the case for the defendant, said the case was briefly that at Constantinople Miss iViedemann was complaisant, and an act of immorality was committed, for which defendant paid £ll5. At the time it would be proved that plaintiff was the Valerie Wiedemann who gave birth to a child at Berlin in 1880, and if sa, she was perjured. Again he charged that she had endeavoured to blackmail a man named De Crenneville, with whom she had had improper relations in Cyprus. On Tuesday, Mr. Walpole, the defendant, in examina- tion, said he never promised marriage, and what took place at the Hotel d'Angleterre, Constantinople, was en- tirely by plaintiff's consent. She was afterwards profuse in her thanks for £lOO, in addition to £l5, but subse- quently made a scene, and said she weuld have £l,OOO. Witness's income was only an allowance of £3OO a year from his mother, but he was ieir to property, on which he had borrowed to a certain extent. He thought £ll5 was a generons sum to give to a woman whom he did not believe to be virtuous. Mrs. Laura Sophia Walpole, mother of the defendant, was also examined, and deposed to the conversation with the plaintiff at the Hotel:Conti- . nental, Cannes, after which witness would have nothing more to do with plaintiff. This evidence and a number of depositions closed the defendant's case, and the court . adjourned. On Wednesday Mr. Baron Pollock, in summing up, put it to the juiv whether there was a promise of mar- riage. Practically the question was breach of promise or nothing. There wasan action for libel, but that, he , imacined, would depend on the question of the promise. The jury, after deliberating an hour and twenty-five minutes, returned a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £3OO. The Judge entered the verdict accordingly, but granted a stay of execution on the question as to corro- borative evidence.

THE PRINCE of WALES has been More About Gam blin having rather a hard time of it a. for the part he took, along with other officers of the army, in shielding the damaged reputation of Sir WILLIAM GORDON-CUMMING. His Royal Highness was also, to a certain extent, shielding himself; but, although a good deal has been heard of the matter as a breach of army disci- pline, it seems to us that this was the lightest part of the offence which ho committed, and that it is fully condoned by the admission made on his be- half, in the House of Commons, on Monday, that "it was an error of judgment." The regulation in question provides that "every commissioned officer of her Majesty's service, whose character or con- duct as an officer and gentleman has been publicly impugned, must submit the case within a reason- able time to his commanding officer, or other com- petent military authority for investigation." It will be seen that the real breach of the regulation was on the part of the culprit in failing to report the accusation which had been made against him. It was doubtless an "error of judgment" on tho part of General OWEN WILLIAMS and the PRINCE of WALES to neglect to advise the sub- mission of the case to the commanding officer; but it is fairly open to argument whether that neglect was in itself an infraction of the regulation; and it is ridiculous to contend, as has been contended, that all three officers stood in the same position in relation to the commanding officer. A much stronger case on civil grounds might be made out against all who were party to hushing up the scandal, in that cheating at cards is a misdemeanour. The law takes direct cogniz- ance of the offence, and in agreeing to shield Sir WILLIAM GORDON-CUMMING, the party at Tranby Croft were themselves committing another offence known as compounding a felony. This would be immediately apparent if the dishonoured Baronet were proceeded against, as he still might be, as a cheat. There is evidence in the matter which has been publicly recorded; and, if no action be taken, it will not be because there is any doubt as to a conviction; but rather because it is thought that world-wide publicity, coupled with discharge from the Army, is punishment which meets the crime. Public opinion is satisfied, and public opinion is equal, in some cases, it seems, to dispensing with the full enforcement of the law.

The sea ndal, and the revelations in the law court which have proceeded from it, have had the effect of directing attention to the grow- ing practice of gambling and betting. Whether the agitation upon the subject will be the means of checking that growth remains to be seen. The vice of gambling would appear from an article in the current issue of the "Westminster Review S' to be as old as civilisation itself. The Greeks and Romans were addicted to it; and "to the Greeks belongs the credit or dis- credit of being the inventors of dice." Betting is of more recent origin : it is the outcome, of our higher civilisation! The Mahommedans are gener- ally spoken of as a bad lot, and yet we are told that—" Games of Chance were prohibited by Mahomet, and in the Koran were placed in the same category as wine-drinking." Gambling was forbidden by Justinian, a Christian Roman Emperor of the sixth century : but he did not interfere with athletic exercises which were engaged .in for money prizes. This is the vier;
