div.p: By Messrs. J. B. and B. LEACH.

which reasonable people take of such matters to- day. Prizes in athletic contests might indeed be Offered by a Young Men's Christian Association, and nobody be the worse for it. It is when bet- ting is added to these things that the mischief begins; or when games are indulged in which are mere games of chance, and when the object in view is money and money only. How demorali sing , this may become has been terribly illustrated in the case of Sir WILLIAM GORDON-CUMMING. It undermines the better natures of high and low, rich and poor, and works mischief in a thousand Ways. It is a poor plea to urge, as is commonly done, that" a sriall stake gives interest to the game." If the interest is over and above the in- terest in the game itself—if it is an interest aris- ing out of a desire to pocket something which has not been legitimately earned—it is a sordid and a vicious interest. Where the game depends entirely or almost entirely upon the skill of the players, there may be betting, especially by those who are I°4:Acing on, but there is little or no disposition to resort to gambling. Thus—the less skill —the more gambling; and what a reflection this is upon that noble creature, man! There is such a thing as the force of habit and association M gambling as in other matters; and it is because the habit is bad— utterly bad in its surroundings and consequences—that men who have at heart the bettering of their kind should set their faces against it. The only safe guide in the matter is the one already indicated : there should be no play where money or money value becomes the object of interest. And this means that raffling at bazaars is objectionable, in that it stimulates the cupidity in human nature which is at the root of gambling. Church or- ganisations have been thoughtless in this res- pect, and much mischief has been wrought. Still, many religious bodiesare now awake to their duty and responsibility; and they are acting with pru- dence and consistency in condemning raffling at bazaars, in order that they may, with the greater effect, condemn gambling and betting in all its forms.

THE by-election in Whitecross " A Moral Ward, Warrington, consequent Victory." upon the elevation of Councillor Gummi, to the Aldermanic Bench has excited more than ordinary interest, and has been, marked by the worst features of Toryism in the conduct of an election. It was claimed, to begin with, that it Was a Tory seat, and charged against the Liberals that they were putting the town to unnecessary expense, when as a matter of fact Councillor GREErTALL had never won, and never could have WOE, the seat as a Tory. He had been placed there by the allocation of the Commissioner on the re- division of the town, mach to the disgust of the electors, who had consequently given him marching orders. It was to avoid being pitched out in a Pitched battle that he was converted into an Alder- man. The Tories seem to have thought that, by Bending the hat round to cover Mr. WOODS' ex- Penses, they could not only induce that sanguine Young gentleman to go into the ring again, but Succeed, possibly, in frightening the Liberal alto- gether out of the field. But they mistook their man trying to intimidate Mr. PLUMPTON, the Liberal candidate, as they now know to their cost. The Tories have not had the opportunity of "yelling themselves black in the face," as Mr. WOODS said they would in case they won. It would have been a pretty picture no doubt; but it was not to be; for the Liberal candidate was returned by a majority of 83, and this in face of calumny and misrepresentation of the most persistent kind. The lies that have been told about Mr. PLUMPTON Would, as the phrase goes, "sink a ship;" and we would put it to "the party of gentlemen 1, whether, even if they had won, it would have been worth their while—not to yell themselves black in the face, but to show themselves black in their hearts. With all their petty trickery and gross mendacity, their candidate did not succeed in increasing the votes recorded in his favour by more than 48. Now, seeing that we'were told after their crushing defeat in November, that the disaster was entirely ow- ing to being short of workers, and the apathy generally of the Tories; and, that according to Mr. JOHN WHrrz, it was just the reverse on Monday,for .there was "no lack of enthusiastic Tory workers," conclusion is inevitable that they are in a hope- leee minority in the Ward. There can be no question that Mr.PLumeroN's majority would have bee, greater if, in order to hide the truth, his bills 1184 not been covered on Sunday night with lying Placards. The work was truly worthy of Church- me n and of the Sabbath! And how clever to print hese slanderous posters in red ink—as if they were us'lled by the Liberals! It was the same with the tere giving instructions how to vote for Mr. v ,°°Ds—they, too, were printed in the Liberal BOlOur. It is the plan of the cut-throat pirate on the _high seas to try to deceive the unwary, and tBLeize an advantage by hoisting false colours; but "8 punishment is death; and, if the Tories meet th their deserts, their piratical practices will lead 100. their political extinction. The tricks which failed on Monday will not be likely to be success- .:ll in November, if they are tried again; for -14iberal electors will be prepared for politicians who Will say anything and do anything to gain a mom- so-tt.— -- y advantage. Lying was certainly reduced to a fine art during the contest ; but, seeing that it ended in failure, it is like speaking of the devil as a gentleman for the chorus at the Conservative Club to describe the result as a "moral victory." They are welcome to such morals, and to such victories ; and it is our earnest hope that they will alwaysbe confined to the Tory party.

- A SCHOOL-MANAGERS and school_ Defective teachers in Warrington and the dis- Bill. trict are somewhat alarmed at the Possible effect of the new Education Bill, if passed in its present form. It is feared that if, as proNsed, fees have to be paid for children under five, the 1.64111 t will be that parents will keep them at home. they will not see the wisdom of paying for the "%tiger children when those who are older have Per head to pay. The proposed allowance of 10s. ',et. head is taken at 3d. per week for 40 weeks' attendance; but in this part of the country the acit.tendance is one of 47 or 45 weeks; and the ilference between the two represents a consider- able loss to the schools. Another element of loss arises from the fact that the 10s. pay- -1,4314 is upon the average attendance; while ths Zaalber of scholars on the books who pay regularly considerably larger than the average attend- Mr. FINNEY, head-master of St. Paurs estimates that the loss to their managers :aid be over £lOO per year. The loss would, B_6, believe, be in a similar proportion in other jounools in Warrington. The usual fee at St. Paul's _4(l. per week ; and under the present bill, with 'll,vv_ allowance of 3d. per head, the school-managers i:ald be in the uncomfortable position of requir- ag_g a id. fee, and at the same time having to face e, tiOUS loss. It is obvious that the bill will have to 3 he amended when it gats into Committee.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Runcorn Bridge is becoming unhappily famous, with two suicides w:thin two weeks. A report in another column gives details of the latest tragedy. It is stated that Molloy,who committed suicide on the 4th instant, was a St. Helens man, and that he was driven to despair through being out of work. General Booth's shelters and workshops would pro- vide for such cases, and thus lessen the sum of human misery.

Mr. Fred Dromgoole, manager of the "St. Helens newspaper," is proceeding with an assize action for assault ar.d battery against Councillm Massey; and it is rumoured that the councillor will respond by an action for libel. But is it not like putting the cart before the horse to fesort to fisticuffs and afterwards resort to law? How- ever, as Councillor Massey is a lawyer, he ought to know what is good for lawyers.

It is stated that Mr. Thomas Robinson who has for many years been connected with Messrs. Mackie and Co., Warrington, has intimated his intention to sever his connection with the firm, having entered into another engagement. He has had his cares of late; and
Care to our coffin adds a nail, no doubt, While every grin, so merry, draws one out. Let us hope that somebody in the future will see him grin.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, a man who gave the name of Thomas Jones was sent to jail for a month, for being at the Griffin Hotel for the purpose of committing a felony. Like "Jim Dalton, the burglar in the "Ticket-of-Leave Man," he carried his tools with him, for he was in possession of a jemmy, a screw-driver, and other useful appliances. It is thought he gave a false name--he was so anxious that his friends should not know he was in trouble. Indeed, if he could only conceal his identity, he felt, like the Tories of Whitecross Ward, that he •had gained." A moral victory." •

Sir Edward Watkin will begin to feel that he is being hard hit as a Railway King. His Channel Tunnel scheme has been for some years under pro- hibition, and now the proposed new railway to Lordon—an extension of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln—is knocked on the head. The rejec- tion of the Bill by the Parliamentary Committee is a surprise and a disappointment. Sir Edward will of course not let his projects drop entirely. He will try again; for he knows that his only difficulty is that he is in advance of his generation.

The Government have got their Education Bill before the House; but the Tnries don't like it. They dissemble their love, and they much wish to kick it downstairs, but they cannot, as ygt, see their way to that without kicking the Government at the same time. As to the Opposition, they feel that they have got the noses of the Tories to the grindstone on this particular job; and they mean to keep them there. If the articl is likely to !JO turned off, in the first instance' in rough state it can be" finished "hereafter in the Liberal work- shop.

It is stated that Mr. Rudyard Kipling is dying of consumption, and that he has been sent to Italy in the faint hope that the climate will have a beneficial effect upon the abscesses formed on his lungs. It is pitiful to be thus struck down when Fame and Wealth were becoming his handmaids. Can it be that his own condition is the origin of his principal story, "The Light that Failed"— the story of the struggling artist who went blind just when the public had discovered that a great painter was in their midst? The parallel is cer- tainly as striking as it is pathetic.

Mr. Chamberlain has been writing to the "Times" to point out that, in a leaflet which has been circulated in:Birmingham entitled IWhat the Liberals propose to do," there is nothing said about Home Rule. He lays the flattering unction to his soul that this means that Home Rule is dead. How blind he has become! What it really means is that the question is beyond argument. It is settled so far as the Liberals are concerned that the Irish must be given the management of their own affairs; and what has now to be considered is "What Liberals propose to dq." Joseph will per- haps have his eyes opened when the 'Liberals . are returned to power.

• The Court of appeal has dismissed the applica- tion for a new trial in the St. Barnabas school 1 case. It is held that the Vicar made a mistake in his minutes ; but that he was not guilty of fradd. Seeing, however, that according to the Master of the Boils" Mr. Proud was rightly elected, " it is a great hardship that he should have been put in the position of not having authority to act. Why should he suffer for the Vicar's mistake ? It is to be hoped, now that the defendants have justified themselves, that a subscription will be raised to assist them in meeting the heavy expenses to which they have been put in fighting a public battle.

In a case of pitch and tois, heard at the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, two magistrates entered a protest against imposing a penalty on the poorer classes, "so long as gambling was passed over in high circles." It certainly seems as if there were one law for the rich, and another for the poor ; and it is satisfactory to observe that public opinion is setting strongly against gambling. But magistrates need to Move cautiously; if they decline to impose pen- alties, they may encourage pitch and toss without affecting high-born sinners. And, besides, the law distinguishes between gaming in public and gaming in private, and it is the duty of magistrates to ad- minister the law as they find it.

A singular objection has been raised in connec- tion with a bill for the extension of the South Pier at Blackpool. It is against dancing in sight of the promenaders; and, at the instance of the Black- pool Corporation, the Select Committee have decided that there shall be no dancing on the pier within 160 yards of the promenade. It is not suggested that there has been anything wrong in the past ; and if people dance at all it can hardly be gainsaid that it is better to dance in the open air than in a crowded ball-room. Still, dancing is an offence to some people, and, as there will be plenty of room beyond the prescribed limit, the restriction has its merits in least dividing public opinion.

The Trades Council of Warrington, which was a very small organisation two or three years ago,has the elements of growth in it, as was shown by the demonstration held on Saturday. If working- men combine in the spirit shown by Mr. TroW, in his speech at the meeting, nothing but good can come of it. "He did not," he said, "wish to organise to rob anyone, but to prevent their em- ployers using force to them. He wished them to organize so that by argument and reason they would be able to secure justice." It was a grand
Hurrah, for the Whitecross Election! 'Twas a case of Radical lick Tory; Though the Tories lied themselves very "red,' And called it "a moral victory !".

The Government i'vere defeated on the Factory Bill, on Thursday night. Contrary to the policy supported at the Berlin Labour Conference, they resisted the proposal to raise the age of half-timers from 10 years of age to 11; and there was a majority of 16 against them. They ought to resign, but will they?

Parr's Banking Company has absorbed, by amalgamation, the London banking firm of Messrs. Fuller, Banbury, Nix, and Co., thus strengthening this large and prosperous institution, and widen- ing the area of its operations. But little change is made in the management, as will be seen from the particulars in another column, and Warrington still remains the centre of business.

At Newton on Saturday, and at Warrington on Tuesday, a considerable number of parents were fined for neglecting to send their children to school. As most of these cases are the result of an impoverished condition which makes it difficult at times to provide school fees, there will be a great reduction in this class of police court business as soon as Free Schools are established.

div.head: SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1891.
div.p: SATURDAY, JUNE 20, 1891.
THE CHESHIRE DAMSON CROP.
LOCAL NEWS.
VAGRANT/3 AT RUNCORN.
On Thursday Mr. J. Brundrit at Runcorn Police Court sentenced fiveyamps to 14 days' hard labour for sleeping out.
Sr. JOHN'S BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.
The members of this temperance organisation had their annual treat on Saturday, when they spent a pleasant day at Mersey View, Overton.
FIALTON WESLEYAN CHURCH.
The anniversary services in connection with the above church took place on Sunday, when the Rev. John Hornabrook, of the Liverpool circuit, preached morning and evening to large congregations.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.

The monthly meeting of the committee was held on Wednesday, Mr. Thomas Riley presiding. During the month 1,790 books had been issued in the lending depart- ment, and 18 books had been consulted in the reference departmont, A number of volumes had been pre- oented.
FREEMASONRY AT RUNCORN.

The annual meeting of the Ellesmere Lodge (No. 758) [ of Free and Accepted Masons was held in the Masonic Hall, Devonshire Square, on Thursday evening. Bro. James Littler, S.W., was elected W.M. for the ensuing year, and Bro. W. R. Wass, P.M., was re-elected trea- surer. Bro. Cooper, W.M., conducted the proceedings. BRUNMVICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The anniversary of this School will be celebrated in St. Paul's Chapel, to-morrow (Sunday). Established in 1880, it is the oldest school in the town and it also has the dis- tinction of being the largest in the town,and the anniver- sary is always a time of deep interest. The preacher will be the Rev. Luke Wisemann, 8.A., who is a powerful preacher, and a leader of the Forward Movement. He has established a successful mission in Birmingham, on the same'lines as Hugh Prices Hughes Mission in London ST. LUKE'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The anniversary of this school was celebrated on Sun- day when the Rev. Principal Holliday of Manchester preached morning and evening in Bethesda Congrega- tional Chapel. There was &large congregation at each service. In the afternoon the Rev. J. Pulford Williams (Presbyterian) delivered an address to parents and children in the schoolroom. Special music was rendered by the choir and scholars throughout the day. The collections in aid of the school funds realised a satisfac- factory amount, TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL HALTON. The anniversary of this School was celebrated in the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Halton, on Sunday. The preacher was the Rev. John Hornabrook, secretary of the Liverpool District. The weather was most favourable, consequently there was a good congregation in the after- noon, and an overflowing Congregation in the evening. On Monday evening the Rev. John Judson (resident minister) preached. The singing at each service was highly appreciated. The collection for the three services amounted to £3O is. DRUNKENNESS IN HALTON VILLAGE. —Edward West was charged at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, with being drunk and disorderly in Halton-road, on the 4th inst. He pleaded guilty. Superintendent Large, in reply to the Bench, said the prisoner had not been up since 1889. He was fined ss. and Bs. 6d. costs.—Philip Taylor and Samuel Finch were also charged with drunk- enness at Halton. P. C. Fryer said they were staggering about. A man named Wilson, who was in their ccmpany. came up afterwards to him (Fryer), and complained that he had been knocked down and kicked by one or both of the defendants. The case was adjourned to next Monday to enable defendants to produce witnesses on their behalf. A DRUNKEN WOMAN'S REVENGE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Harriet Riley, of no fixed abode, was charged with doing wilful damage to the windows of Waterloo Vaults to the extent of £8 ss. —Owen Lencham, manager of the _Vaults for Messrs.

Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd., stated that on Saturday evening, the prisoner, while in an intoxicated condition,. demanded to be served with drink, and he refused to serve her. As she would not leave the premises he put her out, and the prisoner smashed the glass panel of the door with her boot. She was given into the custody of P.S. Clarkson. She was committed to the-Quarter Sessions for trial.

Treacy, sea.; secretary, Mr. J. Treacy. MAIN OF BOWLS AT RUNCORN. •

A main of bowls was played on -t-Ce-Bridge Hotel Green, on Thursday afternoon. The green was in splen- did order. The prizes which were well worth winning consisted of the subscriptions, with £2 added by Mr. James Wood the proprietor. There were 52 entries and the several draws led to some close and exciting games being played. In the semi-final R. Wright met T. Woods and the game was witnessed with much interest. Woods winning by 11-10. In the same round Mr. Snape defeated T. Dean 11-9 and the final ended in Snape, who had played well throughout defeating Woods 11-4. The prizes were divided as follows :-Ist. W. Snape, 2nd, T Woods, 3 and 4R. Wright and T. Dean; other winner. T. Richardson, W. White, W. Rhodes, J. Forster, W. MY, and John Lewis. The main was one of the most successful ever held on the green.
THE RECENT RAILWAY FATALITY AT EARLES- TOWN.

As a consequence of the fatality to George Hol- croft, at the Vulcan Level crossing last week, the divisional engineer of the London and North-Western Railway, visited the spot on Tuesday, and made an inspection of the place, with a view no doubt of carrying out the recommendation of the jury to erect a bridge over the railway. INFLUENZA AT THE CREWE RAILWAY' WORKS. The influenza amongst London and North-Western employes at Crewe has assumed such an epidemic form that quite 10 per cent, of the workmen are away from their employment. Over 6,000 men are employed in Crewe works, and quite 600 are ill. Several deaths have resulted. So many are ill that the remainder of the railway employes are being obliged to work overtime in order to get the work through. The Great Western Railway Company have several hundred workmen- off through the epidemic, which is dislocating the railway service. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.--Gamixo. Warrington. —Advt.

James Cottam, of Boundary-road Bap- tist Chapel, St. Helens, has received a call from the Earlestown Baptists, and has signified his accept- ance of it. Formerly the Baptist congregation at Earlestown had to share a pastor with Park-road Chapel St. Helens, but they have now aecided to abolish that arrangement, and have a minister wholly to themselves, which cannot but be a wise departure. The rev, gentleman will be formally inducted to the Chapel some time in,July. THE RECENT SUDDEN DEATH AT EARLESTOWN. AN UNFOUSDED RUMOUR.. • A statement has this week gone the round of the papers that the body of the man, Charnley who was found dead in an outhouse of the New Market Inn, had been eaten by rats while lying in a a stable, the statement having originated at the meeting of the Guardians, on Wednesday. Mr. Jones, the under- taker, who placed the body in the coffin, has been interviewed, and he states there is not a word of truth in the statement, as there was not a scratch on any part of the body. THE *SUICIDE ON RUNCORN BRIDGE. The body of the man who committed suicide by throwing himself in front of a train on Runcorn Bridge has been identified by Elizabeth Molloy, of Glover-st., as her husband, John Molloy, a chemical labourer, who left St. Helens on the morning of the 4th inst. He had recently returned from America, but had been unable to obtain work. He was in bad health, and this and the fact that he could not find work made him low spirited. His wife had not up to now been able to make inquiries as to his whereabouts, as she was ill. SUMMER FAstiross now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.-Advt. FUNERAL OF AN El-POLICEMAN AT EARLESTOWN. On Wednesday, Thomas Stead who for 20 years was police constable at Croft, was accorded a police funeral at Earlestown. Stead was in the employ of Mr. Melling at the New Market Inn, and after a very short illness died on Sunday morning at the age of 60 years. Ile has been in the receipt of a pension since his retirement from the force. The hearse was accompanied by Police-Sergeant Long- worth and six constables, in uniform, who attended to pay a last tribute of respect to their departed colleague. The Coroner (Mr. Brighouse) said most decidedly they could move the body off the line, but they must not. take it out of the township. lie was not responsible for the idiotic idea that a person could not touch a body until a constable had seen it. On Sunday morning a man named Patrick Garvey, 60 years of age, who lodged at 116, Mercer-st., New- ton, was found dead by the bedside. Garvey has been in failing health for some time, and has been attended by Dr. iVatkins, chiefly for bronchitis. He was apparently in his usual state of health on Saturday, and in the evening transacted some business. When retiring to rest he complained of feeling unwell, but it wag not thought necessary to call in medical aid. On Sunday morning when James Churchill, who slept in the same roam,awoke, he found Garvey by the bedside, partly dressed, dead. D. Watkins has furnished a certificate, so that an inquest has not been _necessary.

VOLUNTEER OFFICERS' MESS AT NEWTON.

On Tuesday evening the officers of the tit-h-V.B. Kings' Liverpool Regiment, were entertained to dinner at The Willows, Newton, by Colonel McCorquodale, Hon. Col. of the Regiment. The brass and reed band attached to the Regiment was in attendance during the evening, under the leadership of Bandmaster Burke, aud played an excellent selection of music, which drew the highest encomiums from a considerable number of inhabi- tants, who enjoyed the pleasure of the musical treat. The members of the baud were entertained to tea at the Pied Bull Hotel, Mrs. Bond's cater- ing giving every satisfaction. The programme of music played by the band was as follows: March, "Britannia," Priests' War march, "Athalie," Ear' act.% " Rosamunde," raise, "Aphrodite," march, "Gipsies' Chorus" from "Preciosa," selec- tion, " Luisa Miller," valse, "Blume!' and Wiege," piccolo solo, "Ben Spatterings," galop, "The fox- hunters."

- At cpe PrvscQtretty Sessions on Tuesday, Robert Huston, a pig dealer, of Orinskirk, was charged with illegally moving six pigs without a license,and he was further charged with using a license for the purpose for which it was not granted. Evidence was called showing that the defendant removed six pigs from St. Helens market toKnowsley while he had only obtained a license for the removal of pigs to Ormskirk. —Mr. R. H. Glover. of Ormskirk, who defended, submitted that no offence was com- mitted, as the defendant held a license for the re- moval of pigs to Ormskirk, and he was entitled to take them round by Knowsley or any other way that he thought desirable. Police-Superinter.dent Barker pointed out that the form of license issued by the county authorities stated that the place to which the pigs were to be moved muss be specifically mentioned.—Mr. Glover said the statement on the license was not the law. Such a provision was not made on the Privy Council Order under which thd proceedings were taken.—The Bench upheld the contentions of Mr. Glover and dismissed the cases. WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COTTRIT. At this Court. on Tuesday morning, before Major Pickmere and M. Ziba Armitage, Mary McCabe Was charged with being drunk at Go'borne, on Monday last. Evidence was given in support of the charge, and the defendant was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. MRS. MAYERICK IN PRIbON. A correspondent states that Mrs. Maybrick was visited in prison on Thursday by her mother the Baroness Von Roque. Mrs. Maybrick's health' has much improved. She spoke gratefully of the con- sideration shown to her by the authorities, and was {very hopeful of establishing her innocence. SUDDEN DEATH AT NEWTON.

div.p: WIDNES WESLEYAN QUARTERLY.
MEETING.

On Monday these meetings .were held in the Lacy-street School. The local preachers met in the afternoon. There was a good gathering. All the usual questions relating to character, attention to appointments, etc., were satisfactorily answered. A resolution embodying the high appreciation of the per- sonal character and work of the late Mr. P. tilover was unanimously carried. The meeting regretted the removal of Mr. R. Bellis from the circuit. Mr. Geo. Bailey and Mr. John Travers passed an excellent examination in theology ond were unanimously received on full plan. Teawas pro- vided by Mr. and Mrs. Brown, of Brookfield, to whick a large number sat down. Tea over, the resolution of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Brown was proposed by Mr. Geo. Davies, seconded by Mr.Swale,and supported by Messrs. Robinson, Ormroyd, Duxbury, and the Rev. Jos. Nield, , whom everyone was glad to see.—The general meeting I was held after tea, when there was a large gathering at representatives from all parts of the circuit. The nume- rical report, read by the Rev. T. Law (chairman), showed that 29 persons haa been received into foil mem- bersihip during the quarter, but the unusually large number of removals and- deaths had more than balanced this number, consequently the report showed ' a decrease of one on the quarter. The financial report, read by the Steward, showed an increase on the quarter, but Was slightly below the expenditure. It was unanimously resolved to hold society meetings through the circuit, at which the circuit stewards should attend. A resolution of condolence with the family of the late Mr. P. Glover was unanimously passed.. As this was the last meeting at which the Rev. 'r. Law would attend previous to his removal to his new sphere, a hearty and unanimous vote of thanks was accorded him for his services daring his three years' residence in the circuit. Sanction was given to certain alterations to the chapel at Ditton.

Speakman who had arrived and taken the chair, thanked the members for their kind- ness in asking him to be president for another year. He felt honoured by the appointment and everything he could do to help forward the Runcorn club in the coming year he would do. As he had suggested some weeks ago' he thought they ought to commence next season by a first class entertainment in the Public Hall, and on that occa- sion they would have an event which would give pleasure to everyone. He wished the members of the team to emulate their ex-captain, and achieve the honours he had received, and he was sure would receive at the hands of the public of Runcorn. (Applause.) A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Speakman for his presence, and that gentleman having replied he took his departure. Mr. W. Carrol conducted the remainder of the business. It was resolved that members who had played for two seasons should be granted tickets at the same price as actite playing members. 1

provide a supply of water for the district and the con- tributory place in which the houses were situated; second, that the whole of the expense of the water supply ought to be charged upon the said district or contribu- tory place; third, that the supply proposed to be pro- vided net being for the solebenefit of one property owner but for several owners, should be a public one. The London and North-Western Railway Company, said Mr. Farrington, were quite willing to pay their share of the cost of providing the supply. The Authority could spend the sum of £lO4. Under the Public Health Act Mr. Linaker's objections must be submitted to the Local Government Board for their decision. The objections simply meant that the township should be charged a rate to provids water for a private individual's property, which he thought was outrageous. It was decided to. forward a copy of the objections to the Lond3n Board for their decision.—Mr. Farrington said the notices to the Ship Canal Company to provide a supply of water to their cottages at Preston Brook had expired, and al- though Mr. Collin had promised on the 16th May to let him know what they proposed to do, he had no since 'heard from them. The amount which the Aut7lority could expend in providing a supply was £ll2 13s. 4d., but he (Mr. Farrington) was of opinion that two wells could be sunk and two pumps fixed for half that amount. —Mr. Whitlow suggested that it would be a good thing for the property owners to get a supply of water from the Liverpool Water Company.—The Inspector was in- structed to communicate with the Ship Canal Company again.—The Inspector drew attention to the defective water supply to Yew Tree Farm, Norton, and he was in- structed to call the agent's(Mr.C. L.Evans's) attention to a letter sent by him in 1888 promising to have a supply from the Liverpool Water Company, when the Vywnry mains were laid.

THE EXAMINER,
A WARNING TO RUNCORN BUILDERS.

William Hall. builder and contractor, was Pum- melled before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, to answer a charge of having on the 9th inst. com- menced to build certain cottages in Grosvenor-st., without giving notice to the Board of Improvement Commissioners of his intention so to do, and with- out leaving at their office a detailed plan showing the position of the buildings contrary to the bve- laws.—The defendant pleaded guilty to a technical offence. He was further charged with having in respect to the same cottages failed to give two days notice to the surveyor of the Commissioners of the commence- ment of the work. The defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. F. A. Lake, law clerk to the Commissioners, prosecuted and called Kr. M. Barker, the surveyor, who said he visited the place on the 9th inst., and found that the defendant had been at work about a week. Next day the defendant sent in plans. He had received no notice flora the defendant of his intention to build.—The de- fendant said he was littildin,g the houses at his own risk. If the plans were wrong he would have to alter the houses according to the bye-laws. In Withies it was quito cus- tomary to commence work before the plans were sub- mitted or passed.—fr. Lake said builders must clearly understand that they could not commence buildings "at their own risk." As the second offence practically arose out of the first he should be satisfied with a penalty on the first and costs on the second offence. Mr. Brundrit said if these irregularities were permitted it was of no use having bye-laws. It might be done in Widnes, but he hoped it would never be allowed in Runcorn.—A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed in the first case, and an order to pay 4s. 6d. costs was made in the second ; total £2 3s. 6d.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presiding. Present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Edwards, Stokes, J. Baguley, Lewis, P. Hall, S. Taylor, T. Lea, Barter, J. Weir, J. W. Baguley, Hewitt, Wilkinson, W. Whitlow, J. Branclreth.—A letter was read from the Secretary of the Prudential Assurance Company with reference to a statement made at the last meeting that that Company had refused to pay the sum assured on the life of a man narn,Nl Roberts. He should be obliged if the members were informed that ' the assurance was not effected in the Prudential Corn- pany.—fhe Chairman said this was the case mentioned by Mr. Aaron; he was sorry he was not present. Perhaps the press would notice the denial.—The Clerk said lie had received notice from the clerk of the peace requesting the call to be paid on or before the 30th June. The call [ amounted to £3,292 10s.—Mr. Stokes: What was the I amount corresponding half-year last year P—The Clerk : £2,036.—Dr. Gastaldi : How much benefit have we de- rived ? (Laughter.)—Mr. Taylor : That is the question. —The Chairman : That is left to the fertility of your own imagination.—Mr. Taylor: What was the call for 1889 half year ?—The Clerk: £1,358 16s. 10d.—Mr. Brandreth : We are getting on.—Mr. Weir: It will be £4,000 in 1892.—Mr. Edwards: £4,500 according to the proportion.—Mr. Taylor said it was no use grumbling and asking questions after the money was paid. He did not know whether it would be out of place or whether the County Council would condescend to reply if they asked what was the reason for the increase. They had to find the money and it was only just they should know the why and the wherefore. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) He made a proposition to that effect.—Dr. Grastaldi seconded. Carried unanimously.
DEATH OF THE RECTOR OF HALEWOOD.

, The Rector of Halewood, the Rev. Charles James Robinson, M.A. (Christ Church College; Oxfotd), died on Tuesday morning at the Rectory. The de- cea:ed clergyman had been unwell for two years past, and under medical treatment. From time to time, however, his condition of health improved, although he was liable to uncertain attacks and internal paroxysms of excruciating pain, rendering him incapable of speech or action. In the hope of gaining strength, he spent some weeks at Buxton, and had only recently returned from Douglas, Isle of Man, where, together with his sis- ter, Mrs. Pearson, he sojourned six weeks, the parish being left under the charge of the Rev. T. B. Hardern, M.A., of Liverpool. Mr. Robinson was out visiting on Friday afternoon last, but was far from well on Saturday. On Sunday he was unable to take duty, the Rev. J. Roberts, curate of Wool- ton, officiating in his place. He was confined to his bed on Monday, but on Tuesday morning arose and break- fasted. Ten minutes afterwards he fell upon the bed- room floor and expired. This sad and unexpected event has thrown a gloom upon the whole parish and district, where deceased was much esteemed for his many ami- able and spiritual qualities. Mr. Robinson, who was unmarried, and was in his 43rd year, was ordained in 1874, by the Bishop of Chester. He held curacies at St. Anne's, Birkenhead.- and St. Matthias'. Liverpool, when in 1888. he was preferred to the Rectory of Halewood by the vicar of Childwall, patron of the living, which is of the value of £3OO a year with residence. The deceased was as enthusiastic member of the Church of England Purity Society, and took much interest in Sunday school work and the recreation of the young, pe pIC of hi parish. He was president of the cricket club, in which he formerly took an active part.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present Rev. Dean Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. R. H. Davies, Mr. S. Quinn, and Mr. G. Danby (clerk).
DISTRICT EDUCkTION.

The District EdiTL'ii-O; Committee reported that dur- ing May (three weeks) there were 115 applications for the payment nf school fees, which were recommended to be paid in 99 cases. 92 persons itppaarecl before the Committee for contravention of the E location Act ; 10 were prosecuted before the magistrates, 8 con- victed, and 2 sent to industrial schools.—The report was adopted.
LABOUR ChATIFICATES.

The School Management Com.nittee recommended that the Board join the Leeds and other school Boards in urging the Education Department to alter the Govern- ment Regulations with regard to the issue of labour cer- tificates and that the seal of the Board be affixed to a petition setting forth the views of the Board on the question.—Dean Finegan in moving the passing of the minnte, explained that many children who had passed the necessary standards were debarred from finding work on account of not being of age. The object of the petition was to remedy this state of things, and allow children who had passed the requisite standards to go to work at once.—The motion was carried unanimously. REPAIRS OF SCHOOL BUILDINGS. On the recommendation of the Sites and Building Committee the tenders of Messrs. Hindley and Co. for a new floor at the Shrun's Cross Infant School ; and of Mr. D. J. Brooks for providing and fixing curtains at the same school were accepted.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended the paymemt of accounts amounting to £793 Bs. The receipts for the month had been £787 is. 7d. Passed on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe. There was no other business of public interest.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Mr. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meet- ing held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse. *Present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Stokes, J. Bagu- ley, Lewis, Wilkinson, W. Whitlow, Edwards, P. Hall, Hewitt, J. W. Baguley, J. Weir, Baxter, J. Brandreth, J. Ashton (clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer),J. Farrington (nuisance inspector). WORKS OF WATER SUPPLY. The proper notices had been supplied upon the property owners. The cottages onthe Preston estate were to be demolished. Mr. C. E. div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

The Law Clerk said the first business was the election of Chairman. Mr. Speakman said he had great pleasure 1 in moving that Mr. Grice be Chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Once was one of the oldest residents in the town, and he felt sure that he would occupy the chair with the same dignity displayed by his predeceFsors,and conduct the business of the town with satisfaction to the Board and the ratepayers.—Mr. White seconded the motion which was carried unanimously. Mr. Once then took the chair amid applause. He thanked the members for the honour they had conferred upon him. It was quite unexpected by him, and as far as his fitness for the position was concerned he was rather sceptical, and thought the choice might have been a better one. At the same time he should be anxious and determined to carry out the duties with credit to himself and satisfac- tion to the Board and to the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) As a tradesman he had been actively engaged in busi- ness in the town for 47 years, and there was no member of that Board, nor of the community that had the in- terests and welfare of the town more at heart tivtn he had, and he should endeavour to discharge th.-2 duties with satisfaction to all. (Applause.)

div.head: THANKS TO MR. TAYLOR.
div.p: THANKS TO MR. TAYLOR.

Mr. Speakman proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Taylor for his services as chairman during the past year ; re- marking that he had had a most successful year of office.—Mr. Imison seconded the motion and remarked that the late chairman might fairly congratulate himself upon the exceptional success of his year of office.— Mr. Taylor had not confined his attention purely and simply to the business of the Board but he had recog- nised the obligations, which every chairman ought to recognise that the position entailed • responsi- bilities besides taking the chair at the mletings of the Board. During the year the aged persons treat had been revived, and, owing to the exceptional weather last winter, a relief fund was started in which Mr. Taylor took great interest. Again, the cottage hospital, which they hoped to bring to a satisfactory conclusion was indebted very much to the energy of Mr. Taylor for the success which they hoped would ultimately attend their efforts. Independently of that he had one oppor- tunity of distinguishing himself which was very excep- tional—the moral courage he displayed in giving his casting vote as chairman in favour of the adoption of the Technical Education Act; and future generations would thank Mr. Taylor for the part he had played. They hoped that whoever might succeed him, would follow his example, and that he might be spared 0 again occupy the position of Chairman. (Applause.) —The Chairman endorsed the sentiments expressed, and the vote was carried by acclamation.—Mr. Taylor thanked them very much for their kind expressions,and said he had endearourod to conduct the business with credit to himzelf and credit to the Board. The Chairman was of very little use unless he had the assistance of the members, and this had been accorded him on all occa- sions, and as a result contentious matters had all been settled to the satisfaction of the Board,and for the benefit of the town. (Applause.)

AN UNSTAMPRD YARD STIC/C.-Arthur John Loins. general dealer, Albert-road, was summoned for having an unstamped yard stick in his possession.—The defen- dant said he sent ten yard sticks to be stamped but this must have been overlooked.—A fine of ss. and costa was imposed.

SWINE FEVER.—Patrick Brehan, f Margaret-st., wag summoned for having neglected to notify the police of a case of swine fever that had occurred on his premises orta the 13th inst. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
PERMIT TO SELL.
At the Borough Police Court on Monday, George Sim- cock obtained a temporary authority to sell at a beer- house in Dallam-lane in lieu of Charlotte Rathcomb. BREACH OF THE WILD BIRDS PROTECTION ACT.

Alfred Tomkins, 9, Pitt-st., was charged at the War- rington Police Court yesterday with unlawfully having in his possession three young thrushes recently taken, contrary to the Wild Birds Protection Act, 1880.—Police- Sergeant Chandler deposed to finding the birds in the de- fendant's house on the 11th inst., and that 'two of them had since died, and said the defendant stated that his little boy had brought the birds in and he did net like to throw them away. The boy was called and said another lad had given him a nest containing the birds and he brought them home. The case was dismissed, his son being cautioned not to bring home young birds again.

div.head: THBFT FROM AN INN YARD.
div.p: THBFT FROM AN INN YARD.

Thomas Leatherbarrow, brush maker, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with stealing from the yard of the Bridge Inn, Warrington, on Friday afternoon, a shawl value ss. the property of Mrs. Hewitt of the Chetwode Arms, Whitley, Cheshire. Mrs. Hewitt had put up at the Inn, and left her shawl under the seat of her conveyance in the yard. On her being about to return home she missed the shawl. Detective Sergeant Monaghan was communicated with and he saw the pri- soner in Bridge-street carrying something bulky under his coat, and asked him what it was. He discovered it was the missing shawl, though the man said he had had it given to him in Bridge-st. The prisoner was commit- ted for trial to the sessions.

div.head: CRUELTY TO .A COW
div.p: CRUELTY TO .A COW

John Evans, butcher, of Lit chford, and John Turner, butcher, of the Market, were charged with cruelly treat- ing a cow by driving it while it was in an unfit state to 'walk, on the 11th inst.—Thomas Peet, butcher, Market- ' :St. the owner of the animal was charged with causing it to be ill-treated.—A constable and Inspector Dowty, N.S.P.C.A., proved the case. The cow was lame, and had a swo'len hip, and was panting and sweating and suffering es'es3ive pain. Turner was walking behind 'tapping it with a stick. Evans was not much to blame, o.s.he was merely wt king in front, having been sent to join Turner.—Mr. Dowty slid he had brought Turner up in case thereim'ght be a dispute as to who was in fault.— The Bench approvea of this course but dismissed Evans; and they fined Turner 23. 6d., and Peet 103. and costs. div.head: AGAIM.
div.p: AGAIM.

it the Police Court, yesterday, Samuel Riley, jun., 349, Winwick-road, was charged with deserting and re- fusing to maintain his wife, Mary Riley. She said they had only been married ten weeks since, but he turned her out of the house a month last Tuesday, with the as- sistance of two men in court, and would not provide her a home, except at his mother's. He had also thumped her on the arm, and he had played her false. He had Promised to bring her money,but had not done so.—The defendant stated that:she took sulks without provocation, and hid her things away, and went to her mother's, and would not come back. He had never struck her. He called a witness who deposed that the defendant's wife had left him, not he hr.---The Court advised the couple to withdraw into an adjoining room, and try to come to an understanding, and they did so, the complainant on her return sobbing bitterly. The defendant promised to provide her a home as soon as he could obtain a house, and he was discharged en this understanding.

div.head: DEN OF IMMORALITY.
div.p: A DEN OF IMMORALITY.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday Charlotte Pc' ighfield was charged with keeping lodgers at tier house Robinson's Yard, Fennell-st., on the 7th inst., it not be- ing registered as a lodging-house. Inspector Spinks said about 3 o'clock on Sunday morning week he visited the house, which consisted of two rooms, one down, and one up, and had only one bed in it, which was in the top room. Downstairs he found a single man and a tnarried woman, sleeping on the floor, and upstairs in the bed he found the defendant and a navy sleeping, and at the bottom of the bed, under some old rags, a woman and two children, aged nine years and seven months respectively. The house was very dirty and quite unfit for a ledgmg-house.—Mr. Norman, Inspector of Nuis- ances, said the house had no license and it was never in- tended to license such houses. It was not only a lodging- house, but, as the Bench had heard, a house of accom- modation too.—The defendant, who did not appear, having absconded, was fined 205., and costs, in default 14 days imprisonment.
A RUFFIAN IN THE MARKET PLACE. - COMPLAINT
AGAINST THE WEIGHING OFFICER,

At the Police Court on Tuesday, William Yates was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the Market Place on Monday night. A constable, Inspector Spinks, and Mr. Simpson proved the case against the prisoner. Se was drunk and using outrageous language, and it took five constables to get him to the bridewell, and they had to take his clogs off to prevent him kicking. In- spector Spinks had received complaints about his con- duct to girls in the Market Place.—Mr. Simpson said about five o'clock on Monday he saw the defendant in the Market Hall standing on the steps apparently about half drunk. Mr. Bailey, earthenware dealer, came to him and asked him why he had struck a little child on the head. He denied that he had, but used some vezy bad language, and said if he had he would serve Mr. Bailey the same. He immediately took his coat and cap off and rolled up his shirt sleeves, and began to use very nasty language to Mr. Bailey. Mr. Rawlinson, the weighing officer, looked on with indifference, and when the man insulted him turned away. Witness drew his attention to the man's conduct, but he did nothing. The prisoner used very nasty lan- guage to some little girls. When the constable came Yates was still conducting himself in a riotous anner, and attempted to strike the officer with a stick, also got on the ground and tried to kick him. If the market officer had taken some action the man would not have got to the pitch he did. The prisoner was sentenced to 21 days' imprisonment with hard labour, and Alderman Chandley said he would see that Mr. Raw- iinson was reported to the Market Committee.

THE CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A SERVANT. Agnes Lee, aged 16, was brought un on remand at the Warrington Police Court on Monday,charged with steal- ing from the dwelling-house of Themas Pilkington, con- tractor, 118, Bewsey-road, five towels, one pair of lady's boots, one pinafore, one piece of cloth, one silk necktie, and one silver brooch, value 30s. in all. She pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable repeated his former state- ment as to the prisorier, with some additional particu- lars. He stated that she had come from Southport with her aunt. Mrs. Arnold, and had been living with her in Chester-road, Warrington. All the articles had been re- covered except the brooch, which she denied taking. She had been sent to a Reformatory at 12 years of age and was there four years.—Mr. Pilkington, unsworn, identi- fied the artidlas produced, and stated that the defendant and her aunt had applied to his wife for a servant's place. for the girl, representing that she had never been in ser- vice which was false. His wife enraged her and a few days after on her return home after being out, found that the prisoner and the articles had disappeared.—Mr. Bunt said the prisoner had been in service at the Mar- quis of Granby, Church-st.—Mrs, Arnold, unsworn,said the prisoner had come back to her, stating that she had left Mr. Pilkington's. Then she went to service at a coffee-house.—Alderman Sutton told Mrs. Arnold she was almost as guilty as the prisoner for not giving her a true .character, and made herself liable to a severe penalty.—

Pressed as to what had become of the brooch, the Bench informing her that they would probably deal more leniently with her if she would, she said she saw it in the drawer, but did not touch it, and she adhered to this statement. She was fined 20s. and costs, in default 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

Alderman Sutton.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Edward Mannion, charged with being drunk and diEorderly in Bold-st., on Saturday afternoon and refusing to quit the Wool Pack Inn when requested to do so, was fined ss. including costs.— William Donovan, drunk and disorderly in the Market Place on Saturday night, 55., including costs.—James Griffin, a militiaman from St. Helens, in Viinwick-st., on Saturday night, 10s. and costs.—Hugh Ross, in Marsh House-lane, on Saturday night. The defendant was guilty of shamefully indecent conduct in front of houses. —Fned ss. and costs.—Robert Roscoe, drunk and disor- derly in Sankey-st., on Saturday-night, ss. including, costs.—Mary Coyne, 44th appearance, drunk and disor- derly in Buttermarket-st.' was discharged on promising to leave the town.—Eliza Smith, married woman, 48th appearance, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night. She had only just come out of jail. and begged hard to be let off, pro- mising to go to the Workhouse if discharged.—The Chief Constable stated that her husband had come over from America lately and "dressed her up," and she might have tone back with him, but would not.—The defendant said he had married another woman and had two children.— Mr. Hunt: He would not have done that if you would have gone with him.—The defendant: I never had the chance of going across the water or I would have gone.— Mr. Hunt: It is a pity there is not a permanent place for such women.—Alderman Sutton: There wants an in- stitution something like a lunatic asylum where they can be kept permanently and have to work hard too.—The defendant was discharged on promising to amend her con- duct and enter the Workhouse.—John Golding, drunk and disorderly, in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, 55., including costs.—Mary Owen, widow, in Robinson's Yard, off Fennell-st., 10s. and costs.—The defendant said she would not pay, and Alderman Harrison said he hoped she would not: it would be better for her.—Annie Hines, in Mersey-st., on the 10th inst.. 53. and costs.—John Tickell, in Back Church Place, on the 7th inst., 103. and costs. Ellison, Joseph Jackson, Isaac Dakin, Wm. Hassell, and Wm. Savage,were charged with playing at pitch and toss, on Sunday, the 7th inst.—Each of them, except Ellison, who could not be clearly identified, was fined ss.
TIIESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman), and
Alderman Harrison:

DRUNK.—Catherine Smith was charged with being drunk in Orford-street, the previous night, also with absconding with clothing belonging to the Warrington Guardians. Mr. B. Shearer prosecuted. He said the prisoner was allowed to leave the Workhouse on Sunday, in Union clothes, and got drunk and did not come back. She was sent to jail for seven days' hard labour.—Bridget Murphy, drunk in Bridge-street, on Monday night, ss. and costs. —AI fred Levitt, a young man, and Mary Clarke an elderly woman were charged with being drunk on Monday night, in Manchester-road. They had been guilty of most indecent conduct together in the cemetery. They were fined ss. and costs each. Moms DELAY. —At this point there was about five minutes' delay in consequence of there beinc, only one magistrate, Alderman Chandley, on the bench", and it being necessary to have another, but the arrival of Alderman Harrison enabled the business to be pro- ceeded with. After some cases had been dealt with which are reported in another column the following were dis- posed of : NON-ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOL—John Mullins, labourer, Bewsev-road, 10s. ; James Mosely, wire drawer, Lovely- lane, Frederick Pritchard, tanner, Cartwright-st., Wm. Spencer, news agent, Mersey-st., Thomas tate, a Sal- vationist, Old Road, Edward Whitehouse, forgeman, Queen-st., ss. each. In the case of Moses Williams, forgeman, Pierpoint-st., Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, mentioned incidentally, that he had found the defendant's house in a most filthy state. there being ex- crement in each corner. Mrs. Williams denied this, and said she was washing at the time, but the place had been like a palace before. The defendant was fined 55., Alderman Harrison remarking that Mrs. Williams must be a disgraceful woman.—Thos. Bate, milkseller, Long- ford-st„ Joseph Gerrard, bricksetter, Hopwood-st., John Gorton, news agent, Latchford, 5,5. each. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fairclough and Alder- man Chandley.

MitrrAnv OFFENCES.—MichaeI .Hunt was charged on his own confession with being a deserter on May Ist from the 2nd West Riding regiment stationed at Newcastle, Jamaica. He was remanded to Strangeways jail to await an escort.—John Cos was charged with making a false answer in attestation on applying for enlistment in tne 3rd Lancashire militia, by stating that he had not served in the army before, he having been in it 12 years. He had tried to enter two other militia regiments. He was fined £5, in default a month's hard labour. DEVNE AND DISOEDERLY.—MichaeI Murray, drunk and disorderly in Lilford-st.. and Clara Ford, a stranger to the town, who called herself a dressmaker, drunk and disorderly early that morning she having been guilty of indecent conduct, were each fined ss. including costs; in default seven days' imprisonment. - - -

- . THURSDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (Chairman), Alder- man Sutton, and Mr. E. M. Crosfield. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Dagr,nall, glassmaker, was charged with not appearing on April 6th to a sum- mons charging him with being drunk and disorderly on the 30th of March. He had surrendered that morning. He was ordered to pay the costs, Bs. ed.
FRlDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (chairman) Alderman

Harrison and Mr. White. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—George Boyle, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Pierpoint-st. the pre- vious night and doing wilful damage to the plate glass window in the off-licensed house of Sarah McCoyne. Mrs. McCoyne appeared and said the prisoner had broken the window but done it accidentally while drunk.—The deputy-magistrates' clerk: Then you will have to put him in the County Court for it.—Alderman Harrison: I am afraid if he did not do it wilfully you would have a difficulty in succeeding there.—He was fined ss. for being drunk and disorderly, and the Chairman said he ought to pay the amount of the damage 4s. The prisoner said he was willing to do so, but had no money then.—John Cairns, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Cross- ley-st.,on Thursday night,and also with assaulting Thos. Taylor, his father-in-law, with whom he 'lived.—P.o Anson said the prisoner was creating a disturbance, and he requested him to leave, but he continued to use bad language and on Taylor coming up, violently as- saulted him.—The prisoner's wife appeared and asked for a separation. He had been working nine weeks, she said, and only brought 245. home during the time. He would not work generally. Taylor lived at their house, and supported them all.—The prisoner : He lodges with me. I pay the rent.—The prisoner was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour. ABSENCE FROMWORK.—MMargretaret Mannion was charged was charged with absenting herself since May 14th from the service of Messrs. J. and J. Wilkinson, fustian cntters without lawful excuse. She was ordered to return to work, and pay the damage and costs, and a is. a week NON-MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN.—BeDjaMin Matthew, was charged with not contributing to the maintenance of his son onboard the Clio, was ordered to pay is. per week.—John Lee, charged with not contributing to the maintenance of his daughter in St. Elizabeth's Industrial School ordered to pay is. per week.—Edward Crutchley was charged with not contributing to the maintenance of his daughter in a reformatory school at Liverpool. The girl is the extraordinary young adventuress who was recently convicted of stealing £5O from her father's house. CHARGE OF DAMAGING HAY GRASS.—Michael Sex- ton,John Stafford, and James Finnegan, were charged with doing wilful and malicious damage, on the 14th inst, to hay grass, in a field belonging to Edward Lunt, behind the Cemetery. Mr. A. Browne appeased for the defence. Evidence was given as to their being seen in the field, one of the witnesses Joseph Beckley said they were tack- ing about the field as though they were looking for birds nest.—Mr. A. Browne said his clients were sent by Mr. Hill the owner of the adjoining field to see whether his horse was all right there. They did not know the neigh- bourhood and got into Mr. Lunt's field by mistake.— Wm . Walker, foreman at Messrs. Cunliffe's tannery, said the defendants kept to the track across the field and did no damage. He knew that Mr. Hill had a horse in the field adjoining.—The Chairman said Mr. White was the agent for the property and therefore would not advise in that case. The defendants were convicted and ordered to pay the cests. NON-PAYMENT OF RENT.—The adjourned case of Wm. Tolley, canal labourer, charged by Robert Lowe, estate agent, with removing his goods to avoid payment of 18s. 3d. rent was called on. ' The defendant did not appear, but Mr. Lowe said the man's wife had paid 103., and as she promised to pay the balance. the case was ad- journed for another four weeks to allow her to do so.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Captain Withington (chairman), • and Major Pickmere DRUNICI CHARGE OF A HORSIC.—JaIIIeS Grimshaw, of Bedford, for being drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Croft, on the 31st ult., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. A 'MANURE NIIISANCE.—Isaac Ashcroft, farmer, was summoned for not obeying an order to abate a nuisance cansed by his leaving a large quantity of manure on one of his fields, near the highway at Orford. Mr. Kerfoot, inspector of nuisances for the Warrington Rural Sanit- ary Authority, said the order was made on the 6th inst., and the defendant had since attempted to remedy the nuisance by covering the manure with straw, but that was not sufficient ; and he asked the magistrates to make

an order for the removal of the manure.—The Bench ordered the defendant to remove it within a month. NON-MAINTIINANCE OF A WIFE.—John Peak was charged with not obeying an order made in September, 1882, to contribute 6s. per week for the maintenance of his wife. The defendant's arrears amounted to £132 135., but the prosecutrix did not ask for payment of any lame amount of arrears. The case was adjourned for a month to allow the defeddant an opportunity of paying two months' arrears, and 6s. a week during the interval. . JUVENILE TRESPASSERS.—Three Sankey youths named William Burgess, George Webb, and Thomas Clark, were charged with trespassing on the 7th inst., on land in the occupation of William Burdon,farmer, and doing damage, to the amount of 35., to a crop of clover.—They were or- dered to pay the damage (Is. each), and Cogs. DRUNK.—Michael Scather, drunk at Croft, on the 31st ult., was fined 53. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Mary Gleave, drunk and disorderly at Warrington, on the 31st ult., was ordered to pay the costs.

The closure was now applied, and after the brief interval Warrington took up the defence at 5.40, Briggs and Hall bowling. The start was disastrous, for only a single had been credited to each batsman, when J. J. in playing back to Briggs, played one hard on to his wicket. With Lee in runs came freely, and at 28 Gunn relieved Hall. The Change worked immediately, for the visiting captain was caught at the wicket with the former's fourth ball, two wickets being down for 28. On Smith joining Lee a useful stand was made, Lee coming in for special notice with his fine drives. At 39, Gunn superceded Hodgkinson, and in his third over got Smith caught at point. With only an addition of two runs, Captain Manson was sent back, but on Clarke joining Lee, the issue was soon beyond doubt. Changes were made in the attack, but to no purpose, and Lee punished the bowling severely, and on the stroke of tithe he completed his 50, which was com- piled by excellent cricket, made up of eleven threes, four twds, and nine singles. The fieldine of Warrington was very Smart, and all round the afternoon's cricket was thoroughly enjoyable. Score :

WARRINGTON V. WERNETH (2ND TEAms).—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. The visitors were fortunate in winning the toss,the wickets being in perfect orderiand shortly after commencing their innings a driz- zling rain further handicapped the bowlers,but Unsworth and Dutton bowled so well that seven wickets were down for 46 runs. Dixon and Turner, however, com- pletely altered the state of affairs, and caused numerous changes of bowling, and not until Smith resumed at his I first end were these batsmen parted,the pair having tak- en the score to 82, Smith quickly finished off the remain- ing batsmen, the total reaching 89. The home team started badly, Adamson being well caught with only one run notched, and Collin was shortly afterwards taken by the same fielder at 26. Jolley played on, and Dun- bobbin failing to score, four wickets were down for 31. Howard and Unswerth played up well, and tcok the score to 60 for the fifth wicket, at which number three more batsmen fell to the underhand bowler. Bibby and Howard played carefully just when the match was going in favour of the visitors, arid were frequently cheered by the spectators as the score slowly rose until the match was won. Two runs later W. Howard was well taken in the long field, the last wicket just raising the total to I 00„ this being the seventh win for the second team, one match being a draw. Score :

WARRINGTON' v. WERNETIL—The return match between these clubs took place at Werneth on Saturday. Only a fortnight had elapsed since the first match was brought to an issue, but the final result then arrived at, when Werneth won by 137 runs to 39, was not at all relished by the home supporters. To show that the verdict was wrong, Warrington made, the journey on Saturday fully bent on reversing the state ?f affairs, and although they lacked the services of Captain Adam, a capital team was placed on the field. Mr. S. M. Crosfield" for Warrington and Briggs for Werneth had both made the journey from Lord's, where They had been assisting Lancashire in the match against Middlesex. On a true wicket Werneth started the defenceNvith Briggs and T. Clegg. Smith and Harrison sharing the attack. .The professional was in a merry mood, and paying particular attention to 'Harri- son, runs came freely. At 37 J. J. Crosfield and Captain Manson took up the bowling, and in the former's third over Briggs skied one to Smith, his 36 having been made in half-an-hour. Hall,.who has a local reputation of being a hard hitter, had a singular career, as after he had been missed c and b, he had a life at cover point, and was then bowled middle stump by Captain Manson. Clegg continued to bat well, an.d now hit out more freely, bringing Harrison on again at 83. Hag,gas was soon disposed of by a smart catch by ' Lee, but Captain Hatch and Clegg played the bowling with ease and rain coming on, these two were in possession when the teams retired. A. fter 45 minutes' absence play was again resumed, and in Manson's third over Hatch got his leg in front of a straight one. Lowe made matters lively, and having had a life had more confidence. With his score at 40 and the total 117, Clegg was bowled by a good ball from Manson. Woodhouse was soon dis.

MEETING OF LABOUR COMNISSION,ERS.

The Labour Commission met for th 3 first time in pub- lic on Wednesday. Lord Derby presided in Group B Agricultdre andTrainsport. The first witness was Mr. Brain, for the dock labourers. fiestated that in the busiest season of the tea industry about 3,503 men were employed, but only about 500 permanently. He depre- cated strikes, and advocated a State Board of Concilia- tion. Mr. T. M. M'Carthy' Decker's Union, said the scarcity of work was owing to shipc4nerS pandering to insane compstition. The uraon,iavoured forty-eight hours work a week, municipalwarkshops, and tha pre- vention of foreign pauper immigration. On Thursday Mr. Frank Friare, recalled, gave evidence as to the grievances of the Thillingsgate fish porters. Mr. Atkins, another man empinyed in the London docks, gave evidence in favour ate. State Board of Arbitration, and the voluntary eight hours day. He said the great trouble at the docks present arose fTom the excessive number of men seekitg employment. div.head: ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MURDER AT
div.p: ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MURDER AT

WIGAN. Early on Sunday morning an attempt at murder took place at Wigan. About four o'clock Police-Constable Hague was on duty in Scholes,when hewas informed by a boy named Joseph Kerfoot, that his mother and a man had been attacked by Edward Kelly. The constable proceeded to Kerfoot's house, which is situated in Mit- chinson's-yard.and entering a bedroom.a shocking scene presented itself. The ceiling and windows were be- spattered with blood. In the room'were Matthew Webs- ter and Ellen Kerfoot, the boy's mother, and both were bleeding from wounds hi the head: Kelly, who is a puddler, had been staying in the house, and entering the room had made a savage attack upcn Mrs. Kerfoot and Webster with a hatchet. Whilst committing the deed Kelly spid to another man who was-also sleeping, in the room, " I am not beawn to touch thee,, but I have kilt the other-2' In the confusion which ensued, Kelly made his eicape. Webster is sufft.ring from a fractured skull and also a serious wound .on the side of the left temple, and it is doubtful whether he will recover. The woman is not seriously injured. The police attribute the motive of the crime to jealousy,.

div.head: ARREST OF 'KELLY.
div.p: ARREST OF 'KELLY.

The Wigan police on Wednesday received telephonic intimation that the man KeUy, .had been apprehended at Tunstall, in Staffordshire. Superintendent O'Brien, of the detective department, was sent for the prisoner, and arrived at. Wigan on Wednesday evening. The injured man still lies in a dangerous condition.. He passed a fair night.

div.head: PRISONER TN. THE DOCK.
div.p: PRISONER TN. THE DOCK.

At the Wigan Borough Mice Cenrt, on Thursday morning, Edward Kelly was brought up in custody in connection. with the Wigan outrage. The Court wls crowded with spectators anxious to have a glimpse at the prisoner. Superintendent! O'Brien stated that from in- formation received from the Staffordshire police, on Wei- nesday, be went to Tunstall. He there charged the pri- soner with attempting to murrler Michael Webster and Ellen Kerfoot on the morning or, the /4th inst. In replY prisoner said, "Yes, that is right enough; I can't deny what I have done. I struck then) both when they we •0 in bed altogether." When asked if he had any objecti,n to make. against the,application for a remand by the Chief Constable, prisoner said he had no objection. Kelly is a powerful, well-built man, and does not appear to realise the gravity of his position. The injured people still continue to improve.

_tirtie Paris " Figaro " states that an influential meeting Imperialist party was held on Wednesday, at the ntlidetice of Prince Victor in Brussels, and tha. import- resolutions were adopted, in regard to which abso- vne secrecy is observed. It is added that nothing is to i)iti.revealed until the Empress Eugenie, Prince Louis, and 411119 ens Letitia have left France, Prince Victor being • Filling that they should be disturbed during their 'visit to Paris.
TRE TRIAL OF THE MANIPUR REGENT.

SENTENCE OF DEATH. , The trial of the Juhraj is concluded. The Prince was '°Und guilty on the first and senond counth of the in- dictnaent, in which he was charged with waging war against the Empress of India, and with aiding and abet- ag the massacre of British officers; but he was ac- quitted on the third count,in which he was charged with Inurder. He was condemned to be hanged,the sentence being, hcwever, subject to confirmation by the Govern- tient of India.

THE HOURS OF EARLESTOWN ENGINEERS.

Sir,—l have been instructed to inform you "That all engineering establishments in Earlestown and Newton- le-Willows have granted the 53 hours, and commenced working the same this week." You are at liberty to publish the above fact. Yours truly, D. WILLIAMS, secretary. Amalgamated Society of Engineers. .240 Earle-q., Earlestown, June 17, 1891.

THE AUTION OF MESSRS. BATTERSBY AND POTTER REPUDIATED. Sir,—l wish you kindly to state in your next issue,that the action taken by Messrs. Potter and Battersby, at the recent election, was upon their own individual responsi- bility, and not by the sanction of our society, and that no party whatever had any authority from us to use our name for political purposes, for we do not recognise any party save that of Trades Unionism.—Yours &c., J. POMFREY, President, Warrington Ftlesmiths', Trades Union. Green-lane Cottages, Padgate, June 16.
"IMMORAL DEFEAT " IN WHITECROSS
WARD.

Sir,—All true lovers of fair play will rejoice at the tory rout in Whitecross Ward last Monday. I very heartily congratulate Mr. Councillor Plumpton on the Victory, and I think he will make a very useful member `of the Corporation. 1 have known him for the last 20 years and can truthfully declare (in face of the scandal- OW; statement by the other side) that he is worthy of the proud position in which the electors of Whitecross Ward have placed him. I see the other side claim the result as a "moral victory" to them. I fail to see where the "moral vic- tory" comes in, when we have returned a Liberal instead of a Tory who held the seat before. In my opinion (and I may say the opinion of honest Conservatives) it is an "immoral defeat." _ _

I might go into the scurrilous things said about Mr. Plumpton, but that will be dealt with by abler hands than mine. There will be a great reaction in favour of the Liberal candidate next November when I feel sure his majority will be largely increased. I think, under the circumstances, he polled well. It is all very well for a Councillor to say that 80 votes had been coerced. I suppose if Mr. Plumpton's majority had been 200 the same gentleman would have had the audacity to say that that number had been coerced likewise. The question is can he prove it? We know all the " artillery "of the Tory party was at work, and those who have had to do with elections know what that means.—Yours gtc.,
"FAIR PLAY."
WARRINGTON Y.31.C.A.

Sir,—Now the Association is moving to larger pre- mises at Friars Green, it is much to be regretted to hear the decision of the Committee that no further Sunday evening Mission services are to be held, when such work has been so beneficial to the numerous congregations which have attended. The Associations' lively enthu- siasm for cricket, football, lawn-tennis, &c., and the evi- dent lukewarmness which it has displayed in regard to its spiritual welfare appears to me somewhat remark- able.

Surely it is high time to speak out, and with no "uncertain sound "when the Committee cut short such a soul-inspiring work. Their efforts should not be to prevent such work, but rather increase the facilities for holding evangelistic services for those young men who do not often come within the pale of the gospel light. If they do not reverse thrir decision and allow these mis- sion services to be continued they will, I think, in the estimation of any right-minded person,be perpetrating a serious wrong. When I brought the subject before the Committee at their last monthly meet in fr,, I regret to say there was none to support me; and if Liverpool and Manchester Christian Associations are doing the work I am now alvocating why should not we? Most assuredly, the first considera- tion should be the spiritual welfare of young men, but with the Warrington Association it seems to be the last. If the Association is to resolve itself into a social club, then it should adopt an appropriate title: 1, however, hope the matter will have their recon- sideration with a favourable result.—l am, sir, yours faithfully,
JOHN ED. HlsLor. 79, Manchester-road, Warrington, June 18th, 1891.
WHITECROSS WARD ELECTION;

Sir,—Would you kindly allow me space in your next issue to ask Mr. William Potter, secretary of the File- smiths' Union, how long the Society has been converted into a machine for political purposes? I think, Sir, the result of the municipal election in the Whitecross Ward has clearly shown that the Tory party have just got their deserts for resorting to such tactics, mainly brought about by the above-named Secretary and Mr. James Battershy. Both of them love unity very much, as I can show. A few months ago some file shops that they call illegal, where there are 50 men working, caused a deputation to wait on Mr. Potter to ask if they could be admitted in the Society by paying £l2 down,and pay for two years before they had any benefit in any shape or form. They were told point blank, "No." There is some unity about that!

I hope, sir, the next time they send anyone to repre- sent the file trade on the Trades Council the two mentioned will authorise the representative to throw off the cloak of darkness, and tell the members of the Council that they have changed the name from the Filestniths' Union into a Political, Sick, and Burial Society. The more ; look at the letters that passed between Potter and Bat- tersby trying to vilify a respectable man like Councillor Plumpton, the more they convince me that both men must have got " intoxicated with the exuberance of their own verbosity." Mr. Battersby, according to one of his speeches at the meeting where they selected the Tory candidate, said he was heart and soul for Trades Union- ism. But at this present time he works at his trade, and also occupies a position at the Post Office. This clearly shows that he would do all the work in Warrington if he could, and I believe he would not care who suffered by it. Thanking you in anticipation for insertion of this letter, I am yours &c. ONE WHO WORKS AT THE TRADE.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE WATER • IN AT LAST
SCENE AT EASTEIAM YESTERDAY MORNING.

Yesterday morning at high water the great gates of the Manchester Ship Canal at Eastham, facing the river Mersey, were opened, being worked by hydraulic power. The great flood ot water caused by the rising tide flowed in, and in a very short time there was 12 feet of water in that part of the canal known ai the Eastham section, which has been constructed and finished between Eastham and Ellesmere Port.

This event has been looked forward to with great interest by the engineers connected with the canal, the Board of Directors. the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, scientific men, and the public generally. It was intended to have opened the gate at Eastham last Monday, but the work would not allow of this being done; but it was satisfac- torily carried out yesterday in the presence of a large number of spectators. When the gate opened and the section filled with water there was a cheer and cries of " Water in the Ship Canal at last." The tide yesterday was about 16 feet on the Mersey, and next week the spring tide will be about 17 feet at Eastham, and hence the water that will then be in the Eastham section of the canal will be of greater depth than it was yesterday.

div.head: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS IN THE BILL.

Sir J. Pease has also given notice of niotion to in- crease the number of Corporation directors from five to eight and to remove the restriction that they shall be members of the Council.
