div.head: RUNCORN BRIDGE MYSTERY.
div.p: A RUNCORN BRIDGE MYSTERY.
A FEAFFUL FALL.

About four o;C-lOCI, on Wednesday morning, a labourer, named Leonard Jackson, found the body of a man lying en his back on a sandbank inside the concrete wall of the Ship Canal and under the shadow of Runcorn Bridge. He was quite dead. Information was at once conveyed to the police and the body was removed to the mortuary. it was afterwards identified as that of William Kay.ft ship- wright, who had lived in Penketh-lane. Whether the man jumped from the Bridge with the idea of committing self-destruction, or accidentally fen over, when viewing the Sl.ip Canal works, or was thrown over is a question involved in mystery. The following evidence was adduced. THE INQUEST

was held by Mr. Worsley, on Thursday morning.— T. Kay,of 27 Scotland-st.,identified the body as that of his brother. He last saw the deceased on Tuesday night between eight and half-past in the Commercial Hotel, Runcorn. He was alone. He was 29 years of age. He had given la ay lately to drink and had done no work for a week—Leonard Jackson, deposed to finding the body, and William Owen, ticket collector at the Runcorn end of the bridge said he issued the return ticket number 31211 found upon the deceased on Tueslay night. Tie had no recollection of the purchaser.—P.S. Gosling described the manner in which the body was lying on the sand, and said in his pockets was 16s. Bd., a pocket book and a reel ot twine used by deceased in his trade. le had evidently been smoking because his pipe was lying besides him. His clothes were not dis- ordered. Deceased was a most quiet inoffensive , man. There was no marks of a struggle on the bridge nor a scratch on the rail to show where he had gone over. The fall would be 80 to 90 feet.— Dr. McDougall, who had made a post-mortem exam- ination, said he attributed the cause of death to laceration of the brain. There was nofracture of any bone except the lower jaw. Deceased had fallen on the right side and his injuries had been caused by a fall.—The Coroner in summing up, said there was no evidence to show how deceased came to his death. It he had been assaulted with a view to robbery his pockets would have been rifled. The safest verdict would be " found dead," and then it would he left open for the police to take advantage of any clue they might get. The verdict suggested was returned.
It has been decided to establish a National Assembly of the Knights of Labour for Great Britain. The central offices will probably be at Birmingham.

div.head: EXAMINER, SAT URDA 1, JUNE '2O, 1891
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDA 1, JUNE '2O, 1891
MRS. LANGTRY.

Mrs: Langtry is the daughter of the Rev. W. C. Le Bret, Dean of Jersey—hence the name of "Jersey Lily," by which she is sometimes spoken of. She was born in the year 1852. She married Mr. Langtry in 1874, and soon became one of ,he chief attractions of Lon- don society. Her success at amateur theatrical perform- ances subsequently induced her to adopt the stage as a

profession. Her first public appearance was at the Hay- market Theatre on December 15th, 1881, when she took the part of Miss llardcastle in " She Stoops to Conquer." Besides playing in Lon- don Mrs. Langtry has starred the provinces, and engaged in a tour in America, where she now chiefly resides. With regard to her experi- ence in the United States it is related that on one occasion she displayed remarkable courage. She was riding in a close conveyance through a place in the Yosernete Valley, when the carriage was assailed with stones by a crowd of the citizens, who exclaimed that they "didn't want no foreign- ers" to compete with their local theatrical stars. All her servants fled, but she opened the carriage door and faced the furious mob, demanding what they wanted. They would make no reply except by yells and groans. She advised them all to go home, and a prominent ruffian promised that they would if she would stand them a drink. She de- clined, asserting that they had had too much al- ready, and imperatively told them to go home. They mechanically obeyed her. This was the only instance in whieli she experienced such a rough re- ception in the Far West. Mrs. Langtry has a fine presence and a clear musical voice, and of late the Press has commented on an improvement in her acting.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS SCHOOL CASE.
div.p: ST. BARNABAS SCHOOL CASE.

APPEAL DISMISSED. "MR. PROUD RIGHTLY ELECTED." The case of Parsons v. Tomlinson came on for hearing before the Court of Appeal on Wednesday. It was an application by the defendant for judg- ment or a new trial on the ground that the consent by which the action was settled was given under a mistake of fact. Mr. Bigham, Q C., who appeared for the appellant said that there were two actions, one by a schoolmistress at St. Barnabas School,War- rington, the other by the schoolmaster for damage for assault. The damage was admitted to be nominal. The defendants were the school management of the Church of St. Barnabas. Five actions were originally brought against different members of the commit- tee,but only two were tried. There were seven mem- bers in the committee. These gentlemen went one morning to the school and told the plaintiff in the action, the schoolmistress, that she must leave. She said she would not go until she was compelled to do so. A hand was laid upon her, when she left and subsequently brought her action. The whole ques- tion in the case was whether the gentlemen who acted thus were members of the committee. The matter really resolved itself into a dispute between the vicar of tile parish and the members of the com- mittee, the vicar supporting the schoolmistress. In support of the plaintiff's case, the vicar was called, and he produced a minute book which he said re- corded what took place at the meetings of the school ' committee. Counsel stated that the contest in the case was whether this book was genuine or not.. Under the date of the 23rd of May, 1889, an entry appeared in the book to the effect that in conse- quence of the illness of one of the members no busi- ness was to be done on that occasion. At this time the committee consisted of the Vicar. Mr. Smith and Mr. Parr,the Churchwardens,Mr. Pierpoint, and Mr. A. G. Allton, the son of the vicar, a young man of 20. There had been disputes between the vicar and some of these gentlemen, and, according to the evidence ot a Mr. Proud, the vicar had asked him if would be willing in the event of the resigna- tion of his son to take his place in the com- mittee. He expressed his willingness to do so. This was in April 1889. The above-mentioned meet- took place on 23rd May, 1889, and according to the evidence of the churchwardens young Mr..Allton ' resigned and Mr. Proud was elected. The Vicar said in his evidence that it was not true that his son resigned and that Mr. Proud was elected, and produced the minute book in support of this asser- tion, showing that in consequence of the absence of Mr. Pierpoint no business would be done. He said that what passed with regard to his son's retirement was this : He saw his son coming out of the vestry and told him he need not come in, as there was nothing to do, whereupon his son retired. The next meeting took place on the Ist June, 1889, and on this occasion the Vicar said there had been some talk about making Mr. Proud the treasurer. The minutes were read, and the meeting was of opinion that it was not made sufficiently clear that Mr. A. G. Allton had resigned, and that Mr. Proud had been elected, and they insisted on an alteration being made. It Was suggested at the trial that the leaf had been torn out of the minute book, and in order to estab- lish this fact an expert was called,who said although several leaves had been torn out one had not been taken from the place referred to. Mr. Bigliam stated that when he heard this he withdrew the charge that he he had made against the Vicar, and consented to accept a nominal judgment for 40s. He was asked for a new trial on the ground that since that time thay had obtained some evidence which strengthened their belief that the book had beell tamnered with. This evidence was from Mr.P.Davies, a solicitor, with whom the Vicar had had some deal- ings, but with whom be bad Aftfillyuds quarrelled, and was in the form of an Affidavit which brought several grave charges against the Vicar, Counsel stated that at the time of the trial he believed that the statement of the Vicar with regard to the minute book was true.

The Master of the Rolls : Well, then, believe it now. The words the vicar wrote were were capable of being read as he read them. His Lordship asked Mr. Bight= under what head of law he made his present application. Mr. Bigham, said under the head of mutual mistake.

Lord Justice Kay: The fact of the case is this: you think you have further evidence from Mr. Davies whereas you have not learnt one fact more than you knew before. Their Lordship proceeded to decide the case with- out calling on Mr. Gully Q.C., who appeared for the respondents. The Master of the Rolls said that the case was a quarrel between the clergyman of the parish and some of hi; parishioners. Those opposed to the Vicar charged him with a wicked fraud. He had not the least doubt that there had been mistakes on both sides. The Vicar was mistaken in his recollec- tion, and Mr. Proud was rightly elected,and he (Lord Esher) had no doubt that Mr.. Allton did resign. Then came the other side,who had got it in their own way that Mr Proud was elected. They had per- suaded themselves that the Vicar committed a wicked fraud by making an entry in the minute book other than that which was found there, and then taken it out. He had not the least doubt that this accusation against the Vicar wars, untrue, and ' that he had never committed that fraud. Then , there came Mr. Davies, the solicitor. He did not mean to say that Mr. Davies had wickedly made false statements,, but he quarrelled with the Vicar and persuaded himself wrongly. His affidavit was founded on a blunder, and the whole case fell to the ground. Mr. Bigham did what was quite right at the trial; he was right to give up the charge against the Vicar, and now they tried to make out that Mr. Bigham had made a mistake. The only thing he could say was the sooner the Vicar and the other people in the parish stopped quarrelling the better. Their comments on their Vicar did not show Christian feeling. If they did dispute, he hoped to goodness they would not come to court again. Lords Justices Lopes and Kay concurredt

OPPOSITION IN THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

The time having expired for depositing petitions in the House of Lords against the Lancashire,Derby, and East Coast Railway Bill, it is found that only six petitioners will appear inopposition to this Bill, as compared with 16 petitioners who entered ap- pearances against the scheme, when it came for con- sideration before a Select COmmittee of the souse of Commons. The petitioners in the House of Lords comprise four railway companies-, viz., the Cheshire Lines Committee, the London and North-Western, the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, and the Midland Railway Companies,. while the remaining two are landowners' petitions,. signed by Lord de Tabley and Colonel Leslie. of Hassop Hall. With the exception of Lord de Tabley,.the whole of, these petitioners were heard before. the Committee of the House of Commons.

FRODSHAM.

ACCIDHNT TO A. MAIL CART DRIVER.—As the evening mail was being driven through Frodsham to Warrington from Helsby, the driver of the vehicle fell from the seat and received injuries to such an extent that it was found necessary to send one of the Frodsham, postmen in charr of the mails. DISTRESSING On Tuesday morning most distressing and determined case of suicide occurred at Five Crosses, near Frodsham, when a man named Joseph Blease, aged about 50)years, shot himself in the head. On Wednesday Mr. Churton, coroner, held an in- quest at Frodsham, on the body of the deceased who had been gardener to Mr. J. C. Sutton of Overton. It appeared from the evidence that the deceased had for SOW weeks past suffered from influenza, and on Tues- day morning he suggestedto his wife that she 'should go to Dr. Robinson who had been attending him and ascer- tain the amount of his bill. She left the house at 7.45 for that purpose and returned at nine. As her husband was not in the house she went into the garden to search for him and in an outhouse she found him lying on his back with a gun across his breast. She gave an alarm to Mr. Sutton's household and went for Dr. Robinson, but when the doctor arrived the unfortunate man was quite dead. There was a deep wound behind the jaw and a quantity of shot was emleddied in the flesh. The back of the head was blown alitibst completely away. P.S. Doyle produced a piece of twine which had been tied to the trigger by means of which the deceased had fired the gun and killed himself.—A verdict of " Suicide whilst temporarily insane" was recorded by the jury.
The Select Committee of the House of Commons yes- terday threw out the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway Bill for a new line to London.

div.head: " STYPENDERRIES."
div.p: " STYPENDERRIES."

Dear Mestur Edditur, wheerfore this din,— Wantin' to fotch a Stypenderry here ? Connot yo see, it wud be a greyt sin, Throwin' eawr taxes an' rates eawt o' gear? Hev we not Majustrates able to judge Aw the known diviltries under the sun? Then, why does somebody tawk sitch deyd fudge, When Law's so wed l an' so thurroly done? Why, they cud settle a thievin' or rape, While sum o'th' Judges wur winkin' thur eye ; And, anny prizoner tryin' t' escape, He'd ha' bad luck wi' his very fost try!

Felony, forjerry, burglerry, poachin'— Aw these are nowt; an' awl' even go furder, They cud be trusted, wi' hawve-an-heatir's coachin', lleaw to dispose ov a red-bonded murder. Gaunt yo believe, if eawr Majustrates' Clerk Geet rayther joobious ovver his law, They'd put him reet wi' a diver remark, An' so be stoppin' sum bledderyed's jaw? Yab, an' ther's several sits on that Bench, Wo, when thay tried, say, a fewtherin' case, Wud tell, at oncet, when thay lookt at the wench, Whether hoo'r modest, or steept i' disgrace. Well, then, its plain as th'owd Parish Church spire, Nay, "Bass's Bitter" wur never moor clear— We winnot hey, for we dunnot require, Rate-raisin', o'erpaid Stypeuderries here. TUX co' PEGS. Warriton, 18, 6, 91.
LABOURERS' UNION MEETING AT RUNCORN.

With the object of forming a branch of the Nay- vies%Bricklayers',Labourers%and General Labourers' Union in Runcorn, an open air meeting was held in DP•vonshire-Square, on Sunday afternoon. A large crowd assembled. The Chairman, known as Bright- on Bill, advised them to support their new organ "The Navvies' Guide" and called on them to face the terrors of the " sack" rather than submit to the terrorism of the contractor.—Mr. Leonard hail, organiser of the society for the Lancashire district, and editor of the" Navvies' Guide," said they bad come that day not to make speeches,but to do busi- ness and they had moreover come to Etay. Flourish- ' ing branches had just been formed at several places. lie advocated" the tanner all round " as the mini- mum wages which a labourer on the canal or else- where should receive. Now that the Manchester Corporation and other elective bodres were likely to be included in the directorate of The canal, the Trades Unions could exercise a direct influence on the directors, which would secure the sixpence an hour and render them less helpless in the hands of the contractors. A London navvy, Mr. M'Cord, said the navvies were resolved to insist that they should be treated as human beings and not as brute beasts. The laboarers of London received 6d. an tour : why should not the Lancashire men, who worked quite as hard, also have the" tanner?" Mr. Robert Gout, a navvy from' Ire/and.moved a resolution "'Mat the ree of 6d. an hour is the lowest wage of out-door labour of all kinds that is consistent with decency and justice, and this meeting pledges itself to give its heartiest support to any organisation including the accomplishment of that object in it pro- gramme." The resolution was carried, and übout a scom of labourers joined the Union.

div.head: VYRNWY PIPE LINE.
div.p: THE VYRNWY PIPE LINE.
THE ALLEGE) BURST/N( IN THE MERDEY

With reference to a report which appeared in a Liverpool paperrin which it was stated that one of the steel pipes across the Mersey at Fidler's Ferry had burst, and in consequence an immense volume of water was escaping down the river, it seems to have been based on an entire misconception. 21 o portion whatever of the pipe has burst; the whole is as sound as when it was sunk in the river. Considerable leakage has taken place, but that arose from a simpler came—through some of the self-acting valves having got out of order. To understand this it should be stated that under each section of the pipes are five boles of half-an-inch. each.. To each of these is at— tached in the pipe a self-acting valve, and all of these are constrn.cted in such a manner that when there is not mucivpressure on they will open and altovrsome of the waterto escape This escaped water will wash away the sand which may accumulate, and thus enable the pipe to-keep its proper position. When heavy pressure occurs fre the pipesthese valves close. The spindles of some olthesevalves have been forced out off the position by thecurrent, and this and not a burst has caused the excessive outflow, the holes referred to not being properly closed by the valves. All the valves are being thoroughly overhauled by the divers. The maim pipes continue to charged, but with slower progress than would have been the case had the valves kept their right position. The officials anticipate that all the valves win in a day or two haw- been examined, and the water then sent on in. greater and adequate volume to Prescot. The work of the divers in the case 'is one of exceptional difficulty, and one of unavoidable delay. Owing to the nature of the bed of the river, the (liver has to wear unusually- heavy weights, andwhen the water became shallow by the ebbing of the tide., it is almost impossible for him to, continue, as he ha& then to bear the weight on his own body. There is no ground for any fears which exagger- ated accounts might prAnce, although the prolonged delay is no doubt irksome. Thework is being proceeded with with all due caution, and those who are cognisant of the details of the situation readily admit that sucl. caution is necessary. All other departments of the work at Fidler's Ferry continue to progress satisfactorily.

div.head: OPENING OF TFIE VALVES AT PRESCOT.
div.p: OPENING OF TFIE VALVES AT PRESCOT.

Yesterday the pipe line from the Mersey to Prestet Reservoir was fully charged ,and at two o'clock the water reached the tank at Prescot at a pressure of nearly 20% lbs. to the square inch. This is ample to throw the water up the tank 15 ft., until it reaches the overflow and enters the reservoir. The valve in the tank was opened slightly-, and about six inches of water of &muddy character wasa4lbwed to enter. The valve outside was then closed, and Mr. Ktrby, superintendent of the reser- voirs, telephoned to Mr. Parry, city water eneneer. The pressure was maintained up to four o'clock, but as Mr. Parry and Mr. Duncanson replied that they were going out at once,. nothing further was done beyond opening the valves. Flags were at once hoisted as an indication that success had attended the scheme.

A waterspout burst directly over the Conception mine at San Louis, Potosi. Mexico, with the result that the mine was flooded almost instantly, and great damage was done to property in the neighbourhood. Twenty- three people were killed, and thirty insured. An extraordinary accident happened on Wednesday evening on board the steamer City of Chicago, lying in the Mersey. During the usual testing process a rocket, instead of taking an upward direction,went right among the cabin passengers who were at the moment getting aboard from the tender. Three passengers wereinjured, one of them very seriously.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.

BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. Runcorn is evidently not congenial soil for Trades Unionism. Out of the thousands of navvies and labourers at present in Runcorn only 20 en- rolled themselves as members of the Navvies and Labourers Union at the demonstration on Sunday. Not one local man supported the delegates on the impoverished platform.

Acting on a suggestion from Mr. S. Taylor, the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday decided to demand from the County Council the why and the wherefore of the great increase of the county rate. The answer will probably be a copy of the budget, which contains a great mass of figures, and which will tax the financial abilities of Mr. Bran- dreth to analyse and present in an intelligible form to his fellow members.

There is no doubt that the County Council as was pointed out by Mr. Speakman a fortnight ago have many more demands on their exchequer than had the magistrates, and they do not receive the ..E15,000 from the Weaver Trust which was paid to the magistrates. Perhaps the Clerk of the Peace will "condescend " to give the Guardians a. full explana- tion.
Parliament has passed a short Act postponing the County Council elections from January to March. Thus is the day of reckoning deferred.

On Wednesday, Mr. S. Taylor retired from the chairmanship of the Board of Commissioners ,carry- ing with him the thanks and good wishes of all. As Mr. Imison remarked, he had during his term of office been not only the chief citizen i-u name but in

Mr. J. J. Grice, hL successcir, is one of the oldest tradesmen in the town, and is highly respected for his business ability and uprightness of character. The traditions of the chair will be safe in his hands.

The scarcity of magistrates at Widnes is becoming a serious block in the way of conducting the police business. Either more magistrates must be ap- pointed by the Lord Lieutenant, or those on the present rota must attend more regularly to their duties. Now that the manufacturers have not the same personal interest in the works of the town, their visits are, like angels', few and far between. Hence the difficulty of getting them to take their positions on the magisterial Bench.

It is highly probable that Mr. T. Snape, C.C., of Widnes and Liverpool, will be invited to become the Liberal candidate for Ileywood Division, at the General Election, in place of Mr. Hoyle, who in- tends to resign.

div.head: FROM AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: FROM AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

It is expected there will be a big crowd at Lyme Park on Saturday, on the occasion of the demon- stration in connection with the Newton Conserva- tive Association, but it is very unfortunate that the miners' demonstration, at Southport, should have been fixed for the same day. However, given a fine day, the Conservatives will find ample means of enjoyment.

The public hall is now the one absorbing topic in Earlestown, and much satisfaction is expressed at the decision of Mr. Owen, the expert, called in by the Commissioners. There is no doubt the plans submitte I by Mr. Beesley more nearly meet the ideas of the Board, but, as Mr. Beesley states, even his idea cannot be carried out for the stipulated sum of £4,500, it is patent to anyone who has gone into the cu estion at all, that to erect a commodious public hall, which will be an ornament and a credit to the town, _on the lines laid down by the plan which secured first prize, a large slice will be taken out of £l,OOO.

The annual election of Commissioners is gradu- ally approaching, and yet the Provisional Order has not been sanctioned by Parliament. Thus it is not known how the election will be conducted; whether the Earlestown and Wargrave people will have to trudge to Newton to record their votes, or whether they will be. able to record them in their own dis- tricts. Apropos of the election, I hear that a section of the ratepayers in Earlestown have matters al- ready cut and dried, and that at least one of the retiring Commissioners will not seek to regain his. seat, if he is called upon to fight for it.

The scene which a good many people witnesse d last week in the neighbourhood of Leigh-st., and Sankey-st., again brings to the front, the question which has long lain dormant, aa to the housing of dead bodies of those who, when alive, were without proper habitation. Of course cales of the kind are very rare, and it may be said that such an instance might not occur again. That may be true, but still it does not alter the fact, that had Earlestown been in possession of a mortuary, suclV an outrage on decency would have been avoided.. I trust the medical men, or perhaps our newly-formed Medical Aid Society, will take this question in hand, and see if something cannot be done to remove any fear of the ozcurrence of a similar case.

llaydock new church has now been completed, and made ready for divine service for several weeka, lint the opening of the sacred building seems as far off as ever. At first I was told some legal difficulty was in the way, but this hast long since been removed, and now I am told the delay rests with the Bishop. I think with a little more push, and a proper representation to theßishopony little difficulty which blocks the way might be removed, and the people allowed to make use of the church for which they have so long and patiently waited.

Mr. Dig?g, the new governor of Newton-Reforma- tory, has hod his hands fairly well filled since he took up hie duties. Something like 70 of the in- mates have been down with the influenza. but happily the•majority have now recovered.
REMOVAL OF CATTLE RESTRICTIONS
IN LANCASHIRE.

A deputation on behalf of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society having recently waited upon the Ptesident of the Board of Agriculture, with a view to ob- taining the removal of the Cattle Restrictive Orders in force in the Hundreds of Salford and West Derby, and to allow cattle being more fully exhibited at this Society's coming show at Bury next month the Secretary has received a reply from the Board which contains the following : "The President has carefully considered the pre- sent condition of Lancashire as regards pleuro pneumonia, and he has decided that the time has now arrived when the district may be relieved from the restrictions. An order is therefore in prepara- tion to release the hundreds of West Derby and Sal- ford and Boroughs from the Scheduled District Restrictions of the Pleuro-Pneumonia Order of 1891. As tharesult of this, there will be no hind- rance to the holding of the show at Bury upon July 23rd and following days."
THE HURLBERT BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.
THE APPEAL FOR A NEW TRIAL.

In the Court a Appeal, on Wednesday, before Lord Esther and Lords Justices Lopes and Kay themotion for a new trial, on behalf of Miss Evelyn, of here breach of 'promise action against Mr. Hurlbert, came on for hearing. Mr. Candy Q.C..„ supported toe motion, which was op. posed by the Attorney-General. Miss Evelyn asked for .a new trial on three grounds—first, surpiim4 as another defence was adopted for that which was on the plead- ings ; second, the improper interference of counsel for the defendant in the course of the judge's summing up, which prevented the jury finding a verdict on the issue as to who wrote the letters ; and third, that the verdict was against the weight of evidence. On Thursday, Mr. Candy, resuming-hiS argument for the appellant„ said the letters of the-defendant described him in the light of a man going about seeking fresh women whom he might devour He would not go be- yond that rough sketch of the defendant.—The Master of the Rolls: I think you have said enough.—Mr. Candy said his case was that Wilfrid Narray was a myth, and that from beginning to end Flurlbert told lies as to the existence of the alleged Wilfrid Murray.—The case was ultimately a, ljourned until next day, when their lord- ships will deliver judgment. Yesterday, Mr. Cock, Q.C. in the abenca of the Attorney-General, continued die argument against the application. Mr. Cock proceeded to show that at the. trial the statement that Huebert met Evelyn at Windsor was disproved, as well as the statement that plaintiff and defendant met at Paris.

Youno* Queen of the Netherlands is suffering from illness, which is said to be accompanied by fever. Mr. Gladstone suffered no ill effects from going out on 'Tuesday. After a long drive in the parks on Wednesday, he spent considerable time at the British Museum, con- sulting works of reference, and in the evening met a company at dinner at Viscount de Stern's.
lATEST NEWS.
The report that the Rev. Canon Legge has been appointed Bishop of LichEeld is incorrect.
-Yesterday the creditors of Lord Pa-ulet, agreed to accept a dividend of 10s. in the pound.
CRICKET. Cambridge, 240 for seven wickets. SUICIDE: OF A BREWER
Mr. Henry Tomlinson, a large brewer, of Sheffield, committed suicide yest3rday by cutting his throat.
TERRIBLE OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.

The dead body of a woman who had apparently been outraged, was found yesterday morning in a field at Cahir, in which place a troop of the 3rd Hussars was billeted last night. Deceased is believed to be a tramp.

div.head: BETTING MEN FINED £5O.
div.p: BETTING MEN FINED £5O.

Yesterday, at the Mansion House, London, William McLachlan was fined £5O for keeping premises in Fen- church-st. for betting purposes. At Oxford, yesterday, Frank Bishall and Charles Harley, billiard-room keepers, were fined £5O each for allowing betting to be carried on on their premises. MURDEit AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. - - -

On Thursday night a young married woman, named Ellen Aldred, living at Ilkeston, jumped into the canal with her youngest child, aged 13 months. Both were got out of the water by two platelayers, but the child was dead. The woman was restored with great difficulty, and was taken to the cottage hospital,where she remains in custody. EXPECTED MARRIAGE OF MR. PARNELL AND

div.head: MRS. O'SFIEA.
div.p: MRS. O'SFIEA.

It is considered very probable that Mr. Parnell and Mrs. O'Shea will be married immediately, and at all events before they are to appear in court in Dublin as hostile witnesses for the "Cork Herald " in the libel action brought against that paper by Mr. H. Campbell, M.P., secretary to Mr. Parnell.

div.head: LEEDS MURDER.
div.p: THE LEEDS MURDER.

At Leeds, yesterday, the mar-i-iiiiiie-r-;nd his mother were charged before the magistrates with the murder and mutilation of Barbara Waterhouse at Horsforth, on the 6th inst., and on the application of Mr. Williams, who represented the Treasury, they were further re- manded until Tuesday, when the charge will be fully gone into. It is alleged that Turner has several times threatened to be revenged upon the deceased's father, who, it seems, some time ago ejected him from a public- house. Mrs. Cotterill, a friend of the prisoners, swore that Mrs. Turner told her that her son, the prisoner Turner, put the body in the coal cellar on Saturday night. Mrs. Turner accordingly dis- covered it there on Monday morning, and afterwards helped her son to carry it to Leeds. The statement made a great sensation in court. THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

Yesterday the fourth Mee e B of the Royal Commission on Labour was held at Westminster Hall, Lord Derby presiding. The first witness called was Mr. Horton, one of the trustees of the Dock and Wharves Foremens' and Clerks' Union. Witness said that the Union numbered from 700 to 800. The employment was very irregular. The average pay of the foremen was 255., and that of the clerks 245,• per weik. The number of hours averaged 68 hours per week. He thought a board of ar- bitration could remedy their grievances.—Mr. Hart Riverside, of the General Labourers' Union,was the next witness called. He objected strongly to piece work, be- cause under that system the man who undertook the work from the employers took more than his share of wages.— Mr. John Costello, of the Dockers' Union, also gave evi- dence.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four.

. In reply to Earl Spencer, Eiri CApcpaANl said the ordi- nance 25 inch maps were on the wholo, accurate. The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill, and the Public Ac- counts Bill were read a second time and the house ad- journed at 25 minutes past 5.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Baron DE Woirsfs. questioned by Mr. Watt as to the Australian defences, said no report had been received from the Australian Defence Commissioners, but it was understood that the South Australian Government was in favour of the fortification of the Island. THE FACTORIES BILL.

The HOME SECDETARY said that the Government op- posed Mr. Buxton's clause last night, because they be- lieved that in so doing they were considering the interests of both the manufacturers and the parents of the chil- dren, but the Government were quite prepared to ac- cept the decision of the House upon the subject. Sir W. Ilaucourrr then addressed the House. He said that at the Berlin Labour Conference, England was behind all"the rest of the world with regard to the limit of age at which children were employed. He asked whether England was to be content to rank in the lowest scale of nations in questions of this character. He hoped the House would not rest content until further progress was made. Mr. LESS defended the position taken by gov- ernment. Mr. SYDNEY Bux.row said,after thedicussion last night, he should not move the subsequent clause stand- ing in his name. The Home Secretary expressed gratifica- tion at the armquncement, and the clause was agreed to. Mr. RANDELY: moved the insertion of the clause including within the provisions of Bill laundries, except domestic laundries.—Mr. Baumann supported the clause, but the Home Secretary opposed it. He believed the great majority of the laundresses in the country were opposed to coming under the provisions of the Blll`. The clause was rejected by 99 to 90.
ATTEMPTED MURDER AT SHEFFIELD.

A murderous assault was committed at Sheffield early on Sunday morning upon a puddler named Garrett. He had lodged witha widow named Bridget Connell, whose son accused her of•being too, friendly with, him. There was a quarrel on Saturday night, and it was alleged that her son Thomas, Connell and another man assaulted Garrett with a heavy hammer, and smashed his skull. An attempt was made on Sunday afternoon to take his despositions, bnt he was scarcely conscions-of what was said. Only Connell has been arrested.
SUDDEN DEATH AT EARMSTOWN.
DISGRACEFUL SCENE IN ME STREET.

On Thursday night, last week,. a. man named Michael Charnley, 65 years of age, who lodged with Mr. Melsip, No. 1; Sankey-st., died very suddenly in an outhouse of the New Market run, Earlestown. The deceased',. it appears, had been in the New Market Inn the greater part of the day, and shortly before eight &clock went out into the back yard. As he did not return within a reasonable time, one of the men in the house went out to, see what had ' become of him, as he had complaiivee during the day of not feeling well: The man who went out, found the deceased huddled in the outhouse, and at once infOrmed the barman, who sent for the police. no. Middleton was soom ort the spot, and after getting the deceased' into the yard, he found he was quite dead. Therewas nnaccommodation for the. body at the New Market Inn, and Middleton pro— cured a hand cart, into which he put the body, and re- moved it to the man'S lodgings. arriving there, the occupier of the house refused to talte the body in, alleg, ing that deceased had left there two days before. FOr some tune the body remained in the street without covering, and surrounded by a crowd composed princi-. pally of 'women andl children, until' a neighbour pravitlect an old sheet, which was thrown ever the corpse. P.C. Cameron then arrived on thescene, and after a consulta- tion. he decided to ask the landiOrd of a neighbouring public-house to find accommodation for the body,, but he refused to have anything to do with it. The, body had, therefore, to remain in the street for some tins* longer, until the barman at the New Market Inn was prevailed upon to allow it ta lie in an outbuildiaz. There the body was conveyed. but about midnight it had to be again removed, and finally found a resting- place in a stable. The facts of the death, were com- municated to the Coroner, but he did not think it neces- sary to hold an inquest.

A Vienna telegram states that Herr Vail Pilinski, Austrian Consul at Prizrend, who had recently been censured by the Foreign Office, has committed suicide. The Premier and Colonial Treasurer of New Zealand proposes in his financial statement just made to establish a graduated income tax, ranging from threepence to a shilling in the pound. He al sr) proposes to abolish the property tax and to levy a graduated land tax. ROBBING A SCHOOL GIRL.—On Tuesday at Prescot Petty sessions,Ann Thompson,a Prescot girl,was charged with stealing a pair of earrings, value 2s. 6d., from another girl named Ethel Mary Holding, whlie on the way from school. She WAZ discharged with a caution.

WHITECROSS WARD ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF WHITECROSS WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Allow me to offer my heartfelt thanks for returning me to the Town Council as your representative by a majority of 83,notwith5tanding the gross and persistent misrepresenta- tion to which the Tory party resorted throughout the contest. Let me thank, too, the zealous and energetic band of workers, without whose voluntary services this victory could not have been won. I shall make it my duty to serve, to thebest of my ability, all classes of ratepayers in the town, and especially those of Whitecross Ward. I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, GEO. FLUMPTON. • 125, Lovely-lane, Warrington, . June 16th. 1891.

COUNTY OF CHESTER 'lO WIT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GlVEN,that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the County of Chester will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clockl in the Forenoon when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirral!, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Ses- sions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester Dis- trict must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of Court on MONDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned to the Court House, Nether, Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the Ist day of July next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Mac- clesfield,and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last- mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House,Knuts- ford ,at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the Ist day of July next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, Bth June, 1891.

RAILWAY ACCIDENI IN AMERICA. FALL OF A TRAIN INTO A RIVER. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY.—A terrible railway accident occurred yesterday, in lowa. A passenger train was approaching a bridge over the Goon River, near flee Coon Rapids, when the engine left the metals. It ran along the permanent way until it reached the bridge, when it struck one of the supports of the structure, and fen over into the river, dragging all the carriages of the trainwith it, with the exception of the sleeping car. Two pas- sengers are known to have been killed and thirty others injured, some fatally. The details are as yet meagre-. • AN ATLANTIC STEAMER ON FIRE. GALLANT CONDUCT OF THE CREW. The Inman steamer City of Richmond arrived at Queenstown from New York on Sunday morning with her cargo partly on fire, and in convoy of the Cunard' steamer Servia. The fire broke out on Wednesday among the bales of cotton in the forward hold, but that which might have resulted in a terrible calamity was averted by the labours of the officers and crew. The passengers, of whom there were 'a rarge number on board, heard , the alarm of fire at two o'clock on Wednesday morning, and they at once rushed on deck, many of them half dressed ; but, there was no panic,, even amongst the women, thanks mainly to the calm and confident demeanour of the officers, who assured everybody that there was no immediate danger and not the slightest reason for fear. Thus reassured, they were able to watch the splendid manner in which officers and men battled with the fire. The Richmond's meu had removed all cause for actual danger by the time. the Harrison liner Counsellor bore down on 'Thursday in response-to signals of distress. She stood by the City of Richmond until, later in the day, the Cunard mail steamer Servia ap- peared upon the scene. The fire was still smouldering on arrival at Queenstown. A large sum of money was sub- scribed among the passengers for the brave crew of the City of Richmond. The vessel arrived in the Mersey on Monday morning, too late to enter the Alexandra Dock. She• acccrdingly anchored outside the dock. The passengers were all landed by 645. For fear of accident, a small detachment of the Bootle Fire Brigade, with suitable appliances, watched the work of unloading on Monday evening, but fertunately their services were not required. • FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN SWITZERLAND: OVER 100 PERSONS KILLED' A Berne correspondent telegraphing on Sunday says : A terrible disaster occurred on Sunday morning on the railway at Mcenchenstein, a village near Basle; by which not lesstlian 47 persons lost their lives and some 20-0 bthers sustained injuries more or less serious. A musical festival' was announced to take place at Mcechensteie on Monday, and as the fixture is an annual and popular one, people flocked to the village from the surrounding country, special excursion trains being run for their• accommoda- tion. To one of these trains, heavily freighted with holi- day makers, the awful disaster occurred. All had gone well until the train neared the village, where the, line crosses a river by means of a bridge. When the train was well on the structure it suddenly and almost completely collapsed. The train, being an exceptionally heavy one. was being driven by two locomotives, and both of these, together with three long carriages packed with people, were hurled headlong into the river, while the terrific shocks smashed some of the carriages which, re- mained on the track, causing injuries to scores of peoptee The three carriages and engines turned 'almost acomplete somersault as they fell, and then struck the water almost as one heap of wreckage. The fete • was aban- doned as soon as news reached the village of the calamity and the villagers were called from their merrymaking to assist in the work of rescue, while help was urgently de- manded and promptly sent from-Basle • and other towns, in the district. The same correspondent in a second telegram , says,:— The train consisted of 16 cars and two -engines, and it appears that it appears that it left• the Tails when onthe. bridge, which was an iron skeleton structure .and the weight being thus thrown to one side caused ale disas- ter. Both the engines and the foremost wagon.were hurled, as already stated, into the river,and everypersoa thus plunged into the water was drowned. The exact number of deaths is still act known, but it is certain. that about fifty perished. Amongst the • dead are the' drivers and firemen of both engines and the conductor chief of the train. Of the great number injared most , are severely hurt ; their injuries generally taking the. form of lacerated and broken limbs. The disaster has caused the greatest excitement in Bale,, where many of the killed and injured resided. DEATH ROLL INCREASING, Up to noon on Tuesday sixty-five bodies badteen-re- covered from the debris of the train wrecked by the col- lapse of a bridge near Basle, and at that time more bodies were seen among the wreckage. lying in the bed of the river. It is feared that the deathsrell; when com- pleted, will number from 120 to 130. The number of in- jured is now stated to be about 300. FUNERAL OF FIFTY VICTIMS. The funerals of fifty of the victims of the -railway dis- aster near Basle took place on Wednesdey. Over 100 bodies have now been recovered, and it is believedahere are at least fifty more bodies to ba got from the-wreck- age in the bed of the river. FURTHER RECOVERY OF ' BODIES. SHOCKING DISCCVERIES. e BERNE, THURSDAY.—Bodies are still being recovered from the wreckage. Over a dozen corpses,. after being photographed, have been interred unrecognised,and each day that passes renders identification impossible ia ether cases, owing to the ravages of decay hastened by the warm weather. The explorers frequently come across headless or limbless bodies. The body of one young girl was found cut clean in two by a, girder. Human arms, legs, and hands have even been recovered in con- siderable numbers from streams leading frone the river Birs and supplying motive power to mills and manu- factories. BASLE, THORSDAY.—The funeral of more of the victims of the recent railway catastrophe.took place this after- noon, without any special rites, but a solemn ceremony will be celebrated in the church next Sunday. ele 711 E LEEDS TRAGEDY- THE PRISONER AND. THE MANN/NGHAM MURDER.. Walter Lewis Turner, who is in custody at Leeds charged with murdering and mutilating a little girl at Horsforth., was on Saturday morning brought before the magistrates and remanded. His mother is still detained in custody. The police haveet is stated,, reason to believe that Turner is implicated in the murder of the boy Gill, at Manningham. near Bradford,. seine time ago. He lived at Bradford at the time of the murder, but he and his mother have changed about from place to place, and little is known of them by anybody. Superintendent Stansfield received an anonymous letter saying that if he charged Turner with the crime he would be sure to confess, and this was theonly clue which led to Turner's subsequent arrest and to-the disclosures which followed. The funeral of Barbara Waterhouse, the little girl murdered, took place on Saturday afcernoon at Hors- forth Cemetery. A Leeds col respendent, says the police are in possession of additional evidence implicating the man Turner as the murderer pf the little girt at Horsforth. A bundle containing the child's clothing has been found in the chimney of the house where the prisoner lived, and blood stains had been traced to a wood in the locality. Evi- dence is also forthcoming that on Wednesday he and his mother were seen on their way to the station carrying a bundle and a trunk. The excitement at Leeds concerning the murder of the child Waterhouse is undiminished. It transpires that Turner visited a friend's house on Wednesday. He had a tin box. The box attracted the attention of a terrier, and Turner hurriedly left the house. It now appears that the Manningham murder has again been relegated to the category of unfathomed mysteries, the Bradford police having satisfied them- selves,after careful inquiry,that there is no ground what- ever for supposing that either of the Turners, now in custcdy at Leeds on suspicion of being concerned in the murder of the girl Waterhouse at Horsforth, had any connection with the murder of the boy Gill at Manning- ham. In interviews with his solicitor on Wednesday and on Tuesday Turner protested his innocence of the girl Waterhouse, made statements regarding his movements after he had, as he alleges, discovered the. bundle con- taining the body in the coal cellar of his mother's house, and repeated his story of the connection of one "Jack the Quarryman" with the tragedy.

LONDON BUSMEN'S STRIKE. WORK RESUMED AND TERMS OF SETTLEMENT. The streets of London resumed their normal aspect on Monday, so far as the 'bus traffic is concerned. Some of the horsekeepers say that they have been discharged, contrary to the terms of the settlement. The men have no doubt obtained very important concessions. The omnibus men's day has so far ranged from fourteen te ssventeen hours; it is now to be a uniform day of twelve hours. Instead of a thirteen days' fortnight, the men can now have a six days' week—that is, if they choose to pay for it. The drivers are advanced from 6. to 6s. 6d. a day, and the conductors from 4s. to 55., and there is an implied promise of a further rise before long, if the extra profits from the new system should justify it.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. - Spot transactions a-r-e estimated at 6,000 bales. Egyptian is down 1-16 d, Brazilian partly so, and Americans favour buyers. Yarns are very quiet and few buyers care to test prices by firm offers for quantity In cloth there is some business in special makes of shirting, and other Eastern fabrics, and also in certain makes of wide cloths for the home and colonial markets, but most staples are difficult to move in quantity, and makers are quite willing to leave quantities over to be "telegraphed out," hoping that. perchance, something good may result.
